Who Holds
the Hammer?

A reply to Dave Snowden's Nailed to the Tides (19 November 2026), in plain English: on the half-answers, the postponed question of power, Fludd's picture and Kepler's ruler, Stacey's abandoned diagram — and the designer who sits in the astrologer's chair.

Mark Downham

Fludd's beliefs, Kepler's methods — and a designer in the astrologer's chair.
A tide cannot be nailed. A frame can.

Defending: Humans Are Not Estuaries · The Compass and the Loom · The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy

Begin reading ↓

At a Glance

On 19 November 2026 Dave Snowden, founder of the Cynefin Company, published Nailed to the Tides[1]. It is a reply to two long critiques I wrote of his ideas: Humans Are Not Estuaries[2], which sets out twenty-four theses, and The Compass and the Loom[3], which sets out twenty-three. He answered all forty-seven in a few thousand words. This is my answer to his answer. It also draws on a third piece, To the Strait-Jacketed, the Other Always Seems Baggy[4], whose central idea turns out to explain his reply better than anything else: we see the constraints other people are under, and are blind to our own.

Snowden's reply is polite, clever and often right. It agrees with more than it first seems to, and those agreements are recorded here in full. But read as a whole, it has a shape, and the shape is the real argument. Three things happen again and again.

  1. He answers half of each thesis. Most of my theses had two parts: a claim about the world ("the constraints that make a community are reproduced when people follow them") and a claim about the person describing the world ("…and when someone maps them"). He answers the first part and leaves out the second. The part he leaves out is always the part about the designer, the mapper, the measurer — about him. (Part III.)
  2. He puts off the central question. Both critiques said the missing piece in his theory is power. His reply says power will be dealt with in a later post. He says this, in one form or another, six times. Every other road in the reply — the triangle diagrams, the questions about his company's software, the use of people's stories to train AI — ends at the same closed door. (Parts III and IX.)
  3. He blames the reader. The Cynefin diagram had to be redrawn because readers took its boundaries as claims it never made. The drift from theory to product is, he says, my invention. My theses, he says, treat a brochure as if it were an academic paper. Each time, his own central principle — that stories change the people who hear them — is applied to everyone except the person telling the story. (Parts III, V and VII.)

Under those three habits lies a deeper problem, and this second edition is built around it. Snowden illustrated his reply with pictures by Robert Fludd, a seventeenth-century English mystic. Fludd lost a famous argument with the astronomer Johannes Kepler. Kepler said Fludd's diagrams were riddles that could not be tested. Fludd said Kepler's measurements missed the living whole. Anthro-complexity — Snowden's name for his theory of human complexity — believes what Fludd believed and works the way Kepler worked. It holds that people are not computers and that meaning lives in the whole; then it turns people's stories into coordinates, pools them, plots them and measures them. The two halves never meet: no measurement is ever allowed to show the theory wrong. And the person who joins them — the designer who chooses the questions and the categories — ends up exactly where Fludd's astrologer sits: outside the thing he draws, curating it. Ralph Stacey, one of the founders of complexity thinking about organisations, faced the same problem with his own famous diagram, and gave the diagram up. Part II tells that story in detail.

The argument in one sentence: Snowden's theory says no one stands outside a human system; his instruments, and his reply, are built by someone standing outside — and the question both of my critiques asked, which his reply puts off, is who that person is and what power they hold.

Against that, this rejoinder sets out thirty theses of its own; goes through every thesis he answered, again, in a question-and-answer format; keeps a ledger of all forty-seven with a verdict for each; accepts the corrections he rightly makes and records them as amendments; accepts his sharpest point — that my critique of harvesting people's stories was itself written with an AI trained on harvested text — as a point against myself; and ends by listing in advance ten tests that his promised post on power will need to pass.

How to read this

In twenty minutes: this page; the thirty theses; Part II (Fludd, Kepler and Stacey); Table 1 in Part III; the ledger of forty-seven; and the final ruling.

In one sitting: add Part I (the epigraph, the pictures and the title), Part VII (on length and the machine), Part VIII (the alternative I proposed, called the Tidal Loom) and Part IX (the ten tests).

In full: each "Question" follows the same four steps. First, the case for Snowden's view, put as strongly as I can. Second, the problem with it. Third, my answer. Fourth, replies to the original case. This is the old university method of disputation, written in plain English. If you are short of time, read "My answer".

The cards. Words in blue open an explainer when you hover over them, tab to them or tap them. Each Part ends with a set of cards you can turn over for a fuller explanation. The Lexicon near the end holds every card in one place and can be searched. Numbers in square brackets lead to the Catalogue of Sources, which lists every work with its link and every place in this text that uses it.

A note on the edition. This is the second edition, rewritten in plain modern English and expanded, with a new Part II on Fludd, Kepler and Stacey. The first edition, in a more elaborate style, is kept in the page's version history. Under the rule I call the Additive Covenant, nothing in it has been withdrawn; it has been restated.

How This Was Written

One of my theses (XXII in The Compass and the Loom) says every instrument should declare how it was made. Snowden turned that against me, fairly. So here it is, before anything else.

This rejoinder, like the two critiques it defends, was written under my direction in a long working dialogue with a large language model — an AI system[5]. The model drafted; I directed, argued, cut, amended, and I answer for every line. The sources were read from the texts themselves: Snowden's reply, my three earlier pieces, and the works listed in the Catalogue of Sources. Factual claims were checked against sources before they were kept. Where a source could only be summarised, it is summarised. Snowden's own words are quoted directly only once, at the point where the whole argument turns on them.

Snowden observed that my critique of harvesting people's stories is itself written with a machine trained on harvested text. That is true. I accept it in Part VII, not as an embarrassment to explain away but as a point against myself — Thesis R21 — and I offer the acceptance as an example of what his reply does not do: apply its own central principle to the person stating it.

Plainly: I do not stand outside the harvest. Neither does he. The difference is that I have said so.

The Thirty Theses of This Rejoinder

Numbered R1 to R30, to keep them apart from the forty-seven theses being defended (numbered 1–24 for Humans Are Not Estuaries and I–XXIII for The Compass and the Loom). Each one says where it is argued. The final ruling records whether each holds.

  1. R1 · Half-answers. The reply answers the part of each thesis that describes the world and drops the part that describes the person describing it. What gets answered is not what was argued. (Part III.)
  2. R2 · The postponed centre. Six times the reply sends power to a later post. A reply that postpones its central question has conceded it until the answer arrives. (Parts III, IX.)
  3. R3 · Pascal supports the long letter. The quotation Snowden uses to tease me about length comes from a series of long letters by an outsider attacking a powerful institution's method — and the long letters were right. (Part I.)
  4. R4 · Fludd is the outside observer. The picture chosen to mock my critique is a picture of a man who reads people's lives from a chart he draws from outside. (Parts I, II.)
  5. R5 · The sailor proves my point. The tide does not notice the sailor. Snowden's image of the reader "inside the tide" brings back exactly the unresponsive medium my thesis complained about. (Part IV.)
  6. R6 · Many identities still belong to one container. Having many identities is not the same as being formed in relationships. A story fragment, rated alone by its teller, treats the person as closed, whatever the theory says. (Part IV.)
  7. R7 · "Safe-to-fail" moves the goal-setting up a level. The outcome is unknown, but the criteria for judging outcomes are chosen in advance by the designer. Safe for whom? (Part IV.)
  8. R8 · Nobody wrote English; somebody wrote the triangle. Comparing a set of rating categories to a language fails exactly where power lies: authorship, interest and the ability to change it. (Part IV.)
  9. R9 · The oblique dilemma. Either the storyteller knows what her ratings will mean (and can game them) or she does not (and cannot properly consent). Indirect measurement cannot have both. (Part IV.)
  10. R10 · The brochure is the evidence. The reply says there is no evidence the practice is becoming more computational. The company's own brochure offers training data for AI automation. (Part IV.)
  11. R11 · A visible outlier is not a protected outlier. Showing unusual stories on a chart does not stop a model fed on them from making them rarer. And the triangle erases one kind of extreme before any model is involved. (Part IV.)
  12. R12 · A deliberate trade-off is still a trade-off. Saying the triangle asks for relative weight, not strength, restates my thesis as a virtue. The known costs of that design should be declared. (Part IV.)
  13. R13 · Two answers that cannot both stand. The reply says "direction of travel" measures escape Goodhart's law, then agrees that any published measure falls under it. (Part IV.)
  14. R14 · The tide in human affairs was a speech. Shakespeare's Brutus announced a turning tide to win an argument; the announcement moved the army; it led to defeat. In human affairs, announcing the tide helps make it. (Part IV.)
  15. R15 · One frame given to many people is still one frame. The reply agrees blindness comes from the task frame, then proposes an instrument that gives everyone the same frame. (Part V.)
  16. R16 · Bees decide by meeting and arguing. The swarm's intelligence lies in scouts who meet, compete and head-butt one another. An instrument whose people never meet keeps the bees' vocabulary and loses their mechanism. (Part V.)
  17. R17 · A crowd that never meets can never object. Keeping people apart does not stop someone speaking for them; it means only the analyst can. (Part V.)
  18. R18 · A question already answered cannot be postponed. By the reply's own test, trademarked products designed by an outside firm are outsiders' products. (Part V.)
  19. R19 · "Readers misread it" exempts the author. A diagram is answerable for the readings it reliably produces. Blaming readers withholds the theory's own principle from the person who drew it. (Parts III, V.)
  20. R20 · The question was never who pays. It was who consents, who sees first, who can change the frame and who benefits — answerable under any funder. And there are more funding options than the reply allows. (Part VI.)
  21. R21 · The AI point binds me too. A critique of harvesting written with a harvested machine stands under its own theses. I accept that. (Part VII.)
  22. R22 · The loom is the method plus five things it lacks. The alternative I proposed is not Snowden's method under a new name; it adds co-authored categories, first sight for storytellers, consent, a rule for disbanding, and a public record of errors. (Part VIII.)
  23. R23 · Recognition runs the wrong way. The Chinese text Snowden accepts says the best leaders are barely noticed and the people say "we did it ourselves". A method-owner saying of a critic's proposal "this is ours" turns that round. (Part VIII.)
  24. R24 · The postponed post is given its tests now. Ten tests, stated in advance, so that anyone can tell whether the promised post on power answers the question. (Part IX.)
  25. R25 · Fludd's beliefs, Kepler's methods. Anthro-complexity holds a Fludd-like view of human beings — whole, tacit, not a machine — and uses Kepler-like methods to study them: signify, aggregate, plot, measure, feed. (Part II.)
  26. R26 · No eight-minute moment. Kepler's greatness was letting eight minutes of measurement overturn his favourite picture. Anthro-complexity names no measurement that could overturn its picture, so its numbers decorate the theory rather than test it. (Part II.)
  27. R27 · The designer sits in the astrologer's chair. Choosing the prompt, the categories, the labels, the order and the display is the act that decides what can be seen. The designer curates; the storyteller is read. (Part II.)
  28. R28 · Curation is power. Choosing the frame through which people describe their own lives is power in its deepest form — the power to shape what people notice. That is why postponing power postpones everything. (Parts II, IX.)
  29. R29 · Stacey gave up his diagram. Ralph Stacey saw his famous matrix turn managers into astrologers and stopped using it. Snowden redraws his diagram and blames the readers. Only one asked what the drawing itself does to the people who use it. (Part II.)
  30. R30 · The third position is taking part. Beyond Fludd's vision and Kepler's ruler lies the participant's position: no map whose maker is exempt from it. That is what anthro-complexity's own beliefs require of its practice. (Part II.)

What Snowden Said: His Reply, Fairly Summarised

In short. Snowden answers the theses rather than the length; agrees on a good deal; disagrees about persons, metaphors, computing, the triangle diagrams and the "drift" towards products; accepts but postpones power; defends his instruments as experimental or misread; corrects two facts; and turns the question of length and AI back on me.

Before arguing, it is only fair to say what the other side said. A critique that misstates its opponent has only refuted something it made up. Here is the reply, in my words, in its own order[1].

How he frames it. He notes that two long critiques appeared within a week — the first about a quarter of a million words with twenty-four theses, the second in four editions under what I call the Additive Covenant (a rule that nothing is ever deleted, only amended). He opens with Pascal's apology for writing a long letter because he lacked time to write a short one, and says he will answer the theses, not the volume — grouping them, agreeing where he can, explaining where he cannot. The post is illustrated with three pictures connected to Robert Fludd: an astrologer casting a horoscope, a woodcut of man as a small world inside the great world, and a portrait. The title is not explained.

Where he agrees. He accepts my first three theses: anthro-complexity is a body of thought in its own right; complexity is not the same as systems thinking; human systems differ in kind from ant colonies and computer simulations. He accepts that a pattern of forces mapped from outside is just a landscape, not the strategic "propensity" the Chinese call 勢 shì, and says his mapping is therefore done by insiders. He welcomes self-signification — people rating their own stories — as a real but partial advance, and adds that more abstract categories make the method more rigorous. He answers my point about instruments losing their accuracy by saying his "vector" measures separate measuring from target-setting. He partly accepts my point about timing, and he accepts my recognition test — that good practice is shown when people can say "we did this ourselves" — linking it to the Chinese classic the Laozi.

Where he partly agrees. On power and interpretation (Theses 13 and 18), he accepts that whoever designs the categories holds power, and answers with an analogy: every language is a frame its speakers did not choose, yet speaking is not coercion. The storyteller's own rating, he says, is the act of interpretation; the analyst works on patterns of ratings, not on the stories. On Thesis 12 he accepts that his original post did not discuss power, says power is different from agency, and postpones it. On Thesis 23 he agrees a more self-aware anthro-complexity is possible, says two of my five proposed additions are already there, and says the rest come from complex responsive processes — the Hertfordshire school founded by Ralph Stacey — complaining that a conversation between that school and Cynefin has been refused.

Where he disagrees. Anthro-complexity, he says, does not assume complete, closed individuals: identity is multiple and spread across contexts, and the unit of analysis is the story fragment; his phrase "the people remain distinct" was aimed at the philosopher Karen Barad, who dissolves people into relations. He accepts that his framework changes its users but denies that practitioners keep a planning mindset, because safe-to-fail experiments exist precisely because outcomes cannot be known. His water metaphors, he says, describe systems that include people, with the reader inside, like a sailor inside the tide. Constitutive constraints come from the philosopher Alicia Juarrero, his source. "Constructors" — a term from physics — can stay able to cause change while being changed in other ways, and are one kind of actor, not a model of people. There is no evidence the practice is becoming more computer-driven, and my claim about lost outliers is simply wrong: the method makes the unusual cases visible. The triangle diagram's trade-off is deliberate, because separate rating scales invite people to say yes to everything. The drift from theory to product is my invention, though the risk is real.

The second critique. On the gorilla study (I), blindness comes from the task, so the cure is many people looking from many angles. Bee quorum decisions (II) are a kind of consensus. The cleaner wrasse (III) was chosen for its virtues, and its imitator is a fair warning; the WRASSE framework is still being developed. The charge of "dual causality" (IV) is my framing; holding back is a gesture (V), but holding back and stirring things up are different gestures. WRASSE has no layers (VI). No one claims unknowns can be mapped (VII), only flagged; he accepts my amended thesis. The I-Space thesis (VIII) misreads its source, though using stories to train AI raises real questions of ownership, benefit and consent. Risk (IX) is partly about relationships but also physical, like a cracked weld. Sources for WRASSE will be acknowledged when it is published (X). Coherence is not the same as uniformity (XI). He accepts the image of Cook Ding the butcher (XII).

The later theses. He welcomes my amendments as a critique revising itself towards his position (VII, XIII). The theses that draw on quantum physics (XIV–XVI) go beyond his physics and their human parallels are unproven, but he accepts the practical points: SenseMaker measures indirectly, built into everyday systems; returns patterns to storytellers; asks for the story before showing the categories; and the research on question order is psychology, not physics. He agrees about Goodhart's law (XVII). On acumen (XVIII) he says the triangle asks only for relative weight; some structure is always needed; the real question is how much and decided by whom — which, he says, leads back to power. He welcomes my use of Kipling's Mariner (XIX) and postpones the question of whether his company, which also builds software, counts as an outsider. He agrees about leverage (XX). On Leviathan (XXI) he says the people in SwarmCompass never gather. He has no quarrel with my three principles (XXII). The Cynefin diagram (XXIII) has been redrawn because readers took its boundaries as claims.

Money, form and the loom. The methods are not members-only; WRASSE is not on the market; SenseMaker and SwarmCompass are trademarked commercial products. The question of a "Pelagian start and Augustinian institution" is fair; the methods are published openly; software costs money; the only realistic funders are consultancies, which would turn the methods into recipes, or tech companies, which would turn stories into products. On form: the old method of disputation suited an age when writing was hard; automated writing makes length meaningless and shifts the burden to whoever has to reply; under my covenant the text can only grow; and a critique of harvesting stories is written with a machine trained on harvested text. My Tidal Loom keeps what he values and removes something he doubts exists; it looks like his own method; a compass assumes a north and a loom a frame, but a north star is a guide, not a destination. In a postscript he admits some answers are too short, postpones power and agency, notes that a brochure is not a paper, and wonders whether he reads the loom too quickly as his own method.

Five things to know first

Anthro-complexity. Dave Snowden's name for the study of complexity in human systems. Its central claim is that human systems are different in kind from ant colonies, weather or computer simulations, because people hold several identities at once, act with intention, think in abstractions — and can change the stories they tell about each other, which changes what happens next[10][11].

Cynefin. Snowden's best-known framework (the Welsh word means roughly "habitat"). It sorts situations by how cause and effect behave in them — clear, complicated, complex, chaotic, with a central zone of confusion — and suggests a different way of acting in each[15]. It is usually drawn as a diagram of domains, and that diagram has been redrawn several times.

SenseMaker. The Cynefin Company's software for collecting large numbers of short stories. After telling a story, each person "signifies" it — places it on triangles and sliders whose labels the designers chose. The software then pools and displays the results as patterns[14].

SwarmCompass. A newer offering, described in a 2025 brochure as "human-AI swarm intelligence" powered by SenseMaker, illustrated with honeybees, radiologists and Abraham Lincoln. It promises to turn unknown unknowns into mapped territory and to produce training data for further AI automation[6][3].

WRASSE. "Weaving Risk and Strategy", a strategy framework launched on the Cynefin Company blog in 2025 and renamed after the cleaner wrasse fish. It crosses two axes — natural versus stimulated emergence, fine versus coarse detail — to give four domains, set on a "substrate" of technology, culture, procedure and networks[7].

That is the reply as fairly as I can put it. Now to its shape.

Anthro-complexity

It positions itself against both systems thinking and the use of ants, flocks and agent-based models as models of organisations.

Humans Are Not Estuaries accepted the distinction and disputed its reason, its reflexivity and its silence on power. The reply defends the first and defers the third.

Turn over ↻
The quaestio in plain English

Each quaestio opens with the strongest case for the position under attack (videtur quod, "It may be urged"); then the decisive counter-consideration (sed contra, "Yet against this"); then the determination (respondeo, "I answer"); then replies to the original objections.

The form is used because it obliges the author to state the adversary's case at its strongest before answering — here, Snowden's reply, paraphrased as fairly as possible — and because each quaestio can be disputed alone.

Part I The Way In: Quotation, Picture and Title

In short. Before a piece of writing makes any argument, it sets the mood with what it puts at the top: a quotation, a picture, a title. Snowden's reply puts up three things: Pascal's apology for a long letter, pictures by Robert Fludd, and the unexplained title Nailed to the Tides. Each one, looked at closely, supports my side rather than his.

The French critic Gérard Genette called these things paratexts — the material around a text that shapes how it will be read before the reader reaches the argument[23]. Reading them closely is not nit-picking. It is the first test of Snowden's own principle: the story you tell about someone changes how they will be heard. His reply read the length of my books, the editions of my critique and the tools I wrote with in exactly this way. It is fair to read his threshold the same way.

Question 1 — Does Pascal's apology count against long critiques?

The case for Snowden's view. At the end of the sixteenth of his Provincial Letters, Blaise Pascal apologised: the letter was long only because he had not had time to make it shorter[18]. Short writing takes work; long writing is what you get in a hurry. A quarter of a million words in a week shows the hurry and skips the work. The quotation says so politely.

The problem with that. Look at where the line comes from. The Provincial Letters (1656–57) were eighteen letters published anonymously by an outsider, writing from the circle of the Port-Royal convent, against the most powerful teaching order of his day, the Jesuits. What Pascal attacked was a method: the casuistry of some Jesuit moralists, a flexible way of fitting moral rules to individual cases which, he argued, ended up serving the convenience of the powerful.

My answer. The quotation works against the person using it, in four ways.

  • In the Provincial Letters, the long letters were the outsider's, and the short replies were the institution's. Readers did not conclude that the short side was right. History sided with Pascal.
  • The sixteenth letter is long because it answers accusations made against Port-Royal. Its length was the burden of the accused, not the indulgence of the accuser.
  • The method Pascal attacked offered, in effect, ingredients rather than recipes: principles that a qualified expert assembled to fit the case. Pascal's complaint was that this put the power of judgement in the hands of the body that certified the experts. That is very close to my own complaint about who certifies, designs and decides in the Cynefin method (Theses 13, 21 and XIX).
  • The Letters grew one at a time, under pressure from replies. Pascal's argument was additive — exactly what the reply finds suspicious in my covenant.

None of this makes me Pascal. It makes the quotation unsafe. Of all the books in the canon, Snowden chose to tease a long critique of an institution's method with a line from the one book in which the long critic was right.

Reply. Length is sometimes the result of haste; granted. But the measure of a disputation is whether its theses can be answered without the full text. The reply did exactly that. The format worked (Part VII).

In one line: in the book Snowden quotes, the long letters were the outsider's — and they were right.

Question 2 — Is Robert Fludd a fair picture of my critique?

The case for Snowden's view. Fludd's books are full of huge, numbered, all-embracing diagrams. A critique issued in numbered editions under a covenant, full of charts and turnable cards, looks rather like that: an attempt to put everything into one picture. The image is gentle mockery, and fair.

The problem with that. Look at what Fludd's pictures show. The banner shows an astrologer casting a horoscope: a man who reads someone else's life from a chart he draws, in which he himself does not appear. The woodcut of man inside the cosmos is a picture of the whole universe made visible to one eye, from outside.

My answer. Fludd is the emblem of exactly the figure my critiques were written against: the observer who maps the whole from outside it. My Thesis 8 complained that the metaphors of anthro-complexity put the reader outside the reading; Thesis 9, that a pattern mapped from outside is only a landscape; Thesis XXIII, that a diagram decides what stands out before the reader asks. The astrologer is all three theses as a picture. And Fludd's famous quarrel with Kepler turns out to be the key to the whole of anthro-complexity. That is the subject of Part II, which follows.

Reply. My own works use large figures and may fail the test I set for them; that is fair. But they do not claim to stand outside what they draw, and they try to mark the difference between what the author asserts and what the eye infers. The astrologer does neither.

Question 3 — Can you nail a tide, and who holds the hammer?

The case for Snowden's view. The title is a light joke. My critique tries to pin down something that is always moving — the tide of Thesis 20, the sailor in the tide of the loom. You cannot nail water.

The problem with that. A title left unexplained is a gesture whose meaning is left to the reader. In the philosopher George Herbert Mead's terms, that is exactly where the meaning of a gesture lives: in the response to it[27].

My answer. Here are three ways to complete it.

The hammer. To nail something you need a nail, a surface and a hand holding the hammer. In a title about pinning down motion, the hand is the one thing not shown. That is the structure of the reply itself: the one thing both my critiques said was missing — power, the hand that fixes the frame — is the one thing it postpones. Nailed to the Tides is a picture with the hammer cropped out.

The church door. The most famous nails in the history of argument are the ones that, according to tradition, fixed Luther's ninety-five theses to a church door in Wittenberg in 1517[22]. Whether he really nailed them is debated; the theses are not. They were short, numbered and posted so that anyone could dispute them without a long book — exactly how the reply used mine.

The tide. A tide is the perfect example of what Snowden says humans are not: a motion that does not change the story it tells about you. You can be carried by a tide, but you cannot argue with it. A title that casts my critique as an attempt to nail a tide casts what I criticise — anthro-complexity, its tools, its author — as a tide: impersonal, unanswerable, beyond argument. That is the very move Thesis 8 complained about. The title does what the body of the reply denies.

Reply. Perhaps this reads too much into four words. But no more than the reply read into the length of a book and the tools used to write it. Both sides may read paratexts, as long as they say so.

In one line: a tide cannot be nailed, but a frame can — and the title shows the water while hiding the hammer.

The way in: cards · 8 cards
Method
Paratext
The threshold where a text negotiates how it will be read.
Turn over ↻
Paratext

Gérard Genette's term (Seuils, 1987; English Paratexts, 1997) for everything that surrounds and presents a text without being its body: title, epigraph, preface, illustrations, notes. Paratexts are not decoration. They dispose the reader before any argument is heard, and they are where an author's stance toward the reader is most visible because it is least argued.

This rejoinder treats the reply's epigraph (Pascal), images (Fludd) and title (Nailed to the Tides) as paratexts in Genette's sense, and reads each as testimony. The method is fair on both sides: the reply read the length, editions and making of the disputations as paratexts too. The covenant asks only that the reading be declared.

The closing apology of the sixteenth of Blaise Pascal's Lettres provinciales (dated 4 December 1656): Je n'ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n'ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte. Snowden uses it as his epigraph, gently suggesting that the disputations' length is the residue of haste.

The rejoinder (Quaestio I) reads the occasion: the Provinciales were eighteen anonymous letters by an outsider attacking the casuistry of a powerful teaching order, whose method adapted rules to cases. The long letter was the outsider's, it answered accusations, and it grew under pressure from replies. History sided with the long letter. The epigraph testifies for the disputation it was chosen to rebuke (R3).

Probabilism and casuistry

In seventeenth-century moral theology, probabilism held that where the lawfulness of an act was doubtful, one might follow any opinion supported by a "grave doctor", even if a contrary opinion was more probable. Combined with casuistry — the art of resolving cases of conscience by adapting principles to circumstances — it produced a supple method in which rules bent to cases.

Pascal's Provinciales argued that this suppleness served the institution: the power of judgement lay with the guild that certified the doctors. The rejoinder notes the family resemblance to a method that publishes "ingredients rather than recipes", assembled to the case by qualified practitioners — and to Theses 13, 21 and XIX, which asked where judgement and certification sit.

Bruno Latour's term (Science in Action, 1987) for the sites — observatories, map rooms, laboratories, head offices — to which inscriptions from far away are brought, combined and made legible, so that those at the centre can act at a distance on what they never see directly. George Herbert Mead (Mind, Self and Society, 1934) argued that a gesture's meaning lies in the social act that the gesture and the other's response together complete. The self arises in this conversation of gestures, by taking the attitude of the other toward oneself.

Mead is used three times in the rejoinder. An unexplained title is a gesture whose meaning is left to its readers' response (Quaestio III). A narrative fragment signified alone by its teller is a gesture cut off before its response — the conversation of gestures with one side removed (Quaestio VIII).
