Part II Fludd's Picture, Kepler's Ruler

In short. Snowden chose pictures by Robert Fludd to illustrate his reply. That choice opens up the most important point in this whole exchange. In 1619 the astronomer Johannes Kepler attacked Fludd's diagrams: they were pictures, not proofs; they could not be measured, so they could not be tested. Fludd answered that Kepler only had the "quantitative shadow" of things and missed the living whole. Anthro-complexity holds Fludd's view of what people are, and uses Kepler's methods to study them. It believes in the whole and works with numbers. The two halves never meet — the numbers are never allowed to put the picture at risk — and the person who joins them, the designer of the instrument, ends up in exactly the position of Fludd's astrologer: outside the thing he draws, curating it. Ralph Stacey faced the same problem with his own famous diagram, the Stacey Matrix, and did something about it: he stopped using it. This Part tells that story in plain terms and draws out what it means.

1 · Two men and a quarrel

Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was an English doctor. He was a Fellow of the College of Physicians in London, he ran a successful practice, and he was also one of the best-known defenders of the Rosicrucians — a loose movement of the early 1600s that promised a universal reform of knowledge through hidden wisdom. Fludd believed the universe was one living whole, made and held together by God, and that a human being was a small copy of it: a microcosm, a little world, that mirrored the macrocosm, the great world. Everything corresponded to everything else. Music, medicine, the stars, the soul and the weather all followed the same harmonies, and the right kind of mind, lit from within by divine light, could see them[19][114][115].

Fludd explained his ideas in huge illustrated books, above all Utriusque Cosmi … Historia — "The History of Both Worlds", the great and the small — published at Oppenheim from 1617. Its engravings are still famous. One shows a giant monochord, a one-stringed instrument, stretched from heaven to earth and tuned by a hand reaching out of the clouds. Another, called the Mirror of the Whole of Nature and the Image of Art, shows Nature as a woman chained by the wrist to the hand of God, and a monkey — Art, human skill, the "ape of nature" — chained to Nature's hand, copying her. Another shows an astrologer casting a horoscope. That is the image at the top of Snowden's reply.

Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) was a German mathematician and astronomer, imperial mathematician to the Holy Roman Emperor. He was not a dry calculator. He was as mystical as Fludd in his own way. His first book, Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596), argued that the spacing of the six known planets was fixed by the five perfect solids of Greek geometry nested one inside another — a beautiful picture of God's design[117]. He believed the planets made a silent music. His book Harmonices Mundi — "The Harmony of the World" (1619) — set out that music, and in its fifth part announced what we now call Kepler's third law of planetary motion[20].

So both men believed the world was a harmony. The quarrel was not between a mystic and a scientist. It was between two ways of showing the harmony: Fludd's way, by pictures read with inner light; and Kepler's way, by numbers that anyone could check.

2 · What Kepler said, and what Fludd replied

Kepler added an appendix to the fifth book of Harmonices Mundi in which he compared his work with two others who had written on the harmony of the world — the ancient astronomer Ptolemy and the living Robert Fludd. About Fludd he was blunt. Fludd's diagrams, he said, were like hieroglyphs: pictures that delighted in riddles and symbols rather than demonstrations. They did not start from anything measurable. You could not check them against the sky. When Fludd drew a harmony, there was no way to find out whether the harmony was really there[20][21].

Fludd replied in 1621 with a pamphlet titled Veritatis Proscenium — "The Stage of Truth"[116]. His answer, in plain terms, was this. Kepler deals only with the outside of things: their sizes, distances and speeds, the "quantitative shadow". Real knowledge of the harmony is knowledge of the whole, and the whole is grasped from the inside, by a mind that is itself a copy of the cosmos. Measurement chops the whole into pieces and so misses what holds the pieces together. Kepler, said Fludd, has the tail of the animal; the true philosopher has its head.

Kepler answered in 1622 with an Apologia — a defence of his book. His reply to the "head and tail" jibe has become one of the best-known lines in the history of science. In the English of Pauli's translator, Kepler says he holds the tail — but I hold it in my hand — whereas Fludd may grasp the head in his mind, but only, Kepler fears, in his dreams[21]. Fludd came back once more, with Monochordum Mundi ("The Monochord of the World", 1622–23), and the two men never met in the middle[116].

Others joined in. The French friar Marin Mersenne and the philosopher Pierre Gassendi both wrote against Fludd in the 1620s, and Gassendi's attack (1630) went to the heart of the matter: Fludd's system could explain anything, so it explained nothing[119]. By the middle of the century the argument was effectively over. Kepler's way became the way of modern science. Fludd became a curiosity — admired for his pictures, not for his proofs.

Table A — The quarrel in one table
FluddKepler
What the world isOne living whole; every part mirrors every otherA harmony too — but one written in number
How you know itFrom inside, by inner light; the knower is a small copy of the wholeFrom outside, by measurement anyone can repeat
What counts as proofA picture that shows the correspondencesA calculation that matches the observations
His charge against the otherKepler has only the "quantitative shadow" — the tailFludd's pictures are hieroglyphs — they cannot be tested
Where he standsClaims to be inside (microcosm) — but draws from God's seatStands outside, with a ruler — and lets the sky correct him
What he got rightThe knower belongs to what is knownA picture must be answerable to something outside itself

3 · What Kepler really got right: the eight minutes

It would be easy to tell this story as "measurement beat mysticism". That would miss what made Kepler great, and it is the part of the story that matters most for anthro-complexity.

Kepler did not win because he measured. Astrologers measured too. He won because he let his measurements overturn his own favourite picture. In his book Astronomia Nova — "The New Astronomy" (1609) — he describes years of work trying to fit the orbit of Mars to a circle, the shape that ancient astronomy, and Kepler's own sense of beauty, said it must have[118]. His best circular model came very close. It missed the superb observations made by Tycho Brahe by eight minutes of arc — about a quarter of the width of the full moon. Almost anyone else would have blamed the data. Kepler did not. He wrote, in effect, that because Tycho's observations were good, those eight minutes could not be ignored, and that they would lead to a reform of the whole of astronomy. He abandoned the circle and found the ellipse.

And he wrote the book as a story of his own mistakes. Astronomia Nova leads the reader through Kepler's failed attempts, one after another, before reaching the answer. It is one of the first great scientific books to show its working, errors included, in public. In the language of my own work, it is an additive book: the wrong turns are kept on the page so that the reader can see how the argument moved.

So Kepler's real lesson is not "count things". It is: let the counting be able to prove you wrong. Three centuries later Karl Popper made a philosophy of it — a claim is scientific only if some observation could show it false[121]. Kepler had already lived it. The eight minutes are the moment at which a measurement was allowed to defeat a beautiful picture held by the person doing the measuring.

In one line: Kepler's virtue was not measuring. It was letting the measurement beat the picture he loved.

4 · What Fludd really got right: the knower is part of the known

Fludd lost the argument, but he was not simply wrong. In the twentieth century the physicist Wolfgang Pauli — one of the founders of quantum mechanics — wrote a long essay on the quarrel, published in 1952 alongside an essay by Carl Jung[21][120]. Pauli found that he sympathised with both men. Kepler stood for the modern scientific attitude, which takes the observer out of the picture so that results are the same for everyone. Fludd stood for something that attitude leaves out: the experience of the person doing the knowing. Quantum physics, Pauli thought, had shown that the observer cannot be completely removed — the act of observing plays a part in what is observed. In that respect Fludd had seen something Kepler had not.

That is exactly the insight anthro-complexity is built on. Human systems are not like planets. When you observe people, they notice, and they change. When you describe them, they hear the description, and they change. The observer is inside the system. That is Fludd's truth, and Snowden's theory rests on it: humans can change the stories they tell about each other, and those stories change what happens.

But here is the twist that this Part is about. Fludd said the knower was inside the whole — a microcosm mirroring the macrocosm. Yet every one of his great engravings is drawn from somewhere no human could stand: from above the cosmos, from God's side of the clouds. The monochord is tuned by a hand from outside the world. Nature is chained to God from above. The astrologer reads a person's fate from a chart in which he himself does not appear. Fludd's doctrine was participation. His practice was cartography — map-making — from a point outside the map. He claimed to be the little world inside the great one, and drew the great one as if he were looking down on it.

In one line: Fludd said the knower is inside the whole — and then drew the whole from outside it. That double position is the one anthro-complexity occupies.

5 · Anthro-complexity's ontology is Fluddian

"Ontology" means a theory of what exists and what things are like. Here is anthro-complexity's ontology, as set out by Snowden in his recent posts and in the Cynefin Company's own descriptions, laid beside Fludd's[10][11]. The match is not exact — Snowden is no Rosicrucian — but the shape is the same.

Table B — The Fluddian ontology of anthro-complexity
Anthro-complexity holds that…Fludd held that…The shared shape
A human being is not a computer and does not run a programme; human cognition is embodied, pattern-based and situatedThe soul is not a mechanism; it is a living mirror of the wholeThe human cannot be reduced to calculation
Meaning is entangled: it exists only in the interaction of people, things and context, and is lost when the interaction is broken upEvery part is bound to every other by sympathies and harmoniesThe whole is in the connections, not in the parts
Much of what matters is tacit — known but not sayableThe highest knowledge is inner illumination, not words or numbersThe most important knowledge cannot be written down
The whole is more than the sum of its parts; it cannot be predicted from themThe macrocosm is a single living beingWholes are real and prior
Humans have three marks — multiple identities, intention, abstraction — that make human complexity different in kindMan is the microcosm, the one creature that mirrors the wholeThe human has a special place in the order of things
Small things can matter enormously; patterns repeat at different scales"As above, so below": the same pattern in the stars, the body and the soulCorrespondence across scales

None of this is a criticism. On most of these points anthro-complexity is right, and so, in his way, was Fludd. Human beings are not computers. Meaning is made between people. Much of what we know we cannot say. The Fluddian side of anthro-complexity is its strength. It is why Snowden has been, for a quarter of a century, one of the most important voices against treating organisations as machines.

6 · Its practice is Keplerian

Now look at what the practice actually does. Take SenseMaker, the Cynefin Company's main instrument, and follow a single story through it[14][2].

Figure 1 — From story to signal. The ontology says the whole cannot be broken into parts. The practice breaks a story into coordinates, pools them, plots them, measures them and passes them on. The designer's choice of frame sits above the whole line.

  1. Signify. A person tells a short story about something that happened to them. Then, on a screen, they place it — one dot on each of several triangles (each corner a quality, such as "for the customer", "for the team", "for myself"), and a mark on several sliders between two words. The story has become a set of numbers: coordinates.
  2. Aggregate. Thousands of people do the same. Their coordinates are pooled in a database.
  3. Plot. The software draws the pooled dots: clusters on each triangle, contour maps, "landscapes" of where the stories fall.
  4. Measure. Analysts look for clusters, outliers, shifts over time. They set "vector measures" — more stories like these, fewer like those — and track movement.
  5. Feed. The patterns go to the client, who decides what to do. Patterns are also returned to the storytellers. And, according to the SwarmCompass brochure, the material can become "training data sets for further AI-based automation"[6][3].

Every one of those steps is Keplerian. It turns lived experience into something that can be counted, compared and checked from outside. The stories are kept — that is a real difference from a survey — but at scale it is the coordinates that make the patterns, because coordinates can be added up and stories, without further processing, cannot.

So the shape is this. The theory says: the whole cannot be broken into parts without loss. The practice breaks the whole into parts, very carefully, and works with the parts. It holds Fludd's view of what people are and uses Kepler's method to study them.

In one line: anthro-complexity believes in the whole and works with the numbers — Fludd's ontology, Kepler's practice.

7 · The worst of both: no eight-minute moment

There is nothing wrong, in itself, with holding a rich view of human beings and using careful methods to study them. Most good social science does exactly that. The problem is how the two are joined.

In Kepler's case, the measurements could defeat the picture. The eight minutes of arc beat the circle. Ask the same question of anthro-complexity: what pattern in the data could ever show that its picture of human beings is wrong? I cannot find one. If the dots cluster, that is a pattern of entangled meaning. If they scatter, that is the diversity of human experience. If a weak signal appears in the tail, the method found it; if none appears, weak signals are by nature hard to see. The theory sits above the data, untouchable, and the data are always read in its light. That is Gassendi's complaint against Fludd: a system that can explain any result explains none[119].

So anthro-complexity does not get the best of both. It gets something closer to the worst of both:

  • From Fludd it takes a picture of the whole that is never put at risk.
  • From Kepler it takes measurement — but not the humility that let measurement overturn the picture.
  • From Fludd again it takes the claim that the knower is inside — while the practice, like Fludd's engravings, is drawn from outside.

This is what Thesis 15 of Humans Are Not Estuaries called "an anti-computational ontology with a computational practice"[2]. The Fludd–Kepler story shows why it matters. The contradiction is not just untidy. It means the theory has no way to learn from its own instruments — no eight-minute moment — and an instrument that cannot teach its makers anything about their theory is not a scientific instrument in Kepler's sense. It is an illustration of the theory, like Fludd's monochord.

7a · Three fair objections to this reading

A reading this sharp should face its strongest objections before going on. Here are three, with my answers.

"Every social science does this." Most social research holds a rich view of people and still counts things. Interviews are coded; surveys are scored. Why single out anthro-complexity? — Because anthro-complexity, unlike most social research, makes the anti-counting view its founding claim. A survey researcher who says "attitudes can be measured" has no quarrel with his own survey. A theory that says "meaning is entangled and is lost when the interaction is broken up" does have a quarrel with an instrument that breaks the interaction up. The tension is sharper because the ontology is stronger. That is a compliment to the ontology.

"The stories are kept; the narrator interprets first; nothing is lost." — The stories are kept, and that matters. But a kept story that nobody reads at scale is an archive, not evidence. What travels to the client, the dashboard and the model is the pattern of coordinates. The first interpretation is the narrator's, but the decisive one — what the pattern means and what to do — is someone else's (Part IV, Question 19). Keeping the story is like Kepler keeping Tycho's notebooks: honourable, and not what the calculation runs on.

"Fludd was a mystic; this comparison is a sneer." — It would be, if the point were that Snowden is a mystic. The point is structural. Fludd believed the whole could be known and drew it from a place no human stands. Kepler measured and let the measurements correct him. Anthro-complexity believes, like Fludd, in a whole that resists counting; it counts, like Kepler; and it draws its frames, like Fludd, from the designer's seat. Neither man is being mocked. Both are being used as mirrors. Snowden chose the first mirror himself when he put Fludd's astrologer at the top of his reply.

Question 4 — Is anthro-complexity's ontology really Fluddian?

The case for saying no. Snowden is a scientist by instinct. He draws on neuroscience, biology and complexity science, not on Hermetic magic. His "whole" is the whole of a complex adaptive system, studied by real science; Fludd's was a mystical body held together by divine sympathy. To call Snowden Fluddian is a cheap trick.

The problem with that. The comparison is about the shape of the belief, not its sources. Both hold that the human is not reducible to calculation, that the whole is real and comes first, that the most important knowledge is tacit or inner, and that the human mirrors the larger whole in a special way.

My answer. Yes, in shape — and the shape is what matters here, because the shape is what creates the tension with the practice. Nobody is saying Snowden believes in Rosicrucian magic. The claim is narrower and, I think, hard to deny: anthro-complexity's view of human beings is holist, anti-mechanical and tacit-first, as Fludd's was, and its instruments are analytic, quantitative and explicit-first, as Kepler's were. The science Snowden draws on is real. But a real science of wholes still faces the question Kepler put to Fludd: how would you know if your picture of the whole were wrong?

Reply to the objection. The "cheap trick" would be to say Snowden is a mystic. I am saying something else: that his ontology, like Fludd's, is never exposed to his measurements. That is a claim about method, and it can be answered by pointing to the eight-minute moment — the pattern that would count against the theory. I would welcome that answer.

Question 5 — Is its practice really Keplerian?

The case for saying no. SenseMaker was designed against the survey. It keeps people's own words. It lets the narrator, not the expert, do the first interpretation. It shows every dot rather than averages. It refuses targets. That is not Kepler's ruler; it is an attempt to keep the whole.

The problem with that. All of this is true, and all of it happens inside a pipeline whose output is still coordinates, clusters and directions — numbers that can be aggregated and compared across thousands of people.

My answer. It is Keplerian in its operations, while being anti-Keplerian in its intentions. The intentions are good; I share them. But the steps — signify, aggregate, plot, measure, feed — are steps of quantification. Keeping the words is like Kepler keeping Tycho's notebooks: valuable, but not what the calculation runs on. And the newer instruments go further along the Keplerian road, not back from it: the SwarmCompass brochure sells "human-AI swarm intelligence" and training data for automation[6]. That is Kepler's ruler handed to a machine.

Reply to the objection. "It shows every dot, not averages." Yes — and a chart of every dot is still a chart. The question is not whether the practice is crude; it is not. The question is whether a practice that turns experience into coordinates can be squared with a theory that says experience cannot be broken up without loss. Snowden's honest answer, I suspect, is that it is a necessary compromise. Then let it be called one, and let its costs be declared.

Question 6 — Does measuring make it scientific?

The case for saying yes. SenseMaker produces real data from real people at scale. It has been used in many countries, on many problems. Its patterns can be shown to the people they describe, who can say whether they recognise them. That is more evidence than most management theories have ever had.

The problem with that. Evidence for a theory is easy to find if the theory decides how the evidence is read. Kepler's science began when evidence could count against him.

My answer. Measuring is necessary, not sufficient. What makes a practice scientific in Kepler's sense is that its measurements can overturn its picture. So the test for anthro-complexity is simple to state: name the pattern that would show the theory wrong. For example: if self-signified patterns turned out to predict nothing that expert coding of the same stories could not predict, would that count against the claim that self-signification captures something experts cannot? If returning patterns to narrators made no difference to what they did next, would that count against the claim that patterns help people see themselves? If the tails of the distribution thinned over successive rounds of capture, would that count against the claim that the method protects weak signals? These are testable. I do not know the answers. The point is that the theory, as stated, does not say what would count — and until it does, its measurements decorate its picture rather than test it.

In one line: a measurement that can never prove you wrong is an ornament, not a test.

Part II, continued The Astrologer, the Designer and Stacey's Diagram

8 · Fludd's astrologer: map-making, not taking part

Look again at the picture Snowden chose. An astrologer casts a horoscope. He sits outside the heavens he reads. He takes the moment of a person's birth, sets it against the positions of the planets, and draws a chart that tells that person what their life is like and will be like. The person does not draw the chart. The person does not choose the categories — the twelve houses, the aspects, the signs. The person is read. Their life becomes a point on a map that someone else made, interpreted in a language someone else controls.

That is what I mean by abstract cartography as opposed to immersive participation. The cartographer stands above the territory and draws it. The participant is in the territory, moving with others, unable to see the whole, making the way by walking it. Fludd's doctrine told him he was a participant — a microcosm, a small world inside the great one. His pictures made him a cartographer. The astrologer is the purest form of that double position: he believes the person and the heavens are one living harmony, and he works by drawing that harmony on paper from a seat outside it.

Now put anthro-complexity's practice into that picture. The narrator tells a story. The narrator places dots on triangles the narrator did not design. The dots join thousands of others and become a chart — a "landscape" — that the narrator never sees whole until, if ever, it is returned. Analysts read the chart. They say: here is a cluster, here is a weak signal, here is the direction to move. The client acts. The person whose story it was has become a point on a map, interpreted in categories someone else chose.

The reply to my disputations says the reader is "inside" the metaphors, as a sailor is inside the tide. The astrologer is inside the heavens too, in a sense: he lives under the same sky. But he does not stand where his subject stands, and his subject does not draw the chart. Inside, in the sense that matters, means able to change the map. Neither the horoscope's subject nor the narrator can.

In one line: believing you are part of the whole does not make you a participant if you are the one drawing the map.

9 · The designer is the one who curates

Who, then, stands in the astrologer's seat? Not the analyst, mainly. Not the client. The decisive figure is the designer — the person who designs the instrument before any story is told.

The designer decides:

  • The prompt — the question that invites a story ("Tell us about a time when…"). This decides which experiences come to mind at all.
  • The signifiers — which three qualities sit at the corners of each triangle, which two words sit at the ends of each slider, which options appear in each list. This decides what a story can be said to be about.
  • The labels — the exact words, which shape how each corner is understood.
  • The order — story first, then signifiers; which triangle first; which slider last. Order changes answers, in measurable, lawful ways[63].
  • The display — how dots are drawn, which patterns are highlighted, what counts as a cluster.

Every one of these is an act of curation: choosing, from the endless whole of human experience, the frame in which it will appear. That is the Fluddian act. It is the hand from the clouds tuning the monochord: the string can vibrate in many ways, but the hand has set its length and its tension. The narrator then plays the string. The analyst then measures the note. But the range of notes was fixed before anyone played.

Fludd's other famous engraving makes the point even more sharply. In the Mirror of the Whole of Nature and the Image of Art, human skill is shown as an ape, chained to Nature's wrist, copying her[19]. Art does not create; it imitates. The designer of an instrument is Fludd's ape: chained to the whole, trying to copy it in a small, manageable form. The copy is never the whole. But once the copy exists, people stop looking at the whole and start reading the copy — and the copy was made by the ape.

Table C — Three roles in the instrument, and who each resembles
RoleWhat they doWho they resembleWhat they can change
The designerChooses prompt, signifiers, labels, order, displayFludd: the hand tuning the monochord; the ape copying NatureEverything — the frame itself
The narratorTells a story; places dots on someone else's frameThe microcosm in Fludd's woodcut; the subject of the horoscopeWhere the dot goes, within the frame
The analyst and clientRead patterns; measure; decide; feed onwardKepler with the ruler — but without the eight minutesWhat happens next, to the narrator

This is why the reply's analogy with language (Part V, Question 19) fails. No one designed English. Someone designed the triangle. And this is why the deferral of power is not a side issue. Curation is power — what the political theorist Steven Lukes called the third face of power: the power to shape how people see their own situation, so that some things never come up at all[96].

9a · One story's journey: a worked example

This example is invented to show how the pieces fit together. It describes no real organisation, project or person.

A hospital trust wants to understand why experienced nurses are leaving. It commissions a narrative study. Here is what happens to one story.

Before anyone speaks. A designer meets the trust's leadership team — the client. Together they agree a prompt: "Think of a shift that made you think about your future here. What happened?" They agree three triangles. One has corners labelled patients, colleagues, myself ("whose needs came first?"). One has workload, management, culture ("what shaped this most?"). One has hope, frustration, resignation. They add sliders and a few multiple-choice questions about grade and ward. No nurse has been consulted yet. The frame is curated.

The story. A ward sister with twenty years' service tells of a night when two agency staff failed to arrive, a patient deteriorated, she missed her break and her own daughter's call, and a manager emailed the next morning about a missed audit. She is exhausted, furious, and still proud of how she kept the patient safe.

The signifying. On the first triangle, patients, colleagues and herself all mattered intensely that night. She puts the dot in the middle. On the second, workload, management and culture all shaped it. Middle again. On the third, she felt hope (she kept him safe), frustration (the email) and resignation (she is thinking of leaving) — all at once, all strongly. Middle. Her story is now three central dots.

The pooling. Two thousand stories come in. Hers joins a large cluster in the middle of each triangle — alongside stories from people who felt nothing much on a quiet shift and could not say what mattered. On the charts, the middle looks like "balanced" or "mixed" experience.

The reading. The analysts notice a smaller cluster near management and frustration, and recommend action on management communication. They set a vector: "more stories like the hopeful ones, fewer like the frustrated ones". The trust launches a programme on manager emails.

The return. Months later, the patterns are shown back to staff. The ward sister sees the middle cluster labelled "mixed experience". She does not recognise her night in it. She did not have a mixed night; she had an overwhelming one.

What went where. Every choice that decided what could be seen — the prompt, the corners, the labels, the order, the display, the reading of the middle — was made by the designer and the client. Her experience entered as data; their frame entered as structure. The intensity of her night was erased by the geometry (Part IV, Question 22), and the meaning of her dots was decided by people she never met (Question 19). Nothing in this example requires bad faith. Every person in it was doing their job well. That is the point: the astrologer's chair does not need a villain in it. It only needs the frame to be drawn from one side.

What the loom would have changed. Nurses would have helped write the corners. An intensity slider would have kept her overwhelming night apart from the quiet ones. She and her colleagues would have seen the pattern of their own stories first, and could have said "the middle isn't mixed — it's everything at once." They could have met to compare. And the trust's list of corrections would have recorded that the first design hid the most important cluster in the study.

Question 7 — Is the designer an insider, or Fludd's astrologer?

The case for "insider". The Cynefin Company says mapping is done by insiders and that signifiers are often developed with the client. Good practitioners test their signifier sets in pilots. Narrators can tick "not applicable". The designer is a craftsman serving the people being studied, not an astrologer reading their fate.

The problem with that. "With the client" is not "with the narrators". The client is usually the organisation that commissions the work — managers, a funder, a government department. The narrators are its staff, its customers, its citizens. A frame designed with the client is a frame designed from the client's side.

My answer. The designer is an insider to the commission and an outsider to the experience. That is precisely the astrologer's position: employed by the person whose chart is cast, or by their family, or by the court — inside the relationship of service, outside the life being read. Piloting a signifier set improves it, as a better telescope improves astronomy, but it does not move the designer into the narrator's seat. Only giving narrators a hand in the frame does that — co-authoring the signifiers, revising them between rounds, seeing the pattern first. Those are threads of the Tidal Loom (Part VIII). Without them the designer remains where Fludd drew himself: beside the hand in the clouds.

Reply. "Not applicable" is a real freedom and I do not belittle it. But it is the freedom to step off the map, not to redraw it.

10 · Stacey's diagram

The problem of the designer standing outside is not new to complexity thinking. One of its founders met it in his own work, and his response is the most instructive thing in this whole story.

Ralph Stacey (1948–2021) was Professor of Management at the University of Hertfordshire and one of the first writers to apply complexity science to organisations[124]. In 1996, in the second edition of his textbook Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics, he included a diagram that became famous[122][127]. It had two axes: how close a group is to agreement about an issue, and how close it is to certainty about cause and effect. Near the corner where both are high, ordinary rational planning works. As you move away from both, you pass through zones where politics or judgement are needed, then a "zone of complexity", and finally, far from both, chaos[125].

Figure 3 — A sketch of the Stacey Matrix as it is usually drawn (after Stacey 1996 and Zimmerman 2001). To use it, you stand outside the chart, decide where an issue sits, and read off an approach. Stacey came to see that this places the user in the astrologer's seat — and stopped using it.

The diagram — soon known as the Stacey Matrix — was enormously popular. Brenda Zimmerman, a Canadian complexity scholar, wrote it up as a practical aid for managers choosing between approaches[125]. Consultants, project managers and the agile software movement took it up. It appeared on countless slides. Many versions changed it in ways that did not match what Stacey had meant[124].

Notice what kind of picture it is. It is a picture of the whole field of organisational life, seen from above, divided into zones. To use it, a manager looks at an issue, places it on the map, reads off which zone it is in, and chooses the matching approach. That is the astrologer's procedure: take the situation, plot it on a chart drawn in advance, read off the meaning. The manager stands outside the situation, deciding what kind of situation it is. The diagram amplified the Fluddian picture — the whole visible at once, from a point outside it — and made it portable. Anyone could now be the astrologer.

11 · Stacey's renunciation

Then Stacey did something very few authors of successful diagrams ever do. He stopped using it. The diagram disappeared from later editions of his textbook. He said publicly that it was a diagram he had come to regret[126][127], and he gave his reason: the diagram was simply interpreted in a way that sustains the dominant discourse — the ordinary language of management — while borrowing the jargon of complexity[126][124]. In the words of a summary of his position, it is too easily read in a way that collapses the paradox of certainty and uncertainty[124].

What did he mean? Put simply:

  • The diagram suggested that complexity is a zone — a place some issues are in and others are not. Stacey came to think complexity is a feature of all human interaction. There is no corner of organisational life where people are not interdependent, unpredictable and responding to one another.
  • The diagram suggested that a manager can stand outside an issue and decide which zone it belongs to, then pick a tool. But the manager is part of the issue. Their judgement about "which zone" is itself a move in the game, which others will notice and respond to.
  • The diagram turned a paradox — we act with intention and cannot know the consequences; we are both certain and uncertain at once — into a choice: here be certainty, there be uncertainty, pick your tool. That is the "collapse of the paradox". It lets ordinary management carry on as before, with new words.

This was part of a larger turn. Around 2000, with Douglas Griffin and Patricia Shaw, Stacey moved away from treating organisations as complex adaptive systems at all[28][124]. He came to see organisations as complex responsive processes of relating: patterns of conversation, power and identity among people who are all inside, all responding to one another, with no one in a position to stand outside and steer. Complexity science became a source of analogies, to be used carefully, rather than a model to be applied[29]. In The Tools and Techniques of Leadership and Management (2012) he went further and asked what tools, frameworks and diagrams actually do in organisations. His answer, developed with Chris Mowles, was that they often function less as instruments of control than as rituals and social defences — ways of managing the anxiety of not knowing, by giving the appearance of a view from above[123][128].

That is the whole of the Stacey challenge, and it is aimed squarely at the designer. It says: the moment you draw the whole and invite people to locate themselves on it, you have put yourself — and them, when they use it — in the astrologer's seat. And the more popular the drawing, the more firmly the seat is fixed.

In one line: Stacey drew a map of complexity, saw that it turned managers into astrologers, and gave it up.

12 · Stacey did Kepler's deed to his own picture

There is a striking parallel here. Kepler loved the circle and gave it up because eight minutes of arc would not go away. Stacey loved his diagram — or at least saw how much others loved it — and gave it up because of something that would not go away either: the way it was used. His "eight minutes" were not an astronomical measurement. They were the steady evidence, year after year, of managers using the matrix to do the opposite of what his theory said was possible.

So Stacey practised the virtue Kepler had and Fludd lacked — he let reality overrule a favourite picture — but the reality that overruled it was social: the life of the diagram among the people who used it. That is the only kind of evidence that really counts for a theory of human systems, because human systems are exactly the ones that learn the picture and change in response. Stacey treated the reception of his own diagram as data about his theory. He applied the asymmetry principle — humans change the stories they are told — to himself.

And then he did not draw a better map. That is the decisive step. He did not produce a Stacey Matrix 2.0 with fuzzier boundaries. He moved to a different position altogether: not Fludd's vision from above, not Kepler's ruler from outside, but the participant's conversation from within. It is a third position, and it is the one this rejoinder has been pointing to all along.

Question 8 — Does Stacey's renunciation bear on Cynefin?

The case for saying no. Cynefin is not the Stacey Matrix. Snowden has long insisted that Cynefin is a sense-making framework, not a categorisation model: its domains emerge from the data rather than being imposed on it, the boundaries matter, and there is a central area of confusion where you do not know which domain you are in. Comparing the two is a common mistake[127][15].

The problem with that. The reply itself says that the Cynefin diagram has been redrawn several times because readers took its boundaries and positions as claims that were never made[1]. That is the same experience Stacey had: a diagram read, again and again, as a map of zones from which to choose a tool.

My answer. Cynefin and the Stacey Matrix are different, and Cynefin's authors have worked hard to make it less of a categorising map. But the two diagrams share a family history and, more importantly, a fate. Both have been widely used as charts on which a manager places a situation and reads off an approach. Stacey's response to that fate was to renounce his diagram and change his position. Snowden's response has been to redraw his diagram and to attribute the problem to readers. Redrawing is not nothing; it is a kind of errata, and I credit it. But it keeps the drawing at the centre and the drawer in the seat above it. Stacey's question to the Cynefin Company would be: what does the diagram do in the rooms where it is used — whom does it place outside, and what anxiety does it soothe? That question cannot be answered by redrawing. It can only be answered by studying the diagram's life among its users, as Stacey did with his.

Reply to the objection. I am not asking Snowden to abandon Cynefin. I am asking him to treat its reception as Kepler treated the eight minutes and Stacey treated his matrix's popularity: as evidence that might overturn something he cares about. If the evidence shows that Cynefin, unlike the matrix, does put its users inside rather than above, so much the better — and I would gladly amend my theses in place.

In one line: Stacey renounced his diagram; Snowden redraws his. Both saw readers take the boundaries as claims. Only one asked what the drawing itself was doing to them.

13 · The third position: participation

We now have three positions, not two.

Table D — Three positions toward a human system
Fludd (the astrologer)Kepler (the surveyor)Stacey (the participant)
Where you standAbove, with a vision of the wholeOutside, with a rulerInside, among others who are also moving
What you produceA picture of correspondencesMeasurements and lawsConversation, reflection, shifts in how people relate
What counts as knowingSeeing the whole by inner lightMatching the dataNoticing what is happening between us, including what I am doing
How you are correctedYou are notBy the data (the eight minutes)By others' responses to you, in the moment and afterwards
The dangerAn unfalsifiable pictureLosing what cannot be countedNever seeing beyond the local; drift; cliques
Anthro-complexity's shareIts ontologyIts practiceIts rhetoric — "insiders", "the reader inside the tide" — not yet its method

The participant's position has dangers of its own, and the reply is right to press them. Open, unstructured conversation can leave power unexamined in a different way; the first confident voice can take over; the least powerful can pay the price; local conversation may never see the larger pattern[16][4]. None of the three positions is safe. But only the participant's position is honest about where the knower stands, and only it is corrected by the people it describes.

That suggests what a practice faithful to anthro-complexity's own ontology would look like. It would not throw away measurement — Kepler's lesson is real. It would not throw away pictures of the whole — Fludd's insight is real too. But it would put both inside the participant's position:

  • The frame would be curated with the narrators, not only for the client (the warp of the loom).
  • The narrators would see the picture of their own stories first, and could say "that is not us" (first sight).
  • The theory would name, in advance, the patterns that would count against it (the eight minutes).
  • The diagram's life among its users would be studied as evidence about the theory (Stacey's step).
  • Every change to the frame would be recorded in the open (the errata).

That is not a new method. It is anthro-complexity's own Fluddian ontology finally given a practice that matches it — a practice in which the person drawing the map is visibly one of the people on it.

Question 9 — Is there really a third position, or only better and worse maps?

The case for "only maps". Any practice that works at scale needs some picture of the whole. Even a participant must eventually summarise, report, decide. The "third position" is a luxury of small groups — Stacey's doctoral seminars, not a ministry or a hospital system. At scale, someone must draw the map.

The problem with that. The argument assumes that whoever draws the map at scale must draw it from outside. That does not follow. Maps can be drawn by those on them, revised by them, and held answerable to them.

My answer. The objection is serious and partly right: scale does need summaries, and the participant's position cannot simply refuse them. But there is a real difference between a map drawn from outside and handed down, and a map drawn by those on it and kept open to revision. OpenStreetMap is a map of the whole world drawn by its users[106]. The Ordnance Survey is a map drawn for the state. Both are maps; they stand in different places. The third position is not "no maps". It is "no map whose drawer is exempt from it". That is achievable at scale. It costs more, it is slower, and it hands power away — which is exactly why it is rarely done, and exactly why the deferred post on power is the place where it must be faced.

In one line: the third position is not "no map" — it is "no map whose maker is exempt from it".

14 · Seven commitments for the designer

If the designer is the person in the astrologer's chair, the most useful thing this Part can do is say, plainly, what a designer could commit to. None of these needs new technology. All of them need a decision about power.

  1. Declare the frame. Publish, with every study, who wrote the prompt and the categories, for whom, and why these and not others.
  2. Share the pen. Write the categories with representatives of the people who will use them, and let them change the categories between rounds.
  3. Keep the intensity. Add a simple "how much of any of this?" measure to every triangle, so the overwhelming and the empty are never confused.
  4. Show them first. Let storytellers see the pattern of their own stories before the client does, and record what they say about it.
  5. Ask before you train. Never use a story to train an automated system, or for any purpose beyond the first, without specific consent, a share in the benefit, and a way to withdraw.
  6. Name the eight minutes. Before each study, state what pattern would count against the theory or the design — and publish it if it appears.
  7. Study the diagram's life. As Stacey did with his matrix, look at how the framework and its pictures are actually used, and treat that as evidence about the theory, not as readers' error.

A designer who made these seven commitments would still be a designer. But she would be standing visibly on the map, with her stake declared and her pen shared — no longer Fludd's astrologer, not merely Kepler's surveyor, but one participant among others.

Robert Fludd (1574–1637)

English physician and Hermetic philosopher whose Utriusque Cosmi … Historia (Oppenheim, 1617–21) filled its pages with engraved diagrams of the macrocosm and the human microcosm nested within it. Snowden illustrates his reply with three Fludd images: an astrologer casting a horoscope, man the microcosm within the macrocosm, and a portrait.

The rejoinder (Quaestio II) reads the choice as self-describing. Fludd's astrologer is the observer who fixes a person's fate from a map of forces in which he himself does not appear — the outside reader of Theses 8 and 9 and the centre of calculation of Thesis XXIII, drawn as a picture. And Fludd's quarrel with Kepler is the quarrel between anthro-complexity's ontology and its practice (R4).

The Kepler–Fludd quarrel

The Kepler–Fludd quarrel

In an appendix to Harmonices Mundi (1619) Johannes Kepler criticised Fludd's cosmic diagrams as hieroglyphic pictures rather than mathematical demonstrations: they could not be measured, so could not be tested. Fludd replied (Veritatis Proscenium, 1621) that Kepler grasped only the quantitative shadow of things and missed the qualitative harmony known by inner illumination; Kepler answered again in 1622.

The rejoinder's claim: anthro-complexity holds Fludd's ontology (the human is not a computer; meaning is entangled and tacit; the whole exceeds its numbers) and Kepler's practice (signify, aggregate, plot, measure, train). Thesis 15 named the contradiction; the reply's banner pictured it. The quarrel is not resolved by choosing a side but by declaring which side each instrument stands on.

Fludd's cosmic monochord

Fludd's cosmic monochord

A monochord is a one-stringed instrument used since Pythagoras to study musical ratios: move the bridge and the note changes in exact proportion. In Fludd's Utriusque Cosmi Historia (1617) a giant monochord stretches from the highest heaven down to the earth. The levels of the universe — elements, planets, angels — are marked along it like notes on a scale, and a hand reaches out of the clouds to turn the tuning peg.

The image says the whole cosmos is one harmony, tuned by God from outside. In this rejoinder it stands for the designer of an instrument: the string can sound in many ways, but someone outside has already set its length and tension. The person who plays it — the storyteller — works within a range fixed before she arrived.

The ape of nature

In Fludd's engraving Integrae Naturae Speculum Artisque Imago ("Mirror of the Whole of Nature and the Image of Art", 1617), Nature appears as a woman chained by the wrist to the hand of God. A second chain runs from her hand to an ape squatting on the earth, measuring a globe: Art — human skill and invention — which can only imitate what Nature makes.

The rejoinder (Part II, section 9) reads the designer as Fludd's ape: chained to the living whole, making a small, manageable copy of it. The copy is never the whole. But once the copy exists, people read the copy instead of looking at the whole — and the copy was made by the ape.

Microcosm and macrocosm

An ancient idea, revived in the Renaissance: the human being is a microcosm (little world) that mirrors the macrocosm (great world). The body's humours match the elements, the soul matches the heavens, and what happens above is reflected below. Fludd built his whole system on it.

It is a doctrine of participation: the knower is inside the whole and can know it by knowing himself. The rejoinder's point is that Fludd held this doctrine while drawing the macrocosm from outside — and that anthro-complexity does something similar: it says the observer is inside, and designs its instruments from a seat outside.

Kepler's Mysterium Cosmographicum (1596)

"The Cosmic Mystery". The young Kepler argued that the distances between the six known planets were set by the five Platonic solids — cube, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron, octahedron — nested one inside another between the planetary spheres. It was a beautiful picture of divine design, and Kepler loved it all his life.

It shows that Kepler was no dry measurer. He started from a Fludd-like vision of cosmic harmony. What made him different was what he did when measurements disagreed with the vision: he let the measurements win.

Hieroglyphic pictures

In the appendix to Harmonices Mundi (1619), Kepler said that Fludd delighted in obscure, riddle-like pictures of reality — "hieroglyphic" images that pointed to hidden meanings — while he himself started from what could be measured and brought obscure things into clear light.

The point was not that pictures are bad. Kepler drew diagrams too. It was that a picture which cannot be checked against anything outside itself cannot be wrong, and so cannot teach us anything. The rejoinder asks the same of anthro-complexity's pictures of the whole: what could show them wrong?

Fludd's replies to Kepler

Fludd answered Kepler first in Veritatis Proscenium ("The Stage of Truth", 1621). He argued that Kepler dealt only with the outward, quantitative side of things — size, distance, speed — and missed the inner, qualitative harmony that a mind lit by divine wisdom could grasp. When Kepler answered in his Apologia (1622), Fludd replied again in Monochordum Mundi Symphoniacum.

The exchange never resolved. Each man thought the other had the wrong idea of what knowledge is. The rejoinder argues that anthro-complexity has taken one side's idea of what people are and the other side's idea of how to study them.

Quote
Head and tail
“I hold the tail, but I hold it in my hand.”
Turn over ↻
Head and tail

Fludd's jibe was that Kepler, the mathematician, had only the tail of the creature — the measurable outside — while the true philosopher grasped its head. Kepler's reply in his Apologia (1622), as translated for Pauli's essay, is that he does indeed hold the tail, but holds it in his hand; Fludd may grasp the head in his mind, but only, Kepler fears, in his dreams.

It is the cleanest statement of the difference between knowledge you can check and knowledge you can only claim. Anthro-complexity, in the rejoinder's reading, claims the head (the whole) and works with the tail (the coordinates) — without saying how the one could correct the other.

Debate
Mersenne and Gassendi against Fludd

Turn over ↻
Mersenne and Gassendi against Fludd

The French friar Marin Mersenne attacked Fludd in the 1620s, and the philosopher Pierre Gassendi published a detailed critique in 1630 (Epistolica exercitatio). Gassendi's central complaint was that Fludd's system of correspondences could account for any result whatever — and a theory that can explain anything has explained nothing.

The rejoinder (Part II, section 7) asks whether anthro-complexity's reading of its own data has the same shape: clustering means entangled meaning, scattering means diversity, a weak signal found means success, none found means weak signals are hard to see.

Finding
Kepler's eight minutes
The measurement that beat the picture he loved.
Turn over ↻
Kepler's eight minutes

Working on the orbit of Mars for Astronomia Nova (1609), Kepler built a circular model that came very close to Tycho Brahe's observations — but missed them by about eight minutes of arc, roughly a quarter of the width of the full moon. Because he trusted Tycho's data, he refused to ignore the gap, and wrote that it would lead to a reform of all astronomy. He gave up the circle and found the ellipse.

This is the rejoinder's test (R26): a theory is scientific in Kepler's sense when some measurement could overturn its favourite picture. What are anthro-complexity's eight minutes? The rejoinder cannot find them stated anywhere.

Astronomia Nova (1609)

"The New Astronomy". Kepler's account of his long struggle with the orbit of Mars, published in 1609, contains his first two laws of planetary motion. Unusually, it is written as a narrative of failed attempts — model after model tried, tested against Tycho's data and abandoned — before the ellipse is found.

The rejoinder treats it as an early example of what the Additive Covenant asks for: corrections made in the open, so readers can see how the argument moved. Kepler's wrong turns are part of his proof.

Concept
Falsifiability
A claim is scientific if some observation could show it false.
Turn over ↻
Falsifiability

Karl Popper's criterion (The Logic of Scientific Discovery, 1934; English 1959): what makes a theory scientific is not that evidence supports it — evidence can be found for almost anything — but that it rules something out, so that an observation could prove it wrong. Theories that can absorb any result, Popper argued, are not scientific, however impressive.

Kepler's eight minutes are a historic example. The rejoinder does not demand that anthro-complexity become Popperian physics. It asks only that it name what pattern would count against it.

Pauli on Kepler and Fludd

Wolfgang Pauli's essay "The Influence of Archetypal Ideas on the Scientific Theories of Kepler" (published with C. G. Jung's essay on synchronicity in 1952; English 1955) examined the Kepler–Fludd controversy. Pauli confessed that he recognised both men in himself: Kepler's drive to quantify, and Fludd's insistence that the quantitative leaves out the qualitative whole.

The rejoinder invokes Pauli not to mystify the dispute but to model the honest posture toward it: to hold both tendencies and say so. A method that is Fluddian in its ontology and Keplerian in its software owes its users Pauli's candour about which is speaking when.

The Fludd-like ontology (R25)

"Ontology" means a view of what exists and what it is like. Anthro-complexity's view of people shares the shape of Fludd's: the human is not reducible to calculation; meaning lives in the connections between people and things; the most important knowledge is tacit; the whole comes first and cannot be predicted from its parts; the human has a special place in the order of things; patterns repeat across scales.

The rejoinder treats this as a strength — it is why Snowden has been right against mechanical management for a quarter of a century. The problem lies only in how it is joined to the practice.

Abstract cartography

The rejoinder contrasts two ways of knowing a human system. The cartographer stands above the territory and draws it; the map can then be read by people who were never there. The participant is in the territory, moving with others, unable to see the whole, making the path by walking it.

Fludd's doctrine (the microcosm) made him a participant; his engravings made him a cartographer. Anthro-complexity's language ("insiders", "the reader inside the tide") is a participant's; its instruments are a cartographer's. The rejoinder asks that the practice catch up with the language.

Concept

Knowing a system from inside it, among others who are also moving.
Turn over ↻
Immersive participation

The position Ralph Stacey moved to after giving up his matrix: there is no place outside human interaction from which to see it whole. We know organisations by taking part in them, noticing what is happening between us — including what we ourselves are doing — and talking about it. Knowledge is corrected by other people's responses, not by a chart.

This position has dangers — it can stay local, drift or become cliquish — and Snowden is right to press them. But it is the only one honest about where the knower stands, and the only one in which the people described can correct the description.

In narrative instruments the designer decides the prompt (what experiences come to mind), the categories (what a story can be said to be about), the labels (how each category is understood), the order (which changes answers, lawfully), and the display (what counts as a pattern). Each is an act of curation: choosing, from the whole of human experience, the frame in which it will appear.

The rejoinder's central claim in Part II: the designer is the figure anthro-complexity never describes, and the one its postponement of power protects. Every half-answer in Table 1 is the shadow the designer casts on the reply.

Steven Lukes distinguished three faces of power: winning decisions; keeping issues off the agenda; shaping what people want and take for granted. Choosing the frame through which people describe their own experience is the third face in its purest form: it decides what can be noticed before anyone notices anything.

Ralph Stacey (1948–2021) developed, with Douglas Griffin and Patricia Shaw at the University of Hertfordshire, the theory of complex responsive processes of relating: organisations are not systems that managers stand outside and steer, but ongoing patterns of communication, power and evaluative choice among interdependent people. Strategy and change emerge in local interaction.

Stacey's analysis of five teleologies (with Griffin and Shaw, 2000) underlies Thesis 7 and Compass Thesis IV. His "Stacey Matrix", which he later set aside because it was being used as a tool for categorising situations rather than as an aid to thinking, is itself a precedent for a figure abandoned because of what readers took from it.

The Stacey Matrix

Turn over ↻
The Stacey Matrix

Introduced by Ralph Stacey in the second edition of Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics (1996). One axis shows how close a group is to agreement on an issue; the other, how close it is to certainty about cause and effect. Near both: rational planning. Further out: politics and judgement. Further still: a "zone of complexity". Far from both: chaos.

It became hugely popular — in management courses, project management and agile software — and was often adapted in ways that did not match Stacey's intent. To use it, a manager stands outside an issue, places it on the chart and reads off an approach: the astrologer's procedure, made portable.

For the later Stacey, organisational life is paradoxical: we act with intention yet cannot know the consequences; we are both certain and uncertain, at once and all the time. In his first phase Stacey applied chaos theory and complex adaptive systems to organisations. Around 2000, with Douglas Griffin and Patricia Shaw, he dropped that application. Organisations, he argued, are not systems but ongoing patterns of conversation, power and identity among interdependent people, none of whom stands outside. Complexity science became a source of careful analogies, not a model to apply. Mead supplied the theory of conversation, Elias the theory of power.

This is the "third position" of the rejoinder: neither Fludd's vision nor Kepler's ruler, but the participant's conversation.

In The Tools and Techniques of Leadership and Management (2012), Stacey argued that management tools cannot deliver the control they promise, because human futures are not predictable; they can support competent performance but not expertise, which goes beyond rules. Chris Mowles developed the idea that tools and frameworks often work as rituals and social defences — ways of managing the anxiety of uncertainty by offering the appearance of a view from above.

Applied to diagrams like Stacey's matrix or Cynefin, the question becomes: what do they do in the room, for whom, and what do they protect people from feeling?

The objection is fair: at scale someone must summarise and decide. The rejoinder's answer is that the third position is not "no maps" but "no map whose maker is exempt from it". Maps can be drawn by those on them, revised by them and held answerable to them — OpenStreetMap is a map of the world drawn by its users.

It costs more, is slower, and hands power away. That is why it is rarely done, and why it belongs at the centre of the postponed post on power.

Part III The Shape of the Reply

In short. Before going through the theses one by one, it helps to look at the reply as a whole. Three habits stand out. It answers the half of each thesis that is about the world and drops the half that is about the person describing it (R1). It postpones power six times (R2). And it puts the blame for misunderstandings on readers rather than on the texts and diagrams that produced them (R19). A table of concessions and a ledger of all forty-seven theses close the Part.

You can read a reply as a list of verdicts. You can also read it as a pattern: what it picks up and what it leaves alone. The sociologist Norbert Elias would call that a figuration; Ralph Stacey would call it a pattern of themes organising experience[25][29]. The second kind of reading is the one my critiques asked for, because both were about one question: where does the person reading a complex human system stand? So the first question to ask of the reply is not "is each answer right?" but "what does the reply, taken as a whole, do with the reader?"

1 · The half-answers

Almost every thesis in both critiques was built in two parts. The first part described something: the metaphors come from nature; the constraints are built into the community; the triangle forces a trade-off; the tide turns. The second part turned that description back on the person doing the describing: …and each one puts the reader outside the reading; …and when someone maps them; …on a frame the storyteller did not choose; …because someone was seen waiting for it. The second part was the point. The first part was the setting.

The reply answers the first part and lets the second drop, with a regularity too steady to be accidental. I do not think this is bad faith. I think it is exactly what the idea at the heart of The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy predicts: we see other people's constraints and not our own[4]. The second part of each thesis is always about the reply's author. It is the part that cannot be seen from where he stands.

Table 1 — The half-answers: what each thesis said about the observer, what the reply answered, what is left
ThesisThe part about the observerWhat the reply answersWhat is left unanswered
7…and a planning mindset for the practitionerExperiments exist because outcomes are unknownWho chose the criteria for judging outcomes
8Each puts the reader outside the readingThe reader is inside, like a sailor in the tideThe tide does not notice the sailor (R5)
9…includes the strategist's own positionMapping is done by insidersWho convenes them, supplies the canvas, reads the map afterwards
10…and when someone maps themThe idea comes from JuarreroWhether mapping changes what it maps

13…whoever designs the categories, receives the pattern and carries the remaining riskLanguage is a frame nobody choseWho receives the pattern and carries the risk (R8)
14…on a frame the storyteller did not chooseAbstract categories are more rigorousWho chooses the abstraction (R9)

18…the in-between step is where the designer sitsThe storyteller interprets; the analyst reads patternsThe designer between them
19People learn what the camera wantsVector measures separate measure from targetContradicted by the reply's own answer to XVII (R13)
20…because someone was seen waiting for itThe turning is what mattersThe visibility of the one waiting (R14)
I…undercuts "find the 17%" as individualsThe cure is many frames at scaleOne frame given to many is one frame (R15)
V…assumes someone who can decide to leave things aloneWaiting and stirring are different gesturesWho chooses, and from where

Fifteen theses, fifteen half-answers. In every row the second column points, in the end, at whoever designs, convenes, measures, publishes or reads. In every row the third column answers a question about the system. The reply is an excellent account of human complex systems with the observer taken out. That is exactly the kind of account my theses were written against — given again, in reply.

Part II showed where this comes from. A theory that holds Fludd's beliefs about the whole and uses Kepler's methods on the parts needs someone to stand in between: to choose the frame, run the instruments and read the results. That person is the designer, and the designer is the one figure the theory never describes. The half-answers are the shadow the designer casts on the reply.

Question 10 — Isn't leaving out half of each thesis just a fair way to keep a reply short?

The case for Snowden's view. Anyone answering forty-seven theses in a few thousand words must choose. He answered the substance and left the flourish. The second halves are rhetorical flourishes — clever turns that add colour, not content.

The problem with that. The second halves are where the theses meet. Theses 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 18, 19, 20 and 23 of the first critique, and IV, V, XIV–XVII, XXI and XXIII of the second, all say the same thing in different ways: a theory whose founding idea is that human systems respond to how they are described must apply that idea to its own instruments and its own author. Take the second halves away and each thesis becomes a small point that is easy to concede. That is why so many of the reply's disagreements turn out, on inspection, to be agreements.

My answer. It is not shortening; it is substitution. The reply supplies a different thesis — one that can be answered from where its author stands — and answers that. Logicians have a name for this: ignoratio elenchi, refuting a claim other than the one made[93]. It is the most forgivable mistake in argument, because it is so often made in good faith. Here it is also the most important, because the claim substituted is, every time, the one without the respondent in it.

Reply. Brevity does force choices. But choices that fall the same way fifteen times are a finding. One dropped clause is economy. Fifteen show us where the author cannot see.

In one line: my theses were about the person reading the system; the reply is about the system — the reader has left the room again, taking the pen.

2 · The postponed centre

Thesis 12 said that a theory of human complexity with no account of power is just ordinary complex-systems theory with nicer adjectives. Thesis 13 turned Snowden's own criticism of power back on the designer of his categories. Thesis 23 named the "power gradient" and "consent to the harvest" as two of five things a more self-aware anthro-complexity needs. Compass Theses V, XIX and XXI named the observer who decides to leave things alone, the outsider who designs the "substrate", and the person who speaks for the crowd. Power was not one thesis among forty-seven. It was the centre of both critiques.

The reply's answer to that centre is, in the only words of his I shall quote directly: Power and agency in particular are deferred to a separate post[1].

That postponement is made at six places, and other roads in the reply lead to the same door.

  1. Thesis 12. His original post did not deal with power, which is different from agency. Postponed.
  2. Thesis 23. Two of my five additions are already present; the power gradient and consent to the harvest belong to the later post. Postponed.
  3. Thesis XVIII. Some structure is always needed, so the question is how much and decided by whom — which, he says, leads back to power. Postponed.
  4. Thesis XIX. Whether a company that also builds software is an outsider selling a product is left for later. Postponed.
  5. Thesis VIII. Using stories to train AI raises real questions of ownership, benefit and consent. Acknowledged, not answered. Postponed.
  6. The postscript. Power and agency are postponed again, with agency described as the three human capacities and power as what happens when those capacities meet position and resources. Postponed.

A seventh road — who pays for the software — stops just short of the door, at the assurance that the company stays alert to the risk. Alertness is how the powerful feel about their power. It is not an account of it.

Part II adds a reason why this matters more than it might seem. The designer's choice of frame is power in its deepest form: the power to shape what people notice about their own lives. Every road that ends at the postponed door is a road that leads to the designer's chair.

Question 11 — If you postpone a question, have you given it up?

The case for Snowden's view. Postponing a question can be a sign of taking it seriously — giving it room of its own. He has offered a working distinction (agency as capacities; power as capacities meeting position and resources) and promised more. A reply cannot be blamed for not being two replies.

The problem with that. Postponing is an action with consequences — what the philosopher J. L. Austin called a speech act[49]. It does not just delay. It decides that the other answers can be given now, without power, and power added later as an extra. That is exactly what Thesis 12 denied. Thesis 12 did not say power was a further topic; it said that without power the other answers are answers about something else.

My answer. A postponed centre is a conceded centre for as long as it is postponed. Every answer that ends "which leads back to power" is an answer not yet given — a signpost to a place where it will be. Until that place is built, the theses that point to it stand. That is simply what it means for a question to be open. The honest form of the postponement — and Snowden is an honest opponent — would be to say: on power, the theses stand until I answer them. His postscript nearly says it. I say it for him, and in Part IX I set out in advance the tests the later post will need to meet.

Reply. The distinction he offers is useful. It is also, very nearly, Thesis 12 itself: the three marks are capacities, and none of them is power. What is still owed is what Thesis 13 asked for: an account of the position and resources of whoever designs the categories, receives the patterns and carries the risk.

In one line: there is a hole in the middle of the reply, every road that reaches it says "later", and until later comes the theses stand.

3 · Blaming the reader

The third habit is quieter. At five points the reply puts the cause of disagreement in the reader rather than in the thing read:

  • The Cynefin diagram has been redrawn several times because readers took its boundaries and positions as claims it never made (XXIII).
  • The drift from theory to product is my construction (22).
  • Dual causality is my framing, not the method's (IV).
  • The I-Space thesis misreads Boisot and SenseMaker (VIII).
  • Several theses treat a brochure as an academic paper and an instrument still in development as a finished product (postscript).

Some of these may be right in detail, and Parts IV and V look at them in detail. But as a pattern they share a structure: the theory's own principle, withheld. Anthro-complexity says humans change the stories they tell about each other, and those stories change the people who hear them. A diagram is such a story. When readers take its boundaries as claims, the diagram has changed how they think — that is what diagrams do. To call this misreading is to say the story changed its readers in a way the storyteller did not intend, and that this is the readers' fault. Applied to anyone else's diagram, anthro-complexity would call that an effect of the diagram. Applied to its own, it calls it the reader's mistake.

Ralph Stacey, faced with the same thing — readers using his matrix as a map of zones — drew the opposite conclusion. He did not blame them. He decided the diagram was doing it, and stopped using it (Part II, section 11).

Question 12 — Is a writer responsible for how a diagram is read?

The case for Snowden's view. No. An author cannot control every reading. Some readers will misread anything. Holding authors responsible for every misreading would make communication impossible.

The problem with that. A diagram redrawn several times because readers keep drawing the same unintended conclusion is not being misread at random. It is being read reliably, in a way that tells us something about what it invites. Psychologists call this an affordance: what a thing invites you to do with it[50]. The Gestalt laws of perception show that the eye groups things by closeness, enclosure and alignment before thinking starts[51]. Draw a boundary between zones and it will be read as a boundary.

My answer. A writer is responsible for the readings a diagram reliably invites, though not for every reading it merely permits. That is the principle of Compass Thesis XXIII, and Snowden's own history of redrawing is evidence for it: redrawing was the right response, and it was a response to what the figure invited, not to readers' errors. So the redrawing should be recorded as the figure's errata — corrections made in public — rather than as a correction of readers. That is a small change of wording. It is also the whole difference between a theory that applies its central principle to itself and one that does not.

Reply. Communication would not become impossible. It would become accountable. The disputation format exists for exactly this: the author states a claim sharply, the critic says what he reads in it, and the record shows both.

A rejoinder that only attacks is no better than a reply that only postpones. Snowden concedes a lot, and it matters. Here it is, in full and without discount.

Norbert Elias
Power is a structural characteristic of every human relationship.

Norbert Elias

Sociologist (1897–1990) whose process sociology — The Civilizing Process (1939), What Is Sociology? (1970; English 1978) — replaced the image of individuals confronting "society" with figurations: webs of interdependent people whose balances of power shift over time. For Elias power is not a possession but a balance, present in every relationship, from parent and child to state and citizen.

Elias stands behind the complex responsive processes tradition (Stacey, Griffin, Shaw, Mowles) and behind Theses 4, 5 and 12. The rejoinder uses him to read the reply as a figuration — a pattern of what it takes up and what it leaves — and to frame the deferred post on power (Part VIII).

Ralph Stacey (1948–2021) developed, with Douglas Griffin and Patricia Shaw at the University of Hertfordshire, the theory of complex responsive processes of relating: organisations are not systems that managers stand outside and steer, but ongoing patterns of communication, power and evaluative choice among interdependent people. Strategy and change emerge in local interaction.

Stacey's analysis of five teleologies (with Griffin and Shaw, 2000) underlies Thesis 7 and Compass Thesis IV. His "Stacey Matrix", which he later set aside because it was being used as a tool for categorising situations rather than as an aid to thinking, is itself a precedent for a figure abandoned because of what readers took from it.

Literally "ignorance of the refutation": Aristotle's name (Sophistical Refutations) for an argument that proves a conclusion other than the one in dispute. It is the most forgivable fallacy because it is so often made in good faith — the respondent genuinely believes he is answering the question.

The rejoinder's charge (Quaestio IV) is not that the reply argues in bad faith but that it systematically substitutes a thesis it can answer from where it stands — the descriptive half — for the thesis argued, whose force lay in its reflexive clause. Fifteen instances are tabulated in Table 1.

J. L. Austin (How to Do Things with Words, 1962) distinguished what an utterance says from what it does — promising, warning, appointing, naming. John Searle systematised the theory. A speech act has force independent of its content.

The rejoinder treats the reply's deferral of power as a speech act (Quaestio V). It does not merely postpone; it allocates, deciding that the other answers can be given now without power and power added later. That allocation is what Thesis 12 denied. Affordance

James J. Gibson's term (The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception, 1979) for the possibilities for action that an environment offers an animal: a surface affords standing, a handle grasping. Don Norman carried the term into design: a well-designed object makes its affordances visible.

A diagram's boundaries afford reading as boundaries. When readers consistently infer claims a figure "never made", the figure is not being misread at random; its affordances are being read reliably. The rejoinder (Quaestio VI) argues that a text is answerable for the readings it reliably affords — the principle of Compass Thesis XXIII.
