Gestalt grouping

Max Wertheimer's laws of perceptual organisation (1923) — proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation, common region — describe how the eye groups elements into wholes before any deliberate interpretation. A line around a region makes it a region; things placed together are seen as belonging together.

For diagrams this means that an author cannot draw a boundary between domains and disclaim its being read as a claim about domains. The grouping is part of what is drawn. Compass Thesis XXIII asked that honest diagrams mark the difference between the author's drawn assertions and the eye's inferred groupings.

The rejoinder's first and most general finding. The reply answers the descriptive half of each thesis and drops the reflexive half, with a regularity too steady to be accident. The rejoinder attributes this not to bad faith but to the predicate of The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy: we see the constraints of others and are blind to our own. The reflexive clause is always the clause about the reply's author, and so always the one that cannot be seen from where he stands.

Part IV Humans Are Not Estuaries, Argued Again

In short. This Part goes back through the twenty-four theses of the first critique, in the groups the reply used. For each, I set out Snowden's answer as strongly as I can and then respond. The main findings: his sailor image supports Thesis 8 (R5); the story fragment treats people as closed whatever the theory says (R6); safe-to-fail experiments move goal-setting up a level rather than removing it (R7); comparing categories to a language fails where power lies (R8); indirect measurement cannot have both rigour and consent (R9); the company's own brochure is evidence of a more computational practice (R10); the triangle erases one kind of outlier before any model is involved (R11, R12); two of the reply's answers contradict each other (R13); and in human affairs, announcing the tide helps make it (R14).

Question 13 — Does "nobody said humans are estuaries" answer Thesis 8? (R5)

The case for Snowden's view. Nobody in the anthro-complexity literature has claimed that humans are estuaries. The estuarine framework maps systems that include humans, where human and non-human things act on each other[12]. A title that denies something nobody said is attacking a straw man, and Thesis 8 inherits the mistake.

The problem with that. Thesis 8 did not say anyone claimed humans are estuaries. It said the guiding metaphors of the practice — tide, estuary, river, wave, waterfall — come from natural systems that do not respond to being observed, and that each one puts the reader outside the reading. A title of the form "X are not Y" can deny an implication as well as a statement. The philosopher Max Black showed that a strong metaphor works by carrying a whole set of associations from one thing to another, whether or not anyone says the two are the same[42]. The philosopher of science Mary Hesse added that every model has a "neutral" part — the features nobody has checked yet — and that is where it does its unnoticed work[43].

My answer. Snowden's own image proves the point. The reader, he says, is placed inside the metaphor, as a sailor is inside the tide. Very well: what is the relationship between a sailor and a tide? The sailor reads the tide. The tide does not read the sailor. The sailor's skill is to anticipate a motion that does not care about him and does not change because he is seen to anticipate it. He is inside the tide as a cork is inside the sea — carried, not answered. That is exactly the relationship Thesis 8 described. The reader is inside, but the system is pictured as something that does not respond to being read. In human systems, the tide is other sailors, and they are watching the one who says he can read them.

In Hesse's terms: the estuary's useful likenesses (many actors, mixing flows, things that change fast and slow) are real. Its acknowledged differences (estuaries have no intentions) are noted. But its unchecked likeness — the one doing the hidden work — is that the estuary does not learn the map. Every one of the guiding metaphors shares it. That is what the title denied.

Part II gives this a history. Fludd's astrologer also lives under the sky he reads. But the sky does not read the astrologer, and the person whose horoscope he casts does not draw the chart. Being "inside" a medium that cannot respond to you is not participation. It is the astrologer's seat with water in it.

Reply. The metaphors do describe systems that include humans; Thesis 8 never denied it. The question is whether the estuary, as a picture, can show humans reading it back. A system full of people reading the mapper is not an estuary with people in it. It is a hall of mirrors with water on the floor.

In one line: the sailor is inside the tide, but the tide is not inside the sailor — and that asymmetry is the whole of Thesis 8.

Question 14 — Do multiple identities answer the charge of "closed persons"? (Theses 4–5; R6)

The case for Snowden's view. Anthro-complexity does not assume complete, closed individuals. Identity is multiple — each of us is many people in different settings — and spread out. The unit of study is not the person but the story fragment. "The people remain distinct" was aimed at Karen Barad's view that people dissolve into relations; people are partly made by their relationships but not reducible to them[34][33].

The problem with that. Having many identities is not the same as being formed in relationships. Someone with ten identities is still the holder of them; the identities are still properties — plural now — of one container that has them before any relationship begins. Elias's "closed person" was never a person with one identity; it was a person whose identities, however many, were his own before they were anyone else's[25]. The closed person can be very full inside.

My answer. A dilemma, and then a point about the fragment.

The dilemma. The reply takes the idea of multiple identity from Alicia Juarrero[32]. In Juarrero's work, what gives a complex whole its identity is a web of context-dependent constraints — interdependencies that bind parts into a whole and keep it going. If anthro-complexity takes identity from there, then identities are formed in relationship: they are not capacities a person brings to relationships, but patterns relationships create. Then Thesis 4 holds: what makes human complexity different lies in how people are formed together, not in properties they carry. If, on the other hand, identities are capacities people carry — one of the "three marks" — then they exist before relationships, and Thesis 5 holds: anthro-complexity starts from separate parts. The reply cannot take identity from Juarrero and keep the three marks as capacities. One has to go.

The fragment. The most important sentence in this part of the reply is that the unit of study is the story fragment. Think about what a fragment is in practice. Someone tells a short story about something that happened, then, alone, rates it on a set of triangles and sliders. The fragment arrives in the database with its teller's ratings attached and no one else's. But for Mead, the meaning of a gesture is not in the gesture; it is in the social act that the gesture and the response complete together[27]. A story told to no one in particular and rated by its teller alone is a gesture cut off before anyone responds. The unit of study is therefore exactly the closed person — not as a belief about people, but as a procedure applied to them. The theory may be about relationships. The unit is not.

I owe one admission. In Humans Are Not Estuaries itself I agreed, with the sociologist Margaret Archer, that people do remain distinct: persons with powers of their own, who can say no; and that Snowden was right to reject Barad[2]. That stands. It narrows the dispute as it should. The question is not whether people can be reduced to relationships — they cannot — but whether what makes human complexity special lies in what people have or in how people are formed. Archer's persons are formed in relationship and then have powers of their own. The fragment captures the powers and throws away the forming.

Replies. To "partly made by relationships": agreed; the dispute is over which part does the distinguishing work. To "the unit is the fragment, not the person": that is the point. A fragment is a person's act with its audience removed. A method built on fragments is built on gestures without responses.

In one line: a person with ten identities is still a container, and a story rated alone is still a gesture with no reply.

Question 15 — Do safe-to-fail experiments remove the planner's mindset? (Theses 6–7, IV; R7)

The case for Snowden's view. In Stacey, Griffin and Shaw's terms, a "rationalist" mindset means moving towards a goal chosen by reason[28]. Safe-to-fail experiments exist precisely because you cannot choose an outcome in advance: you run several small experiments at once, build on what works and stop what does not, because you cannot know beforehand which will work. The practitioner acts with intent but without a chosen outcome. Thesis 7 confuses intent with goal-setting, and the "dual causality" of Compass Thesis IV is my framing.

The problem with that. As published, the practice asks the designer to say, for each experiment, in advance, what would count as success and failure, how each would be recognised, and what would be done to amplify or dampen it[13]. The outcome is unknown. The way of judging outcomes is chosen in advance by the person who designs the set of experiments.

My answer. Safe-to-fail does not remove the planner's mindset; it moves it up a level. At the level of outcomes, there is no chosen goal. At the level of judgement, there is a chosen frame: success and failure criteria, signs to watch, actions to take, and the limit of acceptable loss that makes an experiment "safe". Someone chooses all that, by reason, in advance, and the system's behaviour is then sorted by it. In Stacey's terms that is exactly dual causality: the system is allowed to unfold; the person who designs and reads the experiments keeps a planner's relationship to it. The goal-setting has moved from the destination to the sieve.

Then the question Thesis V asked: safe for whom? "Safe" is not a property of an experiment. It is a judgement about whose losses are acceptable, and that judgement reflects a position. An experiment safe for the organisation may not be safe for the team that runs it, the community it is run in, or the person whose story becomes its evidence. The word "safe" in the name of the practice is a promise made by the designer on behalf of the people who will carry the risk. That is Thesis 13 by another road — and it ends at the postponed door.

Finally, the reply concedes Thesis 6: Cynefin changes the people who use it. But you cannot concede Thesis 6 and reject Thesis 7. If the framework changes its users, then the person designing the experiments is inside the system being experimented on. Announcing success criteria is a gesture the system responds to; teams learn what "amplify" will look like and produce it. The planner's frame is not only held; it is learned by the system, which reorganises around it. That is what Stacey called transformative causality — and the theory, by keeping the practitioner's frame outside, cannot see it.

Reply. Intent is not goal-setting; agreed, and Thesis 7 never confused them. The dispute is whether the frame for judging intent is subject to the same responsiveness the theory claims for human systems. The reply says the outcome is open. The thesis says the sieve is closed.

In one line: the outcome is unknown, but the sieve is chosen — the goal-setting has not gone, it has moved.

Question 16 — Does mapping by insiders meet the standard of 勢? (Thesis 9)

The case for Snowden's view. He agrees with Thesis 9 that a pattern mapped from outside is a landscape, not a 勢 shì — the "propensity" or strategic potential of a situation — and answers that estuarine mapping is done by insiders[81].

The problem with that. In François Jullien's account, shì is not satisfied by who is on the payroll. It requires that the situation include the strategist's own position — that the person reading the propensity be one of the things whose propensity is read, and that the reading change it.

My answer. The concession is bigger than the reply allows, and the remedy smaller. Bigger, because if a pattern mapped from outside is a landscape, then every map that is pooled, compared across sites, reported to a client or published is, from that moment, a landscape. Insiders may draw it; it is read from outside the moment it leaves the room. Smaller, because "insiders" is not either/or. Insiders map on a canvas the method supplies, in a session run by a facilitator trained in the method, using categories the method defines — what counts as a constraint, how its cost of change is scored. Their positions enter the map as data. The method's position enters as the frame. 勢 needs the second in the picture too.

The Chinese military classics Jullien draws on make this plain. The general who reads shì is not a surveyor; he is one force among others, and the enemy reads him as he reads the ground[82]. A map of forces that leaves out the force created by the map — who made it, using what method, and who will act on it — is a landscape with insiders' fingerprints on it.

Reply. This does not ask for an impossible completeness. It asks for one line on every map: this is the method, this is the convenor, and this is their stake. In the 道理勢 scheme I use across my work, that line is where 理 — the grain of things — is read by someone who is himself in the grain, and where 勢 begins.

Question 17 — Does knowing where "constitutive constraint" comes from answer Thesis 10?

The case for Snowden's view. The difference between governing constraints and constitutive constraints comes from Juarrero, whose work is the source of Cynefin's whole theory of constraint. The thesis accuses anthro-complexity of lacking an idea it has always had.

The problem with that. Thesis 10 had two parts, and the second was the thesis: constitutive constraints — the ones that make a community what it is — are reproduced when people follow them, and when someone maps them.

My answer. Knowing where an idea comes from answers neither part. Having a concept in your family tree is not the same as using it in your tools. The test is practical: when a group maps its constraints — names them, puts them on a canvas, scores how hard each is to change — is the mapping itself treated as one of the acts that reproduces or changes those constraints? A group that writes its unspoken rule on a whiteboard has done something to the rule. It has made a hidden constraint visible, and in doing so has either weakened it (it can now be negotiated) or strengthened it (it is now official). The philosopher Ian Hacking called this a "looping effect" when it happens to categories of people[36]; it happens to constraints too. An estuarine map is not a photograph of constraints; it is an intervention in them. The reply does not mention this, because the second part of the thesis was dropped (Table 1). The idea is in the theory's ancestry and missing from its procedure — exactly what The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy found when it asked whether "governing" and "enabling" were enough to describe the rooms in dispute[4].

Reply. If good practitioners already know this, let it be written into the method as a step. A practice that knows its mapping changes what it maps, and does not say so in its method, has an unspoken rule of its own.

Question 18 — Can a "constructor" that changes in other ways rescue the idea? (Thesis 11)

The case for Snowden's view. In constructor theory — a programme in physics developed by David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto — a constructor is something that causes a change and stays able to cause it again, like a catalyst[37][38]. It can be changed in other ways while keeping that ability. And constructors are one kind of actor in anthro-complexity, not a model of people.

The problem with that. Thesis 11's point was not that constructors cannot change. It was that in human affairs everyone is changed by acting. The ability a person uses is altered by using it.

My answer. The rescue gives the thesis away. If constructors are one kind of actor and not a model of people, then the idea supplies a label for the non-human parts of human systems — rituals, objects, institutions — and nothing special about humans. That is exactly what Thesis 11 said. Gregory Bateson's levels of learning explain why: every time we learn to do something, we also learn something about the kind of situation we are in, so our ability to do it next time has changed[35]. A teacher is not the same teacher after teaching a class; a negotiator who closes a deal has a different ability to close the next. Deutsch and Marletto's constructors are an ideal that real catalysts only approach, and the ideal is exactly what fails for people. And the best candidates for human "constructors" — the ritual, the institution, the method — are the constitutive constraints of Thesis 10, which change as they are used. There is no actor in human affairs that is not, to some degree, changed by acting. The method itself is one.

In one line: in human affairs every catalyst is also changed — including the method.

Part IV, continued Power, Signs, Machines and Tides

Question 19 — Is a set of rating categories like a language? (Theses 12, 13, 18; R8)

The case for Snowden's view. Every language is a frame its speakers did not choose, yet speaking is not coercion. Grammar limits what can be said without dictating what is said. A set of rating categories is a small, purpose-built language for describing experience. To call it a site of power is to call every vocabulary a tyranny.

The problem with that. The comparison holds where it is harmless and fails at the three points Thesis 13 pressed on.

My answer. A language and a set of categories differ in three ways — authorship, interest and the ability to change it — and those three are what make a frame a site of power.

Authorship. Nobody wrote English. A set of categories has authors: named designers, working to a brief, for a client. The comparison with language works only because language is the classic example of a frame with no author. Once a frame has an author, it is not like a language; it is like a designed language, and the history of designed languages is not reassuring. Orwell's Newspeak in Nineteen Eighty-Four is frightening not because it is a language but because it was designed to make certain thoughts unsayable[48]. I suspect no such intent. I only point out that the comparison, run properly, points the other way: designed frames are exactly the ones whose design must be declared.

Interest. A language belongs to everyone. A set of categories is commissioned and paid for; the patterns it produces go to whoever paid; and someone carries the risk of acting on them. Thesis 13 named all three — designs the categories, receives the pattern, carries the remaining risk. The reply answers the first, by comparison, and leaves out the second and third (Table 1).

Change. Speakers change their language as they use it. Mikhail Bakhtin showed that every word we use is half someone else's and is constantly being given new tones[45]; his colleague Valentin Voloshinov called the sign an arena where social struggle happens[46]. A storyteller cannot change the triangle while placing her dot on it. Her only way to change it is to refuse — to tick "not applicable" where that is offered, or to stop. The language she speaks there has one grammar and no grammarians among its speakers.

And even language is not innocent. Pierre Bourdieu showed that the language no speaker chose is still a market in which some accents count for more than others, and that "proper" language is the language of those already entitled to speak[47]. Pressed, the comparison does not clear the categories. It charges language too.

Interpretation. The reply adds that the storyteller's own rating is the act of interpretation — the "interpretant" in the philosopher Charles Peirce's terms — and that the analyst works on patterns of ratings, not on stories. But in Peirce, interpretation is not a single act. It is the effect a sign has on someone, and that effect is itself a sign calling for further interpretation, without end[44]. The storyteller's rating is one interpretation. The pattern across a thousand ratings is a new sign, whose shape — a scatter on a triangle, a cluster, a "direction" — was fixed by whoever designed the capture and the display. The analyst's reading of that pattern is the interpretation that leads to action. Saying the analyst reads patterns, not stories, does not take the analyst out of interpretation. It says the analyst interprets a sign the storytellers never saw. That is what Thesis 18 meant: the in-between step is where the designer sits — the curator of Part II.

Reply. Not every vocabulary is a tyranny. Every designed vocabulary carries its designer's position, and the cure is not to abolish vocabularies but to name their designers, share their revision with the people who use them, and let those people see the pattern first. Those are three of the five threads of the Tidal Loom (Part VIII).

In one line: nobody wrote English, somebody wrote the triangle, and the comparison breaks exactly where the power is.

Question 20 — Do more abstract categories make self-rating more rigorous? (Thesis 14; R9)

The case for Snowden's view. Yes. The more abstract the categories — triangles of qualities rather than leading questions — the less the storyteller can guess what the analyst wants, the less she can game the instrument, and the more her rating reflects her experience rather than her expectations. This is indirect ("oblique") measurement: measuring sideways so the measure does not become a target. It is a real improvement on surveys that announce their purpose.

The problem with that. Abstraction does not remove the frame the storyteller did not choose. It hides it.

My answer. I call this the oblique dilemma. Indirect measurement protects the instrument from gaming by making sure the storyteller does not know what her rating will mean to the analyst. Either she knows, or she does not.

  • If she knows what each corner of the triangle means for the client's purposes, the protection against gaming is gone, and the instrument falls under Goodhart's law — which the reply accepts at Thesis XVII.
  • If she does not know, then the meaning that counts — what her dot will be taken to mean, by whom, for what — belongs entirely to the analyst, and her agreement to the use of her story is agreement to something whose meaning was kept from her by design.

Indirect measurement cannot have both rigour and informed consent. The more rigorous it is against gaming, the less the storyteller knows; the less she knows, the further interpretation has moved from her to the analyst. So the claim that abstraction increases rigour is true — and it proves Thesis 14 rather than answering it. Rigour, in this design, is bought with the storyteller's ignorance of what her own rating means. That can be a reasonable trade in many settings. It is not a neutral one, and it should be declared as a trade.

There is another cost. Researchers on participatory sense-making argue that meaning is made between people as they coordinate their interaction[40]. An abstract triangle, given to a storyteller alone after she has told her story, asks her to make meaning with an instrument instead of with another person. The more abstract it is, the more of that meaning-making it demands — and the more it replaces an interlocutor's response with the designer's categories.

Reply. Her own words are kept, and that is a real advance, which Thesis 14 acknowledged. But at scale it is not the words that make the patterns; it is the coordinates (Question 22). The words are the archive. The dots are the evidence.

In one line: indirect measurement buys rigour with ignorance — she cannot game what she cannot see, and cannot fully consent to it either.

Question 21 — Is there evidence the practice is becoming more computer-driven? (Thesis 15; R10)

The case for Snowden's view. None. Software in the practice shows patterns to people; it does not replace their judgement. The theory says the brain is not a computer; the practice uses computers to help people see their own experience at scale. No contradiction, no drift.

The problem with that. The company's own material. The SwarmCompass brochure, as recorded in The Compass and the Loom, lists among its deliverables the creation of "epistemically balanced & multi-perceptive training data sets" for further AI-based automation, and sells "human-AI swarm intelligence"[6][3].

My answer. The evidence the reply says does not exist was published by the reply's author's company. A deliverable described as training data for further automation is, on any reading, a step towards a more computational practice: people's noticing is gathered not only to be shown back to people but to train systems that will notice in their place. That is what I called the harvest loop[2]. Elsewhere the reply concedes that training AI raises real questions of ownership, benefit and consent. It cannot both concede the questions and deny the practice that raises them.

Perhaps the brochure overstates, or the deliverable has not been built. Then the brochure makes a claim about the practice that the practice does not support — which is the subject of Question 38. Either the brochure is evidence of computation, or it is a marketing claim that is not true. It cannot be neither.

In the terms of Part II: this is Kepler's ruler being handed to a machine. The Keplerian half of anthro-complexity is growing; the Fluddian half stays where it was, untested.

Question 22 — Is Thesis 16 simply wrong because the method shows the outliers? (R11)

The case for Snowden's view. Yes, it is wrong outright. SenseMaker was designed against the tyranny of the average. Its displays show every dot; outliers are not averaged away; people use the method precisely to find the unusual story at the edge. Far from erasing the tails of the distribution, it makes them visible.

The problem with that. Thesis 16 is conditional: repeated learning on harvested stories erases the tails; an instrument that feeds a model can starve itself. It is about a feedback loop, not a chart.

My answer, in three steps.

First, the reply answers a different thesis. Nobody disputes that a scatter plot shows its outliers. The thesis is about what happens when the stories are fed to a model, and the model's sense of what is typical shapes what is collected, flagged or noticed next. The mechanism is well documented. In 2024, Shumailov and colleagues showed in Nature that AI models trained repeatedly on data produced by earlier models gradually lose the rare cases: each finite sample under-represents them, each model trained on that sample learns even fewer, and so on, until the model knows only a narrow version of the typical[56]. Thesis 16 applied that to an instrument whose own brochure proposes training data for automation (Question 21). The reply does not discuss the mechanism.

Second, visible is not protected. A rare case on a chart is one the analyst may see. A protected rare case is one the loop between instrument and model cannot thin out. The first is a feature of a display; the second is a property of a feedback loop. An instrument can do the first perfectly and fail the second completely, because the thinning happens upstream — in which categories are kept for the next round, which patterns are flagged, which stories are invited. There is a well-known way to guard against this: Good–Turing estimation, developed by Alan Turing and I. J. Good, which estimates how much you are not seeing from how many things you have seen only once[57]. The reply mentions no such discipline.

Third, and most important, the triangle erases one kind of extreme before any model is involved. On a triangle, a storyteller places one dot whose three coordinates add up to one. A story in which all three qualities were intensely present and a story in which none was present at all both land in the middle. The spread of intensity — how much of anything there was — is not thinned by repetition; it is removed by geometry. The overwhelming story and the empty one look the same. That is Thesis 17, and it shows that Theses 16 and 17 were really one thesis in two forms.

Figure 2 — The triangle records only relative weight. A story where every quality was intense and a story where none was present land on the same point. The difference — how much was going on — is lost by the geometry itself, before any analysis or model is involved.

Reply. The method is designed against the average of what it captures. Thesis 16 is about what it does not capture, or captures and then feeds to a learner. A method can be against the tyranny of the average and still exposed to the tyranny of the typical.

In one line: an outlier on the screen is not an outlier in the loop — the model does not read the chart, it reads what the chart was made from.

Question 23 — Is a deliberate trade-off an answer to the charge? (Thesis 17, XVIII; R12)

The case for Snowden's view. Separate rating scales invite people to say yes to everything — the well-known "acquiescence bias". The triangle forces a choice of relative weight among three qualities in one situation. It does not ask how strong each was. The trade-off is a design decision, not a flaw.

The problem with that. Thesis 17 said the triangle builds a trade-off into its geometry and cannot tell strong-in-everything from weak-in-everything. The reply says it asks for relative weight, not strength. That is the thesis, restated as a virtue.

My answer. A deliberate trade-off is a confirmed trade-off — and a deliberate one carries three obligations the reply does not meet.

Say what is lost. Designs that ask for relative weight are what psychologists call ipsative: each person's scores add up to a fixed total. The research on ipsative scores is decades old and clear. You cannot compare them across people for overall level; the scores are forced to pull against each other; standard statistical techniques give distorted results[58][59]. None of this is a reason never to use forced choice. It is the known price. A design that pays it on purpose should say so, so that nobody reading a cluster near one corner thinks the quality at that corner was strong, when it was only stronger than the other two.

Use the right statistics. A point on a triangle is a composition — a set of parts of a whole. Since Karl Pearson's warning in 1897 about false correlations between ratios, and John Aitchison's work in the 1980s, statisticians have known that such data need special treatment (log-ratio transforms) before averages, spreads and clusters are calculated, or the results can be artefacts of the constraint[61][60]. Whether SenseMaker's analytics use such methods, I do not know; the reply does not say. A design whose trade-off is deliberate should say whether its statistics respect the geometry it chose.

Consider the alternatives. The choice is not just between separate scales and a triangle. Forced-choice designs can be scored with Thurstonian models that recover overall level from comparisons[62]. Separate scales can spot the yes-to-everything respondent as a pattern and allow for it. Most simply, a triangle with one extra slider — how much of any of this was there? — would keep relative weight and restore the lost extreme at the cost of one more mark.

And Compass Thesis XVIII. The reply says the triangle does not try to capture the combination of salience, sapience and sentience that Snowden calls acumen; it only asks for their relative weight. But if acumen is the combination — all three together — then a relative-weight instrument is the one instrument that cannot register it: the person in whom all three are high and the person in whom all three are absent land on the same spot. An instrument for acumen built on a triangle cannot tell the sharp from the inert.

Reply. Separate scales have biases too; entirely agreed. No instrument is innocent. The thesis did not say separate scales were better; it said the triangle "in that respect" loses more. The respect is strength. The reply concedes it.

In one line: in the middle of the triangle the overwhelmed and the unmoved sit together, and the pattern cannot tell them apart.

Question 24 — Do "direction of travel" measures escape Goodhart's law? (Thesis 19, XVII; R13)

The case for Snowden's view. Thesis 19 assumes an instrument that never changes. SenseMaker uses vector measures — "more stories like these, fewer like those" — rather than targets. By separating measures from targets, you can use one without turning it into the other.

The problem with that. Answering Compass Thesis XVII, the reply agrees that any instrument that publishes its findings enters the loop of measure, target, respond and drift, and that its time of good fit is the time to be most careful.

My answer. The two answers cannot both stand. If vector measures escape Goodhart, the agreement with XVII goes too far; if every published measure falls under Goodhart, the answer to Thesis 19 fails. The second is right, for a reason the reply's own terms supply. A vector is a direction: more of these, fewer of those. A direction is a target in the only sense Goodhart and Campbell need — something whose movement will be rewarded[52][53]. Once people learn that a certain kind of story is wanted "more", they tell more stories of that kind, or tell their stories in that way. Robert Lucas made the same point about economic policy: people adjust to the rule[54]. George Soros made it about markets: what people believe about a measure changes what is measured[55]. Thesis 19 put it in a line: human systems learn what the camera wants. A vector is a camera with an arrow on it.

Reply. Vector measures are harder to game than levels at first; agreed. That is what "the time of good fit" means. The agreement with XVII is the right answer. It should be the answer to Thesis 19 too, and the instrument's documentation should say when its good fit is expected to end and how that will be noticed.

Question 25 — Is the turning of the tide what matters? (Thesis 20; R14)

The case for Snowden's view. Kairos — the right moment — is a real feature of time. Being seen to wait matters, but it is only one part of how a tide turns. The turning is what matters: the skill is to recognise it and act.

The problem with that. The thesis was its second half: in human affairs the tide turns partly because someone visible was seen waiting for it. Granting that as "one part" and going back to the turning drops it (Table 1).

My answer, from the most famous tide in English. In Act 4 of Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Brutus tells Cassius:

There is a tide in the affairs of men,
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
Omitted, all the voyage of their life
Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
On such a full sea are we now afloat,
And we must take the current when it serves,
Or lose our ventures.[85]

This is not a reading of a tide. It is an argument — against Cassius's better judgement — for marching to Philippi rather than waiting for the enemy to come to them. Brutus names the flood in order to make it: the naming persuades Cassius, the army marches, and the tide Brutus announced becomes the tide they ride. It carries them to defeat and death. Brutus misread the situation, and his misreading, spoken by the man everyone was watching, created the very movement that destroyed him. That is Thesis 20 as tragedy: in human affairs the tide is partly made by the person seen to read it, and a confident reading can manufacture the flood it claims to have found.

That is why the second half is not one part among many. In a real estuary the tide turns regardless of who watches. In a human system, announcing the turn is one of its causes. An instrument that tells an organisation "the tide is turning here" is not reporting the moment; it is intervening in it. A practice of human complexity has to answer for the floods it announces.

In one line: Brutus did not read the tide; he announced it — and the announcement carried him to Philippi.

Question 26 — Is the drift from theory to product just my invention? (Theses 21–22)

The case for Snowden's view. The distinction between human and other complexity makes the method and the institution possible; it does not undermine them. The path from theory to product is drawn by the critic, not followed by the theory. The risk of institutionalisation is real, but a risk is a warning, not a certainty.

The problem with that. Thesis 22 never said the drift was certain. It said the drift is the path along which self-awareness is lost. A path is not a destiny. Admitting the risk is real is admitting the path exists.

My answer. The drift is in the public record, not in my imagination. It runs: a framework for making sense of situations[15]; a software platform for collecting stories[14]; trademarked commercial products, which the reply confirms SenseMaker and SwarmCompass to be; a brochure selling "human-AI swarm intelligence" and training data for automation[6]; a strategy framework launched on the company blog[7]. Each step can be defended. Together they are the path. I did not draw it. The company walked it and published each step.

On the "three jobs" (Thesis 21): the reply says the theory makes the method and the institution possible. That is the problem, not the answer. The institutional job of a distinction is to draw a border — between this school and its neighbours, between people trained in the method and people not. The sociologist Thomas Gieryn called this boundary-work: the effort by which a field separates itself from what it is not, and gains authority in doing so[98]. Elias and Scotson showed that every such border creates insiders and outsiders, and that insiders tend to describe outsiders by their worst members[26]. The reply's complaint that a conversation between Stacey's school and Cynefin has been refused is itself boundary-work: a border described from one side. The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy was partly an attempt at that conversation, and it found that each school saw the other's constraints and not its own[4].

Reply. A warning is not a certainty; agreed. Then build the warning into the institution: a public list of corrections for each instrument; a named point where self-awareness is checked; a stated answer to the question of consent. A warning that is not built in is just a mood.

Question 27 — Are two of my five additions already there? (Thesis 23)

The case for Snowden's view. Multiple identity (via Juarrero) and constitutive constraint are already in the theory; "the reading of the reader" and the power gradient belong to Stacey's school; consent to the harvest will be dealt with alongside power.

The problem with that. Being in the theory is not the same as working in the instruments (Questions 14 and 17).

My answer. How the reply sorts the five additions is itself the finding. The two it says are already present are the two that can be held without changing what any instrument does. The three it sends elsewhere — the reading of the reader (to Stacey's school), the power gradient (postponed), consent to the harvest (postponed) — are the three that would change the instruments: who sees the pattern first, who can change the frame, what the storyteller agrees to. The self-aware programme has been accepted in principle and declined in practice. That is Thesis 21 in miniature.

Question 28 — Has the recognition test, once accepted, been passed? (Thesis 24)

The reply accepts the recognition test and connects it, rightly, to the Laozi. That is the most important concession in the reply, because it gives us a test the reply can be held to. Part VIII holds it there, and asks whether a method-owner recognising the critic's proposal as "our method" passes the test or turns it upside down.

Newspeak

Newspeak

In George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), the official language of Oceania, engineered to narrow the range of thought by removing the words in which heresy could be expressed. Its appendix, "The Principles of Newspeak", describes vocabulary design as a political act.

The rejoinder (Q. XIII) does not suggest any such intent behind signifier sets. It uses Newspeak to show that the reply's analogy, run correctly, points the other way: language is harmless as a frame because it has no author; designed frames are precisely the ones whose design must be declared.

Bakhtin: the double-voiced word
Every word is half someone else's — and being re-accented.

Bakhtin: the double-voiced word

Mikhail Bakhtin ("Discourse in the Novel", 1934–35; Speech Genres, 1986) held that language is heteroglot — stratified into many social voices — and that every utterance is addressed, anticipates a response, and re-accents words that already belong to others. Speakers do not merely use language; they contest and transform it in use.

The rejoinder (Q. XIII) contrasts this living revisability with the signifier set, which the narrator cannot re-accent while placing her dot. Humans Are Not Estuaries also used Bakhtin's addressivity to name what the fragment loses: to whom the story was told.

Voloshinov: the sign as arena

Valentin Voloshinov (Marxism and the Philosophy of Language, 1929; English 1973), associated with Bakhtin's circle, argued that the sign is "an arena of the class struggle": different social groups use the same signs with different accents, and the dominant group strives to make the sign uniaccentual, eternal and above conflict.

Applied to the reply's analogy (Q. XIII): even language, the frame no speaker chose, is a site of contest. A signifier set fixed by its designers and closed to its speakers' re-accenting is a sign made uniaccentual by construction.

Bourdieu: the linguistic market

Pierre Bourdieu (Language and Symbolic Power, 1991) treated language as a market in which utterances have unequal value depending on the speaker's position and the legitimacy of their speech. "Legitimate language" is the language of those already authorised to speak; symbolic power works through the misrecognition of this arbitrariness as natural.

The rejoinder (Q. XIII): pressed, the analogy of language does not exonerate the signifier set; it indicts language too. A frame no one authored can still be a site of power. A frame someone authored is a site of power twice over.

The reply says the narrator's signification is the interpretant and the analyst works on patterns. The rejoinder (Q. Oblique measurement

A principle of SenseMaker design: rather than ask people directly about the outcome of interest, ask them to signify their experience on abstract dimensions whose purpose is not transparent, so that they cannot easily game the instrument. The reply adds that more abstract signification is more rigorous, and that capture is built into operational systems.

The rejoinder grants the logic and names its price (Q. XIV): obliquity protects against Goodhart by keeping the narrator ignorant of what her sign will mean. It also distinguishes "oblique" from "weak" (Q. XXXIII): indirect, ambient, continuous capture is not light coupling.

Either the narrator knows, and Goodhart returns — or she does not, and consent is uninformed.

The oblique dilemma (R9)

The rejoinder's formulation of Thesis 14's consequence. Obliquity works by withholding from the narrator what her signification will mean to the analyst. If she knows, the protection against gaming is lost. If she does not, the decisive interpretant is the analyst's and her consent to the use of her story is consent to an act whose meaning was withheld by design.

Obliquity cannot have both rigour and informed consent. That is a defensible trade in many settings, but not a neutral one. It must be declared as a trade — test 5 of the ten tests for the deferred post.

Model collapse
Train on your own outputs and the tails disappear.

Model collapse

Shumailov, Shumaylov, Zhao, Papernot, Anderson and Gal (Nature, 2024) showed that generative models trained recursively on data produced by earlier models progressively lose the tails of the original distribution. Each finite sample under-represents rare events; each model trained on it learns thinner tails; the process compounds until the model converges on a narrow version of the typical.

Thesis 16 applied this mechanism to a weak-signal instrument coupled to a model. The reply's answer — the method makes tails visible — does not address the coupling (Q. XVI; R11). A tail on the screen is not a tail in the loop.

Developed by Alan Turing and I. J. Good at Bletchley Park and published by Good (1953): the total probability of all species not yet observed in a sample can be estimated from the number of species observed exactly once. It is the founding technique for reasoning about the unseen from the seen.

The Compass and the Loom's "Turing's Glass" makes it a discipline; Compass XIII credits Turing with measuring "the mass of the unseen". The rejoinder (Q. XVI): an instrument that wishes to protect its tails must estimate what it is not seeing. Visibility of the sampled tail is no substitute.

The characteristic SenseMaker signifier: a triangle with a quality at each vertex; the narrator places a single dot to show the relative weight of the three in her story. The dot's position is a set of barycentric coordinates — three non-negative numbers that sum to one.

Thesis 17: the geometry builds in a zero-sum trade-off and cannot tell strong-in-all from weak-in-all, which both fall at the centre. Concept
Ipsative measurement
Scores that sum to a constant for each respondent.
Turn over ↻
Ipsative measurement

From Latin ipse, "self": measures in which each respondent's scores are relative to her own other scores — forced rankings, forced choices, allocations of a fixed sum. Hicks (1970) and Clemans (1966) set out the consequences: ipsative scores cannot be compared across respondents for absolute level; their intercorrelations are forced toward the negative; standard factor analysis is distorted.

A triad is ipsative by construction. The rejoinder (Q. XVII) does not object to forced choice; it asks that the known price be declared, so that a cluster near a vertex is not read as strength when it shows only relative strength.

Compositional data
Parts of a whole need their own geometry.
Turn over ↻
Compositional data

Data in which each observation is a vector of non-negative parts summing to a constant — proportions, percentages, barycentric coordinates. Such data live on a simplex, not in ordinary Euclidean space, and raw means, variances and correlations computed on them can be artefacts of the constraint.

John Aitchison's log-ratio methods (1982, 1986) are the standard remedy. The rejoinder (Q. XVII) asks, without presuming the answer, whether SenseMaker's cluster and pattern analytics honour the geometry the triad chose. A design whose trade-off is deliberate should say.

Brutus's tide (R14)

Julius Caesar, Act 4, Scene 3: "There is a tide in the affairs of men…" Brutus speaks the lines to overrule Cassius, who wants to wait for the enemy; Brutus argues for marching to Philippi. The army moves on his reading. At Philippi both men die.

The rejoinder reads the speech as Thesis 20 as tragedy: the tide in human affairs is partly made by the one seen to read it, and a confident reading spoken with authority can manufacture the very flood it claims to find. An instrument that tells an organisation "the tide is turning here" is intervening in kairos, not reporting it.

Sources[85] Shakespeare

Boundary-work
The labour by which a field separates itself from what it is not.

Boundary-work

Thomas Gieryn ("Boundary-work and the demarcation of science from non-science", American Sociological Review, 1983) showed that the line between science and non-science is drawn rhetorically, case by case, by those with an interest in where it falls — and that drawing it confers authority.

Thesis 21 argued that the human/other distinction does institutional work: it marks a school's border. The rejoinder (Q. XX) reads the reply's complaint that a CRP–Cynefin conversation has been refused as boundary-work: a border described from one side.

The Established and the Outsiders

Norbert Elias and John Scotson (1965) studied "Winston Parva", a Leicestershire community in which two working-class groups, identical in class and ethnicity, differed only in length of residence. The established group monopolised positions and stigmatised the newcomers, describing them by their worst minority and themselves by their best.

Cited in Q. XX for the general dynamic of schools and traditions: borders between them generate established/outsider figurations, and each side sees the other's jacket. The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy found exactly this between Cynefin and CRP.

Recognition, not alignment

Thesis 24's test for any practice of human complexity, drawn from Kevin Flinn's account of followership and from Laozi 17: the measure of good practice is not whether people are aligned to a direction but whether, when the work is done, they recognise it as their own — 我自然, "we did it ourselves".

The reply accepts the test. It is the most important concession in the reply, because it is a test the reply can be held to. Part VII (Q. XLIV; R23) holds it there.

Part V The Compass and the Loom, Argued Again

In short. The twenty-three theses on the Cynefin Company's SwarmCompass and WRASSE instruments. The main findings: the gorilla answer accepts the brochure's mistake and then repeats it (R15); bees decide by meeting and arguing, which SwarmCompass removes (R16); the brochure promises twice what the reply says nobody claims; a brochure should meet a higher standard of evidence than a paper, not a lower one; measuring "indirectly" is not measuring "lightly"; the reply has already answered the question it postpones about outsiders (R18); and a crowd that never meets cannot object to whoever speaks for it (R17).

Question 29 — Does "many people looking from many angles" answer the gorilla point? (Thesis I; R15)

The case for Snowden's view. The 2013 radiology study does not contain the episode the brochure added, but the wider research on inattentional blindness covers it[75]. Blindness comes from the task, not the person. The 17% who saw the gorilla were not special; they were just looking differently at that moment. So the cure is many people looking from many angles, at scale.

The problem with that. The study's own findings make the problem sharper. In Drew, Võ and Wolfe's experiment, 83% of radiologists missed a gorilla forty-eight times the size of a typical nodule, and eye-tracking showed most of those who missed it had looked straight at it[74]. They did not fail to look. They looked through a frame that made the gorilla invisible.

My answer. The reply accepts the thesis and then repeats the mistake the thesis named. It accepts, first, that the brochure's story added something the study does not contain — my factual point. It accepts, second, that blindness comes from the task frame, not the person — my theoretical point, which undercuts the brochure's instruction to "find the 17%", since there is no fixed 17% to find. Then it proposes the cure: many angles. But SwarmCompass, as its brochure describes it, gives the same prompts and the same rating frame to everyone. One frame given to a thousand people is not a thousand frames. It is the radiology study's task frame, copied at scale: everyone is looking for nodules because the instrument asked everyone to look for nodules. The cure needs variety of frame, and the instrument standardises the frame so the answers can be pooled. An instrument that really sought many frames would let its participants write their own prompts — which is the first thread of the Tidal Loom.

Part II adds the reason this keeps happening. The frame is chosen by the designer — the curator in the astrologer's chair. However many people look, they look through the designer's window.

Reply. People bring different experiences to the same frame; true, and that is real variety of content. But inattentional blindness is about the frame, not the content. The radiologists had different experiences too.

In one line: they looked straight at it and did not see it — and giving the same question to a thousand eyes gives one frame a thousand times.

Question 30 — Is a bee quorum a kind of consensus? (Thesis II; R16)

The case for Snowden's view. In Thomas Seeley's honeybees, the swarm commits when enough scouts gather at one site; by take-off the dancing scouts have usually come to agree; quorum is how agreement is reached[76]. The bees' "stop signals" prevent early lock-in, which SwarmCompass also tries to avoid. Humans do not share genes as bees do, which is exactly why the tool removes intermediaries. And committing to one site is just what deciding means.

The problem with that. In Seeley's work, quorum sensing is a mechanism that triggers commitment before full agreement is needed. Scouts at a site sense when enough others are there and start "piping", which prepares the swarm to fly, even while other sites may still be advertised[78]. Agreement among the dancers often follows; it is not the trigger.

My answer. The reply keeps the swarm's vocabulary and drops its mechanism, in four places.

Quorum. A quorum is a local threshold sensed by bodies that meet: scouts at the site bump into each other and, in effect, count. It is commitment by being together. SwarmCompass's participants, by the reply's own account, never meet (Question 41). A quorum among people who never meet is not sensed by them; it is calculated for them. That is a vote, counted by the returning officer.

Stop signals. The stop signal — a brief head-butt delivered by a scout from one site to a dancer promoting another — is the swarm's built-in disagreement[79]. It is how bees argue: directly, physically, between rival advocates. The reply says SwarmCompass also avoids early lock-in. But it does so by keeping people apart — stopping them influencing each other at all — while the swarm does it by conflict among advocates who meet. Same name, opposite mechanism.

Shared interest. The reply says humans' lack of shared genes is why the tool removes intermediaries. But Seeley's bees can afford open advocacy because every bee's interest is the swarm's: no scout gains by misleading. Humans have no such guarantee. That is why their disagreements need rules — of advocacy, standing and appeal — not why they need to be prevented. Removing intermediaries does not remove interests. It removes the place where interests could be argued out.

Commitment. For bees, committing to one site is what deciding means, because they must fly together or die. Organisations can, and often should, keep several options open, split, hedge, or come back to a decision. Using the swarm as a model imports the bees' all-or-nothing into human decisions. That was the thesis.

And the factual point stands where the brochure made it. Seeley and Buhrman tested whether swarms choose the best of five sites; they did in four out of five trials[77]. The authors called that "reasonably good". A swarm that chooses best four times in five does not "always" choose best.

In one line: the swarm decides by bees who meet, argue and head-butt — an instrument whose people never meet has borrowed the swarm's name and left its parliament behind.

Question 31 — Was the wrasse chosen for its virtues? (Thesis III)

The case for Snowden's view. The cleaner wrasse was chosen for its adaptability, colour, sex-changing and parasite-cleaning. WRASSE is still being developed. Its mimic is a fair warning about imitators.

The problem with that. You do not choose some of an emblem's properties; it carries them all. The best-known finding about this fish is that it cheats — eating its clients' protective mucus instead of parasites — more when unobserved, and behaves better when other potential clients are watching[80].

My answer. The reply's reading of the mimic is generous and I accept it: an emblem that warns against imitation is a useful one. But the cheating is the wrasse's own, and it has the shape of Thesis XVII. The cleaner behaves well when it is watched by those who will decide whether to come back. That is Goodhart's law on a coral reef: performance tuned to being observed. An instrument named after the wrasse carries, whether its designers like it or not, the best-documented natural example of behaviour that changes when watched. That is a good reason to keep the emblem — and to read it as a permanent warning: this instrument will be gamed when watched, and cheated when not.

Question 32 — Are waiting and stirring different gestures? (Thesis V)

The case for Snowden's view. He accepts Mead's point that holding back is itself a gesture, but keeps the distinction: waiting and stirring things up are different gestures with different results, and the WRASSE axis asks which one is chosen.

My answer. The concession is the thesis, and keeping the axis drops its second half. If holding back is a gesture, then "natural emergence" is not emergence without intervention; it is emergence under the intervention of being watched and not acted on. The axis does not divide natural from stirred; it divides two kinds of stirring, chosen by the same person. And the reply's own words — which one is chosen — point to that person without naming him. Thesis V asked who stands where, to choose. The answer is the strategist who has kept his planner's mindset (Question 15), now choosing between two gestures towards a system that will learn which he chose — the astrologer deciding whether to speak.

Question 33 — Are WRASSE's "substrates" tangled rather than layered? (Thesis VI)

The case for Snowden's view. WRASSE has no layers. Its four substrates — technological, cultural, procedural, network — are tangled together, and people act within them; they are not a growing medium.

My answer. If the substrates are tangled, the word substrate is wrong and should change. In every sense — chemistry, geology, biology, electronics — a substrate is the thing underneath: the surface something grows on, reacts on or is built on. Calling culture a substrate and then saying it is underneath nothing is keeping a word whose meaning you reject. The anthropologist Tim Ingold's distinction between stacked layers and a tangled "meshwork" is exactly the distinction the reply now draws[39]. If WRASSE is a meshwork, call it one, and take the horizontal bands out of the diagrams. If it keeps the bands and the word, the reply is describing a WRASSE not yet drawn — which, since it is still in development, is quite possible, and should be recorded as an amendment to WRASSE rather than a correction of my thesis.

Question 34 — Does anyone claim that unknowns can be mapped? (Thesis VII, XIII)

The case for Snowden's view. Nobody does. Unknowns can be flagged, not mapped. My amended thesis — that the general shape of the unknown can be stated in advance, but not what it will turn out to be — is accepted, and my second edition's concessions move towards the position my first edition attacked.

The problem with that. The SwarmCompass brochure promises, twice, to turn "unknown unknowns" into mapped territory[6][3].

My answer. The reply denies a claim its company published. If nobody claims unknowns can be mapped, the brochure should be withdrawn or amended, because it claims exactly that. The reply's position — flag, do not map — is the right one, and it is my amended Thesis VII. Accepting the amended thesis means accepting that the brochure's central promise was a category error, which is what my first edition said.

On Thesis XIII: the reply reads my second edition's concessions as a move towards the position my first edition attacked. It is not. The concessions — that Tria and colleagues predicted the statistics of novelty, that Cortês, Kauffman, Liddle and Smolin modelled when novelty explodes, that Turing measured the size of what is unseen, that Machta, Transtrum and Sethna showed why complex systems can be summarised[68][69][70] — grant the shape of the unknown and deny its contents. The brochure promised the contents. My critique, amended, still denies that. What moved was not my critique towards the instrument, but my critique away from its own overstatement — which is what the Additive Covenant is for. Snowden welcomes a critique that revises itself. I welcome the welcome, and return it as a question: where is the Cynefin list of corrections?

In one line: the reply says nobody claims the unknown can be mapped; the brochure does, twice — one of them must be amended, and it is not the thesis.

Question 35 — Does Thesis VIII misread Boisot and SenseMaker?

The case for Snowden's view. In Max Boisot's I-Space, moving through the space — codifying, abstracting, spreading, absorbing, applying, scanning — is the social learning cycle; codifying is a phase, not a fall[73]. SenseMaker keeps stories in people's own words. The thesis mistakes a cycle for a decline.

The problem with that. In Boisot, "codifying" means putting things into categories, and "abstracting" means reducing the number of categories needed. Placing a story as a dot on a triangle is codifying and abstracting by definition.

My answer. The reply is right that the I-Space describes a cycle, and Thesis VIII is improved, not refuted, by saying so. The cycle has six phases. The question now is: where do the later phases happen, and for whom? Codifying and abstracting happen at capture, when the storyteller rates. Spreading happens when patterns are displayed — to whom? Absorbing — turning codified knowledge back into practical know-how — happens wherever the patterns are learned from. Applying happens wherever they are acted on. If spreading, absorbing and applying happen among analysts, clients and, according to the brochure, automated systems, then the storytellers supply the codifying and others complete the cycle. The learning cycle runs through the storytellers and finishes elsewhere. That is the harvest, in Boisot's own terms. The reply's concession that AI training raises questions of ownership, benefit and consent is a concession that the later phases may be completed by machines. The thesis asked who completes them.

Question 36 — Is risk a physical fact, like a cracked weld? (Thesis IX)

The case for Snowden's view. Risk is partly about relationships, but a cracked weld is a cracked weld whatever anyone feels about it. Reducing risk to anxiety managed between people, as Shaw, Stacey and Menzies Lyth do, is a mistake of psychodynamic thinking[30][31]. WRASSE's quadrants assign kinds of response, not risk itself.

The problem with that. I have been a receiver since 1989, and I have stood beside a good many cracked welds.

My answer. The reply is right that the crack is physical, and Thesis IX is better for the correction. It should be amended to say risk lives in relationships as well as in things. But the crack is a hazard. It becomes a risk only when it meets exposure: whose building, whose security, whose loan covenant, whose insurer, whose tenants, whose liability, whose decision to inspect or not. The same crack is a nuisance to an owner-occupier with cash, a breach of covenant to a lender, a valuation adjustment to a surveyor, a reason to appoint a receiver, a problem for the receiver selling the property, a claim against a contractor — and a different story to each. The physical fact is one; the risks are many, and they are shared out among the parties by contracts, positions and powers. That is what "risk lives in relationships" meant. And a quadrant that assigns a kind of response to a situation has assigned it on someone's behalf — the someone whose exposure the response protects. The quadrant does not hold risk. It holds a view about whose risk counts.

In one line: the crack is in the weld, but the risk is in the lease, the charge, the policy and the person who decides whether to look.

Question 37 — Genealogy, alignment and the Way (Theses X–XII)

X · Where WRASSE comes from. The reply says WRASSE is in development, that reacting against Rita McGrath's work was one of its starting points, that sources will be credited when it is published, and that Mintzberg and Waters and March measure different things from WRASSE's axes[111][112][113]. The first three answers are gladly accepted; they confirm that the sources are not credited yet. The fourth is half right: the axes differ, but the four domains do not, and the thesis was about the domains. A promise to credit sources on publication is a promise the record can hold. It goes in the ledger as stands pending.

XI · Alignment. The reply distinguishes coherence that allows variety from uniformity, and says the aim is not compliance. But it does not engage with Kevin Flinn's recognition test, or with the brochure's own phrase — "authentic alignment (not just top-down compliance)" — which was the subject of the thesis[41]. The distinction between coherence and uniformity is good; it is not in the brochure. The brochure sells alignment and qualifies it as "not just" compliance, which admits that compliance is part of it. Recognition — the test the reply accepts at Thesis 24 — is the alternative I proposed. The reply accepts it in one place and does not apply it here.

XII · The Way. The reply accepts Cook Ding — the butcher in the Zhuangzi whose knife never dulls because he follows the natural spaces in the ox rather than forcing his way[83] — and says nothing about my claim that both instruments grab 勢 (potential) and lose 道 (the way). That silence is telling. Cook Ding's blade lasts nineteen years not because he reads the ox well but because he does not impose on it. An instrument that supplies the frame — categories, quadrants, substrates — is supplying what the system lacks. Accepting Cook Ding means accepting that the frame should be found in the situation, not brought to it. That is the loom's first thread again — and the opposite of the curator's chair in Part II.

Question 38 — Should a brochure be held to a lower standard than a paper? (postscript)

The case for Snowden's view. A two-page marketing brochure is not an academic paper. It simplifies for a different audience. Disputing it at scholarly length mistakes its genre. Marketing and academic writing have different readers, and writing differently for each is not inconsistent.

The problem with that. A brochure is where claims meet buyers — where a theory becomes something someone pays for.

My answer. A brochure should meet a higher standard of evidence than a paper, not a lower one, and that standard is not mine but the regulator's. In the UK, the CAP Code says that before publishing an advertisement, a marketer must hold documentary evidence for claims consumers are likely to see as objective, and the Advertising Standards Authority may treat claims without such evidence as misleading[109][110]. "The swarm always chooses the best site", "turn unknown unknowns into mapped territory", and a story about radiologists being talked out of what they saw are the kind of claims readers are likely to take as objective. I do not suggest any rule has been broken; that is not mine to judge. I suggest that defending the brochure by its genre turns its responsibility upside down. A paper may speculate and be wrong in public; that is what papers are for. A brochure may not.

On two audiences: the medieval universities had a name for this worry. The doctrine of "double truth" — that something could be true in philosophy and false in theology — was blamed on certain Paris philosophers and condemned by the Bishop of Paris in 1277[91]. Historians doubt anyone actually held it. But the worry it named is permanent: an author who says one thing to buyers and another to scholars has not two audiences but two theories, and owes readers an account of which is meant. The reply says there is no inconsistency. Then let the brochure say what the scholarship says: flag, do not map; four times in five, not always; the gorilla study has no conformity episode.

In one line: a paper may be wrong in public, a brochure may not — the claim that meets the buyer carries the heaviest burden of proof.

Question 39 — Is measuring "indirectly" the same as measuring "lightly"? (Theses XIV–XVI)

The case for Snowden's view. The quantum theses stand without their physics, and their practical lessons are already in the practice. SenseMaker measures indirectly, with capture built into everyday systems; it returns patterns to storytellers so they can compare experiences; it asks for the story before showing the categories; and the research on question order is psychology, not borrowed physics. His own physics stops at undergraduate level, and borrowed authority should be distrusted — the same distrust I apply to bees.

The problem with that. Two of the lessons the reply says it has learned are the reverse of the lessons drawn.

My answer. First, thanks: the reply's caution about physics is exemplary, and it is right that the theses must stand or fall without the physics. They do. Then three distinctions.

Indirect is not light. In physics, a "weak measurement" is one where the measuring device barely touches the system, so each measurement hardly disturbs it, at the price of a lot of noise[65]. "Measure weakly" in Thesis XIV meant touch lightly and seldom, so that measuring does not freeze what it measures — the lesson of the "Zeno effect", where a system watched constantly cannot change[66]. Indirect measurement is something else: sideways, so the person does not know what is being measured. And capture "built into everyday systems" is, if anything, the opposite of light: continuous, ambient and frequent — a measurement folded into every working day. That is the watched needle. The practice has learned "measure indirectly" and turned "measure lightly" upside down.

A fixed order is a fixed bias. The reply says the story comes before the categories, so the categories do not shape the story. Good. But Wang, Busemeyer and colleagues showed across seventy national surveys that question-order effects follow a law — the "QQ equality" — rather than being random[63][64]. If order effects are lawful, a fixed order does not remove the effect; it applies it the same way to everyone, which makes it invisible in the data because there is nothing to compare it with. Story-first changes how the categories are answered, every time, in the same direction. The reply accepts the warning about rotating questions; the deeper warning is that the chosen order is a constant, undeclared intervention — chosen, once again, by the designer.

Sending patterns back is not a meeting. Thesis XV said agreement cannot be broadcast; it can only be discovered when people meet and compare what each lived through. The reply says patterns go back to the storytellers. That is a broadcast: a pattern, made by the analyst from everyone's ratings, sent back to each. The image behind Thesis XV — the no-communication theorem — says the opposite: correlation becomes knowledge only when the parties meet and compare notes[67]. Sending patterns back is good. Letting storytellers meet each other — not just the pattern — is the meeting.

Reply. The bee is at least an animal; granted gladly. My distrust of borrowed authority applies to my physics as to the brochure's bees, which is why Thesis XIII said the opponent wins half. The physics is scaffolding. The building is the three distinctions above, which need none of it.

In one line: "measure lightly" meant touch seldom — capture built into every system touches always, which is not the lesson but its opposite.

Question 40 — Can the question about outsiders be postponed? (Thesis XIX; R18)

The case for Snowden's view. He welcomes Kipling's Mariner, who works from inside the whale, with what is to hand. He agrees that constraints designed by insiders with a stake are legitimate, and that substrates designed by outsiders and sold as products are the problem. He says the methods are published as ingredients, not recipes. And he postpones the question of whether a company that also builds software is an outsider selling a product[86][8].

My answer. The postponed question has already been answered — by the reply. In its section on money, it corrects the record by saying SenseMaker and SwarmCompass are trademarked commercial products. A trademarked commercial product, designed by a company, sold to organisations the company is not part of, supplying the frame (prompts, triangles, substrates) in which those organisations' people describe their experience, is — by the reply's own test — an outsider's substrate sold as a product. You do not have to think that a sin to see that the test has been met. A question answered in the same document cannot be postponed; it can only be declined. The honest answer is available and costs nothing: yes, for our products, we are outsiders; here is how we try to become insiders with a stake. That sentence would open the whale. Without it, the Mariner is still outside, in the curator's chair.

Question 41 — Does a swarm that never gathers escape becoming a Leviathan? (Thesis XXI; R17)

The case for Snowden's view. A crowd becomes a Leviathan — a single body with one voice, in Hobbes's sense — when someone speaks for it; so every gathered crowd needs a rule for breaking up. But the swarm in SwarmCompass never gathers. Its people do not meet or interact. Because humans, unlike bees, are open to influence and herding, they rate alone through abstract categories, and the swarm disperses as it is created.

The problem with that. Hobbes himself: a multitude of men are made one person, when they are by one man, or one person, represented[87]. The state is made not by gathering but by representation.

My answer. The swarm that never gathers does not escape Leviathan; it perfects him. Think of three ways a crowd can be spoken for. A gathered assembly can speak for itself, argue with its representative, and break up. A crowd in the street can at least shout back. A crowd that never meets — whose members rate alone, through abstract categories whose meaning they do not know (Question 20), into a system that pools them — cannot speak for itself at all. It has no voice but the pattern, and the pattern has no voice but the analyst's. Being kept apart from one another is not being kept apart from the representative. It is the condition in which only the representative can speak. Hobbes's sovereign is safest when his subjects cannot combine; the never-gathering swarm is the instrument of that safety.

And the reason given — that people, unlike bees, influence and herd one another — is, in anthro-complexity's own terms, the most revealing sentence in the reply. Influencing each other is what makes human systems human. Identity formed in interaction, meaning made between people, Snowden's own principle that we change the stories we tell about each other — all of these are influence. The research on the "wisdom of crowds" shows that independent estimates pool well and influenced ones herd[71][72]; true — but that is a fact about estimating, where independent errors cancel out. Building a human-complexity instrument on the independence rule means sensing people by first removing the very thing that makes them human. The swarm breaks up as it is created because it is never allowed to become a society.

Reply. Gathered groups do herd. Thesis XXI proposed the remedy: not isolation but a rule for breaking up — a gathered crowd that knows in advance how and when it will disband, and who may not speak for it afterwards. That is a constitution. Isolation is the lack of one.

In one line: a crowd that never meets can never object, and only the person reading the pattern can speak for it — that is not dispersal, it is sovereignty.

Question 42 — The diagram, the three books and leverage (Theses XX, XXII, XXIII)

On XX and XXII we agree, and agreement should be left alone. On XXIII the argument was made in Part III (Question 12) and Part II (sections 10–12): the reply agrees that every figure shapes what stands out, then blames readers for the Cynefin diagram's history of redrawing. The agreement is the thesis; the blaming is R19. Stacey, in the same position, blamed the diagram and gave it up. One more suggestion: the redrawings are the best evidence the Cynefin Company has of its own capacity for self-correction. They should be published together, dated, with the readings each one responded to. That would be the list of corrections — and a gift to the field.

Part V: cards · 30 cards
Concept
Inattentional blindness
Failing to see what is in plain view because attention is elsewhere.
Turn over ↻
Inattentional blindness

The phenomenon made famous by Simons and Chabris (1999): observers counting basketball passes frequently fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. Attention selects; what the task frame does not select is often not seen at all, even when looked at directly.

The reply rightly says blindness is a property of the task frame, not the person. The rejoinder (Q. XXIII; R15) agrees — and observes that an instrument issuing the same frame to every node reproduces the frame's blindness at scale.

Sources[75] Simons 1999
Appears inQuestion 29Cards · Part V The Compass and the Loom, Argued Again

Study
The gorilla in the CT scan
83% of radiologists missed it; most looked straight at it.
Turn over ↻
The gorilla in the CT scan

Drew, Võ and Wolfe (Psychological Science, 2013) inserted a gorilla forty-eight times the size of an average nodule into the last of five chest CT cases read by 24 radiologists searching for nodules. 83% did not report it. Eye-tracking showed that most of those who missed it had looked directly at its location.

The SwarmCompass brochure built on this an anecdote of people talked out of what they saw — an episode the study does not contain (Compass I). The reply concedes this. The rejoinder notes the study's sharpest finding: looking is not seeing, and the frame, not the eye, decides.

Sources[74] Drew 2013
