Thomas Seeley
The honeybee swarm as a parliament of scouts.
Turn over ↻
Thomas Seeley

Cornell biologist whose decades of field experiments, summarised in Honeybee Democracy (2010), showed how a swarm of some ten thousand bees chooses a new home: several hundred scouts inspect sites, advertise them with waggle dances tuned to quality, recruit others, and inhibit rival advertisers; when a quorum of scouts gathers at one site, they trigger the swarm's takeoff.

The brochure used the swarm as an image of "true consensus" that "always" chooses best. Compass II disputed each claim. The rejoinder (Q. XXIV; R16) adds that the swarm's intelligence lies in a mechanism — advocacy and dissent among bees who meet — that an instrument whose nodes never meet cannot keep.

Sources[76] Seeley 2010
Appears inQuestion 30Cards · Part V The Compass and the Loom, Argued Again
↺ Turn back
Mechanism
Quorum sensing
Commitment triggered by co-presence, before consensus is required.
Turn over ↻
Quorum sensing

Seeley and Visscher (2004) showed that scouts at a candidate site sense when the number of other scouts there passes a threshold, and then begin "piping", which prepares the swarm for takeoff. Experiments that dispersed scouts among five identical boxes at one site delayed piping and takeoff, supporting the quorum hypothesis. Consensus among dancers often follows; it is not the trigger.

The reply calls quorum a form of consensus. The rejoinder (Q. XXIV): it is commitment by bodies that meet and count. A quorum among nodes that never meet is not sensed by them; it is computed for them — a vote tallied by the returning officer.

Sources[78] Seeley 2004
Appears inWhat Snowden Said: His Reply, Fairly SummarisedQuestion 30Cards · Part V The Compass and the Loom, Argued Again
↺ Turn back
Mechanism
The stop signal
A head-butt from a rival advocate: the swarm's institutionalised dissent.
Turn over ↻
The stop signal

Seeley and colleagues (Science, 2012) showed that scouts committed to one site deliver brief vibrational "stop signals", often by butting their heads against dancers advertising a different site, inhibiting the rival dance. Part VI Money: Pelagius, Augustine and the Software Bill

In short. The reply corrects two facts, which I accept. It agrees that the question of a "Pelagian start and an Augustinian institution" is fair. It answers with safeguards (open publication; an open network of practitioners) and a dilemma (software costs money; the only funders are consultancies or tech firms). The safeguards are real but partial; the dilemma is false; and the question was never who pays (R20).

First, a short explainer, because the terms are unusual. Pelagius was a fourth-century British monk who taught that people can choose to do good by their own nature. Augustine opposed him: fallen human nature cannot do good without God's grace, and in the settlement that followed, grace came through sacraments given by an ordained priesthood[88][89]. Snowden has called his own approach "Pelagian" — it trusts ordinary people to make sense of their own situations. My question was whether a Pelagian start ends, as movements often do, in an Augustinian institution that hands out the grace of method through its own priests.

Question 43 — Does publishing the methods openly prevent the Augustinian turn?

The case for Snowden's view. Yes. The methods are published openly as components, not recipes; the network of practitioners is not limited to people the company trained; WRASSE is not on the market; nothing is members-only. Openness protects the Pelagian start from an Augustinian end.

The problem with that. The Augustinian church published its scripture too. Open texts have never stopped the institutionalising of interpretation.

My answer. The safeguards are real. They set the Cynefin Company apart from many in its trade. But they work at the wrong level. The Pelagian controversy was not about access to scripture — Pelagius and Augustine read the same Bible. It was about whether people could do good by themselves or needed grace given through the Church. So the question for any open method is not "are the texts published?" but "who administers the sacraments?" For SenseMaker and SwarmCompass, the sacraments are the software: the platform where stories are captured, the analytics that make patterns, the displays that show them. Those are not published as components. By the reply's own correction, they are trademarked commercial products. The texts are open; the altar is owned. Max Weber described the process: a founder's personal craft becomes an institution's procedure, run by people the institution authorises[90]. Open texts are the Pelagian part that remains. The platform is the Augustinian institution.

Part II gives this a sharper edge. The sacrament that matters most is not even the software; it is the act of curation — choosing the frame. Whoever designs the categories stands at the altar, whoever funds them.

Reply. The open network is the strongest safeguard offered. It would be stronger still if practitioners outside the company could change the official descriptions of the methods, as in a commons. That is the difference between an open church and a congregational one.

In one line: the scripture is open and the altar is owned — Pelagius and Augustine read the same Bible.

Question 44 — Must software be paid for by consultancies or tech firms? (R20)

The case for Snowden's view. Software costs money to build and run. The realistic funders are large consultancies, which would turn the methods into recipes, or tech companies, which would turn stories into products. Neither is better; the company stays alert; money has to come from somewhere.

The problem with that. The dilemma leaves out every form of organisation that has actually kept research software going without either.

My answer. The dilemma is false, and it answers a question my theses did not ask.

False. Between consultancy and tech firm lie the forms the Nobel-winning economist Elinor Ostrom studied as "the commons" — long-lasting arrangements in which users govern shared resources themselves[103] — and the forms research software has actually taken: the statistics language R, maintained by a foundation and a volunteer core[104]; the reference manager Zotero, kept going by a non-profit[105]; OpenStreetMap, a world map built and governed by its own mappers through a foundation[106]; public research grants; university consortia; user-owned cooperatives; and data trusts, in which the people whose data it is hold rights over how it is used[107]. None is easy. All exist. A dilemma that names two funders and leaves out the commons describes the options open to a firm, not the options there are.

Beside the point. More importantly, my theses never asked who pays. They asked who consents, who sees first, who can change the frame, and who benefits[2]. All four can be answered under any funder. A company-funded platform can still guarantee that storytellers see the patterns before clients do; that categories are written with representatives of the people who will use them; that no story becomes training data without specific consent and a share in what it trains; that storytellers can withdraw their stories. In the UK, some of this is already law: "purpose limitation" says personal data collected for one purpose must not be used later in a way incompatible with it[108]. A story collected to help an organisation understand itself, later used to train an automated system for other clients, is the textbook case the principle was written for. The software bill decides none of this. Governance does.

Reply. Staying alert to the risk is not the best that can be done. Alertness is a mood; governance is a constitution. The reply offers the first. The theses asked for the second.

In one line: the theses did not ask who pays — they asked who consents, who sees first, who can change the frame and who benefits, which can be answered under any funder.

The four questions (R20)

The rejoinder's restatement of what the political-economic theses asked — not who pays for the software, but: who consents to the use of a narrative; who sees the pattern first; who may revise the frame; who benefits from what the stories train or decide.

All four are answerable under any funder, by governance rather than ownership. They reappear as tests 1, 2, 5 and 6 of the ten tests for the deferred post (Part VIII), and as threads 1–3 of the Tidal Loom (Part VII).

Part VII Length and the Machine

In short. The reply makes three points about form. Length means nothing when text can be generated. The burden falls on whoever has to reply. And a critique of story-harvesting is written with a machine trained on harvested text. The first is true and always was. The second is answered by the format itself, which worked. The third is true, and I accept it as a point against myself (R21).

Question 45 — Does machine-made length put an unfair burden on the person replying?

The case for Snowden's view. The old disputation format suited an age when writing was hard work and length had natural limits. Automated tools can now produce half a million words a week. Length no longer shows engagement, and the person replying faces a burden no human can carry. Brandolini's law — refuting nonsense takes far more effort than producing it — applies with new force[95].

The problem with that. The reply answered all forty-seven theses in a few thousand words, without reading the whole text.

My answer. The format worked exactly as designed. A disputation was never judged by length. Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae runs to thousands of articles, but each article can be argued on its own, because each states its question, the objections, the counter-authority, the answer and the replies[92]. Luther's theses were ninety-five sentences. Numbered theses exist so a long work can be answered without carrying the whole: you go to the thesis, find the argument behind it, and dispute there. That is what Snowden did. It is what the theses, the table of verdicts and the cross-references were built for. The burden he describes is one he did not have to carry, because the format lifted it.

Brandolini's law is about nonsense. The reply calls several theses useful, accepts many and rejects others in a sentence each. That is not the burden of refuting nonsense; it is the ordinary imbalance of debate, where an objection is often shorter than the argument it answers. It was always so. Aquinas's replies are shorter than his objections.

Reply. Length still signals effort to readers, and machine-made length can mislead them; agreed. That is why the form must be declared (Thesis XXII), and it is declared at the start of this work. A reader who knows how a text was made can weigh it.

In one line: the theses were numbered so nobody would have to read the volume — he didn't, he answered them, and that is what theses are for.

Question 46 — Does a critique of harvesting, written with a harvested machine, defeat itself? (R21)

The case for Snowden's view. Yes. A critique that accuses an instrument of harvesting people's stories to train machines is itself written with a machine trained on harvested human writing. The critic stands where he says the criticised stand.

The problem with that. An argument is not refuted by facts about who made it. Rejecting a claim because of its source is the genetic fallacy; rejecting it because the critic does the same thing is tu quoque — "you too"[94]. Neither touches whether the claim is true.

My answer. In logic the objection is a "you too". I accept it anyway — not as a refutation, but as a point against myself, recorded here as R21.

My critiques argued that turning people's stories into machine-readable data raises questions of consent and benefit, and tends to erase the unusual. A large language model is the biggest such harvest ever made: trained on writing by people who were not asked, its unusual voices thinned by the same statistical pressures Thesis 16 described. Writing with one means standing inside the harvest. I do. The theses bind me as they bind the instruments. Whose writing trained the machine I use? Did they consent? Who benefits from what I make with it? Which voices does it make more ordinary — including mine? I do not have good answers to all of these. I do have the obligation to ask them in public, which is what the declaration at the start does.

And here the exchange becomes instructive, because accepting the point shows the very thing in dispute. Snowden's principle says humans can change the stories they tell about each other. Thesis 6 asked that anthro-complexity apply that principle to itself. The reply conceded Thesis 6 in a line and applied it nowhere else (Part III). Now the same principle is turned on me — your story about the harvest is itself a harvest — and the self-aware answer is not to deny it, or to argue my way into innocence, but to say: yes; so the theses apply to me; here is how this was made; here is what I will try to do about it. That is what a self-aware anthro-complexity would sound like. The difference between the reply and this rejoinder is not that one of us is outside the harvest. It is that one of us has said he is inside it.

In the language of Part II: the critic is not exempt from his own map. That is the participant's position.

Reply. Perhaps this acceptance is just rhetoric. Then hold me to it. Under the Additive Covenant, this paragraph cannot be withdrawn.

In one line: the irony is true, it is not a refutation, and I accept it as a thesis against myself.

Question 47 — Does the Additive Covenant mean the text can only grow?

The case for Snowden's view. Yes, and that is a fault: a text that can only grow can never be made concise, and a rule against deleting is a rule against editing.

My answer. The covenant forbids silent deletion, not revision. A thesis can be amended in place, struck through, annotated or replaced — two are amended in this rejoinder, and this whole edition restates the first in plainer English. What may not happen is that a claim, once made, quietly disappears, so readers cannot see the argument move. That is the practice of published corrections, of the scholarly record, and of version control in software; it is how a field learns in public. It is also Kepler's practice: Astronomia Nova kept his wrong turns on the page (Part II). And it is what the Cynefin diagram's history of redrawing most needs.

This is the form of every quaestio in the rejoinder, rendered in plain English. Its point (Q. XXXIX): a long work so built can be answered thesis by thesis without the burden of the whole — which is exactly what the reply did.

Part VIII The Loom Is Not His Method Under Another Name

In short. The reply finds that my alternative, the Tidal Loom, keeps what it values, removes something it doubts exists, and looks very like its own method — which it takes as a kind of agreement. It is a kind of agreement, and a test. The loom is the method plus five things it lacks (R22); a north star is not the only way to navigate; and the recognition test, once accepted, is turned upside down by claiming the loom as "ours" (R23).

Question 48 — Is the Tidal Loom just SenseMaker renamed? (R22)

The case for Snowden's view. The Tidal Loom keeps distributed story-sensing (SenseMaker), attention to what is hard to change (the energy cost of change in estuarine mapping), and many small actions rather than one big bet (parallel safe-to-fail experiments). It claims to remove the observer's privileged position, but there is no such privilege to remove. What is left is the method he already uses.

The problem with that. The reply lists what the loom keeps and finds it familiar. It does not list what the loom adds.

My answer, with a table and an invitation.

Table 3 — The five threads: where the loom differs from the method
ThreadThe method, as describedThe Tidal LoomThesis
1 · The warp (the frame)Categories designed by the method's designers for a clientCategories written with representatives of the people who will use them; the frame is offered by convenors and re-strung by the weavers14, 13, I, XII
2 · First sightPatterns seen by analysts and clients, then returned to storytellersStorytellers see the pattern of their own stories before anyone else, and can comment on it18, XV, 24
3 · Consent to the harvestQuestions of ownership, benefit and consent acknowledged; postponedNo story becomes training data, or is used beyond its first purpose, without specific consent and a share in what it trains; withdrawal honoured23, VIII, 16
4 · A rule for breaking upParticipants never meet; the analyst reports the patternStorytellers can meet to compare; every gathered group says in advance how it will disband and who may not speak for it afterwardsXV, XXI
5 · A list of correctionsDiagram redrawn because readers took claims never madeEvery instrument keeps a public, dated list of what it got wrong, including what its diagrams inviteXXIII, 22, 6

If the loom is the method under another name, the method already has these five threads, and nothing is lost by saying so in its documentation. If it does not, the loom is not the method renamed; it is the method with what my theses said was missing. Either way, the invitation is the same: if the loom is yours, weave it. I would count it the best possible outcome of this exchange if the Cynefin Company adopted any one of the five threads and called it its own.

Notice what the five threads have in common. Each one moves something out of the curator's chair described in Part II and into the hands of the people being studied: the frame (thread 1), the first look (2), control of the material (3), the right to meet and speak for themselves (4), and the record of mistakes (5). The loom is not a better map. It is a way of making the mapmaker one of the people on the map.

On the observer's privilege: the reply doubts there is one to remove. But being unable to see your own privilege is the form privilege usually takes. Donna Haraway called the claim to see everything from nowhere in particular the "god trick", and argued that worthwhile objectivity is situated, partial and accountable[99]. A practitioner who says "there is no privilege here" has not removed it; he has hidden it. Fludd's astrologer did not think he was privileged either. He thought he was reading the harmony of the world.

In one line: if the loom is yours, weave it — the five threads are the only difference between us, and the only ones that matter.

Question 49 — Is a north star a guide rather than a destination?

The case for Snowden's view. A compass assumes a north and a loom assumes a frame, and complexity gives neither. But the next step can still have a direction, and a north star is a guide, not a destination. You sail by it, not to it.

The problem with that. The pole star is useful precisely because it is the one point in the sky that does not move — because it stands outside the motion you steer through.

My answer. The image is exactly right and exactly the problem. The pole star is the perfect example of a fixed reference point outside the system, useful because it does not care who steers by it. A human system has no such star. Every reference point it uses — a value, a vision, a pattern, a category — moves when it is used, because people steer by it and are changed by steering. Micronesian navigators used a different method. In etak, as Thomas Gladwin and Edwin Hutchins described it, the navigator imagines the canoe as still and a reference island, out of sight, moving backwards under a sequence of rising and setting stars[101][102]. The reference frame is inside the voyage; the stars are a path, not a pole; and the navigator's own position is the fixed point. That is the "star-path" of The Compass and the Loom, chapter 15[3]. A north star guides those who can stand outside the sea. Etak is navigation for people who know they are the canoe — Stacey's participant, at sea.

Question 50 — Does the reply pass the recognition test it accepts? (Thesis 24; R23)

The case for Snowden's view. The reply accepts the test — recognition, not alignment — and connects it to the Laozi. Then it recognises its own method in the Tidal Loom. What better recognition than finding that the critic's proposal is already the practice?

The problem with that. The line in the Laozi is spoken by the people about the ruler's work, not by the ruler about the people's.

My answer, from the chapter itself. Chapter 17 of the Laozi ranks rulers[84]. The best are those the people barely know exist (太上，不知有之). Next come those they love and praise; then those they fear; last, those they despise. And when the best ruler's work is done, the people all say: we did this ourselves — 百姓皆謂我自然. The recognition the test asks for is recognition by those inside that the work was theirs. It is passed when the ruler disappears into the people's sense of their own doing.

The reply turns this round. It is the method-owner who looks at the critic's proposal and says: this is ours. In the Laozi's terms that is not the first rank but the second at best — the ruler who wants to be praised — and in terms of the recognition test it is not recognition but appropriation. I say this without unkindness. The reply saw the danger itself, in its postscript, when it wondered whether it reads the loom too quickly as its own method. That postscript is the best sentence in the reply, because it is the one moment its author sees his own constraints. I ask only that the sentence be promoted from the postscript to the method.

Reply. Recognising a likeness is not claiming ownership; true. But the test is not whether the likeness is real. It is who gets to say "we did this ourselves". If storytellers, working under the loom's five threads, said it of their own patterns, the test would be passed. If the method-owner says it of the loom, the test has been turned round.

In one line: the best ruler is the one the people barely notice — he does not say "this is ours"; they say "we did this ourselves".

Part IX The Hammer: What the Postponed Post Must Answer

In short. The reply postpones power to a later post. This Part sets out, in advance, ten tests an account of power in anthro-complexity must pass to answer my theses (R24). Setting them now is not presumption. It is the only way to make sure that when the answer comes, people other than its author can tell whether it is one.

The reply has given the later post its first sentence: agency is about the three human capacities, and power arises when capacities meet position and resources. It is a good sentence. As Part III noted, it is Thesis 12. What follows from it is not more definition but more location: where, in anthro-complexity's own practice, do capacities meet position and resources, and with what result? My theses named the places. Part II added the most important one: the designer's chair, where the frame is curated. The tests below ask that each place be addressed.

The tests draw on three bodies of work any account of power in human complexity will have to meet. The political theorist Steven Lukes described three "faces" of power: winning decisions; keeping issues off the agenda; and shaping what people want and take for granted[96]. Those map exactly onto the three places a sensing instrument holds power: what it decides, what it does not ask, and the frame through which people come to see their own experience. Norbert Elias adds that power is a feature of every human relationship — a balance, not a possession[25]. And Michel Foucault's idea of the dispositif — an arrangement of positions, visibilities and procedures that produces behaviour without seeming to command it — describes what a well-designed instrument is[97].

  1. The test of the categories. Who writes the categories, to whose brief, and can the people who will use them change them before capture? (Theses 13, 14; Lukes's third face; the curator of Part II.)
  2. The test of first sight. Who sees the pattern first, and can storytellers see their own pattern before the client does? (Thesis 18; XV.)
  3. The test of remaining risk. Who carries the risk of acting on a pattern, and who bears the loss when a "safe" experiment is not safe for them? (Theses 7, 13; IX.)
  4. The test of the agenda. What questions does the instrument not ask, and who decided it would not? (Lukes's second face; Thesis 10.)
  5. The test of indirectness. When storytellers do not know what their ratings will mean, what are they consenting to, and how is that consent informed? (Thesis 14; R9.)
  6. The test of the harvest. Can any story become training data, or be used beyond its first purpose, and on what terms of consent, benefit and withdrawal? (Theses 16, 23; VIII; R20.)
  7. The test of representation. Who speaks for a swarm that never gathers, and how can the swarm challenge what is said in its name? (XXI; R17.)
  8. The test of the product. For its trademarked products, does the company stand as an outsider designing substrates, and what does it do to become an insider with a stake? (XIX; R18.)
  9. The test of the border. Who certifies practitioners, who can amend the official methods, and how is the border with neighbouring schools kept open? (Theses 21–22.)
  10. The test of the record — and the eight minutes. Where is the public record of what the methods and diagrams got wrong, who can add to it, and what pattern in the data would count against the theory itself? (XXIII; R19; R26.)

If the later post passes these tests, my theses on power will have been answered, whatever the answers are. If it does not, it will be another sentence like the first: true, and not yet an answer. Either way, readers will be able to tell, and that is the point of setting the tests now.

In one line: the title shows the nail and the tide but crops out the hammer — these ten tests are where the hand holding it will have to appear.

Steven Lukes

Steven Lukes

Steven Lukes (Power: A Radical View, 1974; 2nd ed. 2005) distinguished three dimensions of power: the power to prevail in observable decisions (Dahl); the power to keep issues off the agenda (Bachrach and Baratz); and the power to shape people's preferences and perceptions so that conflicts never arise — the "third face".

The rejoinder (Part VIII) maps the three faces onto a sensing instrument: what it decides, what it does not ask, and the frame through which people come to see their experience.

The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy called the triopticon a dispositif. The rejoinder extends the term to the sensing instrument in general (Part VIII).

Dispositif

Foucault's term (in the 1977 interview "The Confession of the Flesh") for a heterogeneous ensemble — discourses, institutions, architectural forms, regulations, scientific statements — and the network of relations among them, responding to an urgent need and producing conduct without appearing to command it.

A well-designed instrument is a dispositif in this sense: it arranges who signifies, who sees, who decides and what can be noticed, and the conduct follows. That is why its power must be described as arrangement, not intention.

Curation is power (R28)

Steven Lukes distinguished three faces of power: winning decisions; keeping issues off the agenda; shaping what people want and take for granted. Choosing the frame through which people describe their own experience is the third face in its purest form: it decides what can be noticed before anyone notices anything.

That is why the rejoinder says postponing power postpones everything. The triangle, the Mariner, the harvest and the reflexive programme are all questions about the curator's chair.

The Final Ruling

In short. What stands, what falls, what has been amended, and what is still open.

What the reply wins

Two factual corrections (members-only; WRASSE on the market), recorded as amendments. A refinement of Thesis IX (risk lives in relationships as well as in things) and of Thesis VIII (the I-Space is a cycle, and the question is where it finishes). The point that its emblem's mimic is a fair warning. By its caution, the point that the quantum theses must stand without their physics — and they do. The irony of the machine, accepted as a point against myself. And my sincere thanks for a reply that took the theses seriously enough to answer them one by one.

What the reply concedes

The common ground (1–3); that its own principle applies to its own framework (6); that a mapped pattern is a landscape, not 勢 (9); that power is missing from the three marks (12); that whoever designs the frame holds power (13); that self-rating is only partial (14); Goodhart's law for every published instrument (XVII); the shape of the unknown but not its contents (VII, XIII); that holding back is a gesture (V); that AI training raises questions of ownership, benefit and consent (VIII); that every figure shapes what stands out (XXIII); the recognition test (24); the fairness of the Pelagian question; and, in a postscript, that it may read the loom too quickly as its own.

What the reply does not answer

The second half of fifteen theses (R1). The centre, postponed six times (R2). The second and third parts of Thesis 13 (R8). The oblique dilemma (R9). The brochure's training-data deliverable and its double promise of "mapped territory" (R10; Question 34). The feedback loop of Thesis 16 (R11). The statistics of the triangle (R12). The contradiction between its answers to 19 and XVII (R13). The second half of the kairos thesis (R14). One frame given to many (R15). The mechanism behind the swarm's vocabulary (R16). Who speaks for the swarm that never gathers (R17). The outsider question it has already answered (R18). Its own principle, applied to its own diagram (R19). The four questions that are not about who pays (R20). The five threads (R22). The direction of the recognition test (R23). And, beneath all of these, the problem of Part II: a Fludd-like picture of human beings, studied with Kepler-like methods that are never allowed to test it, joined by a designer who curates from the astrologer's chair (R25–R30).

Last word

The idea behind The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy was that we see the constraints others are under and are blind to our own. The reply has shown that again, with real intelligence and in good faith. It sees the length of my books, the editions of my critique, the machine I write with, the brochure I read as a paper — and, until its postscript, not the hand that holds the frame. I have tried in this rejoinder to see my own: the machine is declared, the irony accepted, two facts amended, the corrections thanked. Whether I have managed it is not for me to say. That is the whole point.

Kepler gave up the circle because of eight minutes of arc. Stacey gave up his matrix because of what it did to the people who used it. Both let something outside themselves overrule a picture they cared about. That is the only thing my critiques have asked of anthro-complexity: not that it give up its picture of human beings, which is largely right, but that it name the evidence that could correct it, and let the people it studies hold the pen.

A tide cannot be nailed. A frame can. The question both critiques asked, and this rejoinder asks again, is not whether anthro-complexity is right about human systems — on much it is, and more right than most — but whether it will let the humans it studies read it back. When the post on power is written, I will read it as I hope it will be written: as the place where the hand holding the hammer is finally drawn into the picture.

Finally: the sailor reads the tide and the tide does not read the sailor — but in human affairs the tide is other sailors, and they have been watching the one who says he reads them.

Mark Downham · Principia Humanitatis · London · 20 November 2026 · Second edition

The Lexicon: Every Card

208 reversible explainer cards. Every term in blue, every thesis of the rejoinder, and every figure, study and concept the argument relies on. Filter by word or by kind; select a card to turn it over. Each card lists its sources (linked to the Catalogue) and the places in the text where it appears.

Concept
Abstract cartography
Map-making from above, rather than taking part from within.
Turn over ↻
Abstract cartography

The rejoinder contrasts two ways of knowing a human system. The cartographer stands above the territory and draws it; the map can then be read by people who were never there. The participant is in the territory, moving with others, unable to see the whole, making the path by walking it.

Fludd's doctrine (the microcosm) made him a participant; his engravings made him a cartographer. Anthro-complexity's language ("insiders", "the reader inside the tide") is a participant's; its instruments are a cartographer's. The rejoinder asks that the practice catch up with the language.

Concept
Acquiescence bias
The tendency to agree with whatever is asked.
Turn over ↻
Acquiescence bias

A well-documented response style in surveys: some respondents tend to agree or rate highly regardless of content ("yea-saying"). The reply's defence of the triad rests on it: independent scales invite people to say yes to everything.

The rejoinder grants the bias and notes that independent scales can detect a yea-sayer as a pattern and model it, whereas an ipsative design hides it by removing magnitude for everyone. No instrument is innocent; the question is which loss is chosen and whether it is declared.

Concept
Acumen
Salience, sapience, sentience — as a conjunction.
Turn over ↻
Acumen

Snowden's term in a recent series of posts for a quality of judgement compounded of salience (noticing what matters), sapience (wisdom) and sentience (feeling). Compass XVIII argued that as a conjunction it cannot be represented by a barycentric triad, and read it through Boyd (orientation that can destroy and rebuild itself) and Deleuze (collective acumen as refrain).

The reply: the triad does not claim to represent the conjunction; it asks relative weight. The rejoinder (Q. XVII): then the instrument cannot register acumen at all, since the person with all three high and the person with all three absent are plotted at the same point.

Concept
Affordance
What an object reliably invites, whatever its maker intended.
Turn over ↻
Affordance

James J. Gibson's term (The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception, 1979) for the possibilities for action that an environment offers an animal: a surface affords standing, a handle grasping. Don Norman carried the term into design: a well-designed object makes its affordances visible.

A diagram's boundaries afford reading as boundaries. When readers consistently infer claims a figure "never made", the figure is not being misread at random; its affordances are being read reliably. The rejoinder (Quaestio VI) argues that a text is answerable for the readings it reliably affords — the principle of Compass Thesis XXIII.

Constraints that constitute wholes, not merely limit parts.

Alicia Juarrero

Philosopher whose Dynamics in Action (1999) and Context Changes Everything (2023) develop a theory of constraint as the source of coherence in complex systems. Context-dependent constraints bind parts into wholes with their own identity and causal powers; enabling constraints open possibilities; governing constraints regulate. Cynefin draws its constraint theory from her.

The rejoinder uses Juarrero twice: against the reply's claim to multiple identity (if identity is constituted by context-dependent constraint, it is relational — Q. VIII) and on constitutive constraint (provenance is not procedure — Q. XI).

Theory
Anthro-complexity
Complexity theory for human systems, as distinct from ants or weather.
Turn over ↻
Anthro-complexity

Dave Snowden's name for the study of complexity in human systems, which he holds differ in kind from other complex systems because humans have multiple identities, act with intention and work with abstraction — and can change the stories they tell about one another, and so the constraints under which they act. It positions itself against both systems thinking and the use of ants, flocks and agent-based models as models of organisations.

Humans Are Not Estuaries accepted the distinction and disputed its reason, its reflexivity and its silence on power. The reply defends the first and defers the third.

Astronomia Nova (1609)
A great science book that kept its own mistakes on the page.
Turn over ↻
Astronomia Nova (1609)

"The New Astronomy". Kepler's account of his long struggle with the orbit of Mars, published in 1609, contains his first two laws of planetary motion. Unusually, it is written as a narrative of failed attempts — model after model tried, tested against Tycho's data and abandoned — before the ellipse is found.

The rejoinder treats it as an early example of what the Additive Covenant asks for: corrections made in the open, so readers can see how the argument moved. Kepler's wrong turns are part of his proof.

Bakhtin: the double-voiced word
Every word is half someone else's — and being re-accented.
Turn over ↻
Bakhtin: the double-voiced word

Mikhail Bakhtin ("Discourse in the Novel", 1934–35; Speech Genres, 1986) held that language is heteroglot — stratified into many social voices — and that every utterance is addressed, anticipates a response, and re-accents words that already belong to others. Speakers do not merely use language; they contest and transform it in use.

The rejoinder (Q. XIII) contrasts this living revisability with the signifier set, which the narrator cannot re-accent while placing her dot. Humans Are Not Estuaries also used Bakhtin's addressivity to name what the fragment loses: to whom the story was told.

Concept
Bateson's levels of learning
Every act changes the context in which the next act is learned.
Turn over ↻
Bateson's levels of learning

Gregory Bateson ("The Logical Categories of Learning and Communication", in Steps to an Ecology of Mind, 1972) distinguished Learning 0 (fixed response), Learning I (change in response within a set of alternatives), Learning II (change in the set — learning to learn, the formation of character) and Learning III (change in the system of sets).

The rejoinder (Q. XII) uses Bateson to name why no human actant is a constructor: every Learning I alters the context-markers of Learning II, so the capacity to do something is changed by doing it. The teacher, the negotiator and the method itself are reagents.

Sources[35] Bateson 1972

Concept
Black's interaction theory of metaphor
A metaphor projects a system of commonplaces whether or not anyone asserts the identity.
Turn over ↻
Black's interaction theory of metaphor

Max Black (Models and Metaphors, 1962) argued that a strong metaphor is not an abbreviated comparison but an interaction: the "system of associated commonplaces" of the primary subject is projected onto the secondary, selecting, emphasising and suppressing features of it. "Man is a wolf" organises our view of man.

On this account, "no one has said humans are estuaries" does not answer Thesis 8. The governing metaphors do their work by projection, not assertion. The thesis concerned what the estuary, as a projected system, brings with it: a medium that does not read the reader.

Max Boisot (Information Space, 1995; Knowledge Assets, 1998) mapped knowledge on three dimensions: codification (assigning phenomena to categories), abstraction (reducing the number of categories needed) and diffusion (how widely it is shared). Compass VIII said SenseMaker codifies and abstracts, moving narrative down the I-Space into training data. The reply says this misreads a cycle as a descent. The rejoinder (Q. XXIX) accepts the cycle and asks where its later phases complete, and for whom.

Thomas Gieryn ("Boundary-work and the demarcation of science from non-science", American Sociological Review, 1983) showed that the line between science and non-science is drawn rhetorically, case by case, by those with an interest in where it falls — and that drawing it confers authority.

Thesis 21 argued that the human/other distinction does institutional work: it marks a school's border. The rejoinder (Q. XX) reads the reply's complaint that a CRP–Cynefin conversation has been refused as boundary-work: a border described from one side.

Bourdieu: the linguistic market
The frame no one chose still prices some accents above others.
Turn over ↻
Bourdieu: the linguistic market

Pierre Bourdieu (Language and Symbolic Power, 1991) treated language as a market in which utterances have unequal value depending on the speaker's position and the legitimacy of their speech. "Legitimate language" is the language of those already authorised to speak; symbolic power works through the misrecognition of this arbitrariness as natural.

The rejoinder (Q. XIII): pressed, the analogy of language does not exonerate the signifier set; it indicts language too. A frame no one authored can still be a site of power. A frame someone authored is a site of power twice over.

Julius Caesar, Act 4, Scene 3: "There is a tide in the affairs of men…" Brutus speaks the lines to overrule Cassius, who wants to wait for the enemy; Brutus argues for marching to Philippi. The army moves on his reading. At Philippi both men die.

The rejoinder reads the speech as Thesis 20 as tragedy: the tide in human affairs is partly made by the one seen to read it, and a confident reading spoken with authority can manufacture the very flood it claims to find. An instrument that tells an organisation "the tide is turning here" is intervening in kairos, not reporting it.

Data in which each observation is a vector of non-negative parts summing to a constant — proportions, percentages, barycentric coordinates. Such data live on a simplex, not in ordinary Euclidean space, and raw means, variances and correlations computed on them can be artefacts of the constraint.

David Deutsch's programme (2013), developed with Chiara Marletto, reformulates physics in terms of which transformations are possible and impossible. Finding
Kepler's eight minutes
The measurement that beat the picture he loved.
Turn over ↻
Kepler's eight minutes

Working on the orbit of Mars for Astronomia Nova (1609), Kepler built a circular model that came very close to Tycho Brahe's observations — but missed them by about eight minutes of arc, roughly a quarter of the width of the full moon. Because he trusted Tycho's data, he refused to ignore the gap, and wrote that it would lead to a reform of all astronomy. He gave up the circle and found the ellipse.

This is the rejoinder's test (R26): a theory is scientific in Kepler's sense when some measurement could overturn its favourite picture. What are anthro-complexity's eight minutes? The rejoinder cannot find them stated anywhere.

"The Cosmic Mystery". The young Kepler argued that the distances between the six known planets were set by the five Platonic solids — cube, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron, octahedron — nested one inside another between the planetary spheres. It was a beautiful picture of divine design, and Kepler loved it all his life.

It shows that Kepler was no dry measurer. He started from a Fludd-like vision of cosmic harmony. What made him different was what he did when measurements disagreed with the vision: he let the measurements win.

The rejoinder's reading of the reply to Compass XXI. A convened assembly can argue with its representative and disperse; a street crowd can shout back. A multitude whose members signify alone, through abstract signs whose meaning they do not know, into a system that aggregates them, has no voice but the pattern — and the pattern has no voice but the analyst's.

Ian Hacking ("The looping effects of human kinds", 1995) argued that human kinds differ from natural kinds: when people are classified, they become aware of the classification and change in response, which changes the kind. George Herbert Mead (Mind, Self and Society, 1934) argued that a gesture's meaning lies in the social act that the gesture and the other's response together complete. The self arises in this conversation of gestures, by taking the attitude of the other toward oneself.

Mead is used three times in the rejoinder. An unexplained title is a gesture whose meaning is left to its readers' response (Quaestio III). A narrative fragment signified alone by its teller is a gesture cut off before its response — the conversation of gestures with one side removed (Quaestio VIII). And withholding is itself a gesture, as the reply concedes at Compass Thesis V, so that "natural" emergence is emergence under the intervention of being watched (Quaestio XXVI).

The French friar Marin Mersenne attacked Fludd in the 1620s, and the philosopher Pierre Gassendi published a detailed critique in 1630 (Epistolica exercitatio). Gassendi's central complaint was that Fludd's system of correspondences could account for any result whatever — and a theory that can explain anything has explained nothing.

The rejoinder (Part II, section 7) asks whether anthro-complexity's reading of its own data has the same shape: clustering means entangled meaning, scattering means diversity, a weak signal found means success, none found means weak signals are hard to see.

An ancient idea, revived in the Renaissance: the human being is a microcosm (little world) that mirrors the macrocosm (great world). The body's humours match the elements, the soul matches the heavens, and what happens above is reflected below. Fludd built his whole system on it.

It is a doctrine of participation: the knower is inside the whole and can know it by knowing himself. The rejoinder's point is that Fludd held this doctrine while drawing the macrocosm from outside — and that anthro-complexity does something similar: it says the observer is inside, and designs its instruments from a seat outside.

Model collapse

Shumailov, Shumaylov, Zhao, Papernot, Anderson and Gal (Nature, 2024) showed that generative models trained recursively on data produced by earlier models progressively lose the tails of the original distribution. Each finite sample under-represents rare events; each model trained on it learns thinner tails; the process compounds until the model converges on a narrow version of the typical.

Thesis 16 applied this mechanism to a weak-signal instrument coupled to a model. The reply's answer — the method makes tails visible — does not address the coupling (Q. XVI; R11). A tail on the screen is not a tail in the loop.

Kepler's measurements could defeat his picture. The rejoinder asks what pattern in anthro-complexity's data could defeat its picture of human beings, and finds none stated. The threshold where a text negotiates how it will be read.
Turn over ↻
Paratext

Gérard Genette's term (Seuils, 1987; English Paratexts, 1997) for everything that surrounds and presents a text without being its body: title, epigraph, preface, illustrations, notes. Paratexts are not decoration. They dispose the reader before any argument is heard, and they are where an author's stance toward the reader is most visible because it is least argued.

This rejoinder treats the reply's epigraph (Pascal), images (Fludd) and title (Nailed to the Tides) as paratexts in Genette's sense, and reads each as testimony. The method is fair on both sides: the reply read the length, editions and making of the disputations as paratexts too. The covenant asks only that the reading be declared.

The closing apology of the sixteenth of Blaise Pascal's Lettres provinciales (dated 4 December 1656): Je n'ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n'ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte. Snowden uses it as his epigraph, gently suggesting that the disputations' length is the residue of haste.

The rejoinder (Quaestio I) reads the occasion: the Provinciales were eighteen anonymous letters by an outsider attacking the casuistry of a powerful teaching order, whose method adapted rules to cases. The long letter was the outsider's, it answered accusations, and it grew under pressure from replies. History sided with the long letter. The epigraph testifies for the disputation it was chosen to rebuke (R3).

The rejoinder invokes Pauli not to mystify the dispute but to model the honest posture toward it: to hold both tendencies and say so. A method that is Fluddian in its ontology and Keplerian in its software owes its users Pauli's candour about which is speaking when.

In seventeenth-century moral theology, probabilism held that where the lawfulness of an act was doubtful, one might follow any opinion supported by a "grave doctor", even if a contrary opinion was more probable. Figure
Ralph Stacey
Organisations as patterns of conversation and power, not systems to be steered.
Turn over ↻
Ralph Stacey

Ralph Stacey (1948–2021) developed, with Douglas Griffin and Patricia Shaw at the University of Hertfordshire, the theory of complex responsive processes of relating: organisations are not systems that managers stand outside and steer, but ongoing patterns of communication, power and evaluative choice among interdependent people. Strategy and change emerge in local interaction.

Stacey's analysis of five teleologies (with Griffin and Shaw, 2000) underlies Thesis 7 and Compass Thesis IV. His "Stacey Matrix", which he later set aside because it was being used as a tool for categorising situations rather than as an aid to thinking, is itself a precedent for a figure abandoned because of what readers took from it.

Sources[28] Stacey 2000[29] Stacey 2001

Test
Recognition, not alignment
Whether those inside can say: we did this ourselves.
Turn over ↻
Recognition, not alignment

Thesis 24's test for any practice of human complexity, drawn from Kevin Flinn's account of followership and from Laozi 17: the measure of good practice is not whether people are aligned to a direction but whether, when the work is done, they recognise it as their own — 我自然, "we did it ourselves".

The reply accepts the test. It is the most important concession in the reply, because it is a test the reply can be held to. Part VII (Q. XLIV; R23) holds it there.

Finding
Recognition or appropriation (R23)
Who gets to say 'we did this ourselves'?
Turn over ↻
Recognition or appropriation (R23)

The rejoinder's distinction. Recognising a likeness — the loom resembles the method — is not wrong. But the recognition test asks who may say "we made this". If narrators, convened under the five threads, said it of their pattern, the test would be passed. If the method-owner says it of the critic's loom, the test is turned around.

The reply's own postscript saw the danger, wondering whether it read the loom too quickly as its own method. The rejoinder calls that the best sentence in the reply and asks that it be promoted from the postscript to the method.

Finding
Redraw or renounce?
Two responses to a diagram read as a map of zones.
Turn over ↻
Redraw or renounce?

Stacey's matrix and the Cynefin diagram met the same fate: readers placed situations on them and read off approaches. Stacey's response was to renounce the diagram and change his position. Snowden's has been to redraw the diagram and attribute the readings to readers who took boundaries as claims never made.

The rejoinder credits redrawing as a kind of correction, but notes that it keeps the drawing at the centre and the drawer above it. Stacey's question — what does the drawing do to the people who use it? — can only be answered by studying the diagram's life, not by redrawing it.

Robert Fludd (1574–1637)

English physician and Hermetic philosopher whose Utriusque Cosmi … Historia (Oppenheim, 1617–21) filled its pages with engraved diagrams of the macrocosm and the human microcosm nested within it. Snowden illustrates his reply with three Fludd images: an astrologer casting a horoscope, man the microcosm within the macrocosm, and a portrait.

The rejoinder (Quaestio II) reads the choice as self-describing. Fludd's astrologer is the observer who fixes a person's fate from a map of forces in which he himself does not appear — the outside reader of Theses 8 and 9 and the centre of calculation of Thesis XXIII, drawn as a picture. And Fludd's quarrel with Kepler is the quarrel between anthro-complexity's ontology and its practice (R4).

Sources[19] Fludd 1617[20] Kepler 1619[21] Pauli 1955

Concept
Routinisation of charisma
The founder's craft becomes the institution's procedure.
Turn over ↻
Routinisation of charisma

Max Weber (Economy and Society, 1922) described how charismatic authority, resting on a leader's extraordinary qualities, is transformed after its founding moment into traditional or legal-rational authority: offices, rules, credentials, succession. The movement survives by becoming an institution.

The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy used Weber on the triopticon; the rejoinder (Q. XXXVII) uses him on the Pelagian/Augustinian question. Open texts are the Pelagian residue; the platform and accreditation are the routinised institution.

Sources[90] Weber 1978

Safe-to-fail probes

A Cynefin practice for complex situations: run several small, parallel, coherent experiments; for each, state beforehand what success and failure would look like, how they would be recognised, and how one would amplify or dampen; keep each within a tolerable loss. Act, sense, respond.

The reply cites the practice against Thesis 7: probes exist because outcomes cannot be known. The rejoinder (Q. IX; R7) agrees about outcomes and disputes the frame: criteria, indicators and the bound of "safe" are chosen in advance by the portfolio's designer. And "safe" is a deontic claim about whose losses are tolerable — Thesis 13 by another road.

Self-signification

The core SenseMaker move: after telling a story, the narrator herself places it on the instrument's signifiers, so that the first interpretation is hers rather than an expert's or an algorithm's. Thesis 14 called it a real advance that moves interpretation to the narrator only partly, on a frame she did not choose. The reply agrees it is partial and adds that abstraction increases rigour. The rejoinder (Q. XIV) shows the price of that rigour: the oblique dilemma.

勢 shì — propensity
The disposition of things, including the strategist's own.
Turn over ↻
勢 shì — propensity

The Chinese term variously rendered as configuration, momentum, potential, propensity. In the military treatises (Sunzi) the general creates and exploits 勢 as water released from a height or a round stone rolled down a slope. François Jullien (La propension des choses, 1992) made it a key to Chinese efficacy: not imposing a plan but riding the potential of a situation.

Thesis 9: 勢 includes the strategist's own disposition in the configuration; a propensity mapped from outside is a landscape. The reply concedes. The rejoinder (Q. X) argues the concession covers every aggregated or reported map, and that "insiders" mapping on a method's canvas is not yet 勢.

"Parameter space compression underlies emergent theories and predictive models" (Science, 2013) showed that in many multiparameter models only a few combinations of parameters matter for behaviour at observable scales; most are "sloppy". This is why simple effective theories work for complex systems.

Smooth and striated space
Always mixed: the question is how much striation, and by whom.
Turn over ↻
Smooth and striated space

Deleuze and Guattari (A Thousand Plateaus, 1980, plateau 14) contrast smooth space — nomadic, directional, occupied without being counted — with striated space — metric, gridded, counted in order to be occupied. The two are always mixed, passing into each other.

Compass XVIII warned that "creating the substrate" risks striating the smooth space it means to nurture. The reply agrees that some striation is the condition of action, so the question is how much and by whom — which leads, it says, to power. That is deferral four of six.

Sources[100] Deleuze 1987

Concept
Speech act
Saying is doing: a deferral allocates as well as postpones.
Turn over ↻
Speech act

J. L. Austin (How to Do Things with Words, 1962) distinguished what an utterance says from what it does — promising, warning, appointing, naming. John Searle systematised the theory. A speech act has force independent of its content.

The rejoinder treats the reply's deferral of power as a speech act (Quaestio V). It does not merely postpone; it allocates, deciding that the other answers can be given now without power and power added later. That allocation is what Thesis 12 denied. A deferred centre is a conceded centre for the duration of the deferral.

Sources[49] Austin 1962

Spurious correlation of ratios

Turn over ↻
Spurious correlation of ratios

Karl Pearson ("On a form of spurious correlation which may arise when indices are used in the measurement of organs", Proc. Royal Society, 1897) showed that variables expressed as ratios to a common quantity will be correlated even when the underlying quantities are independent. Proportions that must sum to one are the limiting case.

The rejoinder (Q. XVII) cites Pearson to show that the problem of reading patterns in triads is old and well understood — which is why its handling should be declared rather than assumed.

Sources[61] Pearson 1897

Finding
Stacey gives up his diagram
“Simply interpreted in a way that sustains the dominant discourse.”
Turn over ↻
Stacey gives up his diagram

Stacey dropped the matrix from later editions of his textbook and said it was a diagram he had come to regret. His reason, widely quoted, was that it was simply interpreted in a way that kept ordinary management thinking going while using the language of complexity. It made complexity look like one zone among others, and managers like people who could stand outside and pick.

The rejoinder (R29) sets this beside the Cynefin diagram's history: both were read as maps of zones; Stacey gave his up and asked what the drawing did to its users; Snowden redraws his and attributes the problem to readers.

↺ Turn back
Turn
Stacey's turn to complex responsive processes
From complex adaptive systems to people relating, around 2000.
Turn over ↻
Stacey's turn to complex responsive processes

In his first phase Stacey applied chaos theory and complex adaptive systems to organisations. Around 2000, with Douglas Griffin and Patricia Shaw, he dropped that application. Organisations, he argued, are not systems but ongoing patterns of conversation, power and identity among interdependent people, none of whom stands outside. Complexity science became a source of careful analogies, not a model to apply. Mead supplied the theory of conversation, Elias the theory of power.

This is the "third position" of the rejoinder: neither Fludd's vision nor Kepler's ruler, but the participant's conversation.

Sources[28] Stacey 2000[29] Stacey 2001[124] “Ralph D 2021

Figure
Steven Lukes
Power has three faces.
Turn over ↻
Steven Lukes

Steven Lukes (Power: A Radical View, 1974; 2nd ed. 2005) distinguished three dimensions of power: the power to prevail in observable decisions (Dahl); the power to keep issues off the agenda (Bachrach and Baratz); and the power to shape people's preferences and perceptions so that conflicts never arise — the "third face".

The rejoinder (Part VIII) maps the three faces onto a sensing instrument: what it decides, what it does not ask, and the frame through which people come to see their experience.

Sources[96] Lukes 1974

Biochemistry: the molecule on which an enzyme acts. Geology: underlying rock. Microbiology: the medium on which organisms grow. Electronics: the wafer on which circuits are built. In every sense, a substrate is below what it supports.

SwarmCompass®

A Cynefin Company offering described in a two-page 2025 brochure as powered by SenseMaker, organised in four stages, and illustrated by honeybees choosing a hive, radiologists missing a gorilla, and Lincoln's "think anew and act anew". Its deliverables include turning "unknown unknowns" into mapped territory and creating training data sets for further AI-based automation.

The subject of The Compass and the Loom, Theses I, II, VII, VIII, XI and XXI. The reply calls it a trademarked commercial product and says its swarm never convenes.

Rule
The Additive Covenant

Turn over ↻
The Additive Covenant

The rule governing every Principia Humanitatis work: text is added, never silently removed. Theses may be amended in place, struck through, annotated or superseded, but the original stands beside the amendment, so the reader sees the argument move.

The reply notes that under it "the text can only grow". The rejoinder (Q. XLI) answers that the covenant forbids silent deletion, not revision — it is the practice of errata, of the scholarly record and of version control — and enters two amendments of its own. It also asks for a Cynefin errata.

Finding
The amputated clause (R1)
What is answered is not what was argued.

The amputated clause (R1)

The rejoinder's first and most general finding. The reply answers the descriptive half of each thesis and drops the reflexive half, with a regularity too steady to be accident. The result is an excellent account of human complex systems with the observer subtracted — which is the account the theses were written against.

The rejoinder attributes this not to bad faith but to the predicate of The Strait-Jacketed and the Baggy: we see the constraints of others and are blind to our own. The reflexive clause is always the clause about the reply's author, and so always the one that cannot be seen from where he stands.

The ape of nature

Turn over ↻
The ape of nature

In Fludd's engraving Integrae Naturae Speculum Artisque Imago ("Mirror of the Whole of Nature and the Image of Art", 1617), Nature appears as a woman chained by the wrist to the hand of God. A second chain runs from her hand to an ape squatting on the earth, measuring a globe: Art — human skill and invention — which can only imitate what Nature makes.

The rejoinder (Part II, section 9) reads the designer as Fludd's ape: chained to the living whole, making a small, manageable copy of it. The copy is never the whole. But once the copy exists, people read the copy instead of looking at the whole — and the copy was made by the ape.

Form
The article of the Summa
Question, objections, sed contra, determination, replies.
Turn over ↻
The article of the Summa

Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (1265–74) is divided into some three thousand articles, each of which can be read and disputed alone: a question; objections (videtur quod); a contrary authority (sed contra); the determination (respondeo dicendum); and replies to each objection.

This is the form of every quaestio in the rejoinder, rendered in plain English. Its point (Q. XXXIX): a long work so built can be answered thesis by thesis without the burden of the whole — which is exactly what the reply did.

The banner of Snowden's reply shows an astrologer casting a horoscope, from Fludd's 1617 book. The astrologer sets a person's birth against the planets and draws a chart that tells them who they are. The rejoinder uses the astrologer's chair as the name for the designer's position: inside the relationship of service (paid by the client), outside the life being read (choosing the frame for someone else's experience). Nobody needs to be a villain to sit in it.

The asymmetry principle

A foundational claim of Snowden's anthro-complexity: human systems differ from other complex systems because humans can change the stories they tell about one another, and in doing so change the constraints under which they act. Ants and starlings cannot.

Thesis 6 argued that the principle applies to the theory that states it: Cynefin, SenseMaker and estuarine mapping are stories that change constraints. The reply concedes this. Anthro-complexity's asymmetry principle holds that only humans can change the story they tell about the other. The characteristic SenseMaker signifier: a triangle with a quality at each vertex; the narrator places a single dot to show the relative weight of the three in her story. The dot's position is a set of barycentric coordinates — three non-negative numbers that sum to one.

Labroides dimidiatus removes parasites from client fish at "cleaning stations" — and prefers to eat client mucus, which is cheating. The rejoinder's name for the neutral analogy shared by tide, estuary, river, wave and waterfall. None of them changes in response to being mapped; none has a story about the mapper; none learns what the mapper expects. Human systems do all three.

Finding
The five threads (R22)
Warp, first sight, consent, dispersal, errata.
Turn over ↻
The five threads (R22)

1 · Warp: signifiers co-authored with those who will signify. 2 · First sight: narrators see their pattern before anyone else, and may annotate it. 3 · Consent to the harvest: no narrative becomes training data or is used beyond its first purpose without specific consent and a share; withdrawal honoured. 4 · Dispersal rule: narrators may meet to compare; every convened group declares how it dissolves and who may not speak for it after. 5 · Errata: a public, dated record of what each instrument got wrong, including its affordances.

If the method has these, nothing is lost by saying so. If not, the loom is not the method under another name.

"Ontology" means a view of what exists and what it is like. The rejoinder treats this as a strength — it is why Snowden has been right against mechanical management for a quarter of a century. The problem lies only in how it is joined to the practice.

The Kepler–Fludd quarrel

Turn over ↻
The Kepler–Fludd quarrel

In an appendix to Harmonices Mundi (1619) Johannes Kepler criticised Fludd's cosmic diagrams as hieroglyphic pictures rather than mathematical demonstrations: they could not be measured, so could not be tested. Fludd replied (Veritatis Proscenium, 1621) that Kepler grasped only the quantitative shadow of things and missed the qualitative harmony known by inner illumination; Kepler answered again in 1622.

The rejoinder's claim: anthro-complexity holds Fludd's ontology (the human is not a computer; meaning is entangled and tacit; the whole exceeds its numbers) and Kepler's practice (signify, aggregate, plot, measure, train). Thesis 15 named the contradiction; the reply's banner pictured it. The quarrel is not resolved by choosing a side but by declaring which side each instrument stands on.

Form
The quaestio in plain English
It may be urged · Yet against this · I answer · To the objection.
Turn over ↻
The quaestio in plain English

Each quaestio opens with the strongest case for the position under attack (videtur quod, "It may be urged"); then the decisive counter-consideration (sed contra, "Yet against this"); then the determination (respondeo, "I answer"); then replies to the original objections.

The form is used because it obliges the author to state the adversary's case at its strongest before answering — here, Snowden's reply, paraphrased as fairly as possible — and because each quaestio can be disputed alone.

The sailor's skill is to anticipate a motion indifferent to him, that does not change because he is seen to anticipate it. He is inside the tide as a cork is inside the sea: carried, not answered.

That is precisely the relation Thesis 8 named. In human systems the "tide" is other sailors, who are watching the one who claims to read them. The image confirms the thesis it was offered to refute.

Appears inCards · Part IV Humans Are Not Estuaries, Argued Again

Image
Theses on the door
Short, numbered, posted so that anyone could dispute them.
Turn over ↻
Theses on the door

Tradition holds that on 31 October 1517 Martin Luther nailed ninety-five theses to the door of the Castle Church at Wittenberg. Whether the nailing happened is debated by historians; the theses, and their printing and spread, are not. They were short, numbered and offered for disputation.

The rejoinder (Quaestio III) reads Nailed to the Tides as an unintended echo: the most famous nails in the history of disputation fixed theses where they could be answered without the volume behind them. That is exactly the use the reply made of the forty-seven theses — which is to say that the form worked (Part VI).

The six deferrals

The reply defers power at six places: Thesis 12 (power differs from agency; deferred); Thesis 23 (power gradient and consent to the harvest; deferred); Compass XVIII (how much striation, and by whom — leads back to power); XIX (whether a software company is an outsider with a product); VIII (ownership, benefit and consent acknowledged, not answered); and the postscript. A seventh road, funding, ends at "alertness to the risk".

The rejoinder (R2) argues that a reply whose centre is deferred has conceded its centre for the duration of the deferral; and (R24, Part VIII) pre-commits the deferred post to ten tests so that its success can be recognised by others than its author.

The social learning cycle
Scanning, codification, abstraction, diffusion, absorption, impact.
Turn over ↻
The social learning cycle

Boisot's six-phase cycle through the I-Space: scanning for patterns in diffuse data; codifying them; abstracting; diffusing the codified knowledge; absorption, as it is internalised into new tacit know-how; and impact, as it is applied in concrete practice — which generates new uncodified experience to scan.

The rejoinder's question (Q. XXIX): if narrators codify at capture, but diffusion, absorption and impact occur among analysts, clients and (per the brochure) automated systems, the cycle runs through the narrators and completes elsewhere. That is the harvest in Boisot's own terms.

Diagram
The Stacey Matrix
Agreement against certainty: a map of zones for choosing how to manage.
Turn over ↻
The Stacey Matrix

Introduced by Ralph Stacey in the second edition of Strategic Management and Organisational Dynamics (1996). One axis shows how close a group is to agreement on an issue; the other, how close it is to certainty about cause and effect. Near both: rational planning. Further out: politics and judgement. Further still: a "zone of complexity". Far from both: chaos.

It became hugely popular — in management courses, project management and agile software — and was often adapted in ways that did not match Stacey's intent. To use it, a manager stands outside an issue, places it on the chart and reads off an approach: the astrologer's procedure, made portable.

The stop signal
A head-butt from a rival advocate: the swarm's institutionalised dissent.
Turn over ↻
The stop signal

Seeley and colleagues (Science, 2012) showed that scouts committed to one site deliver brief vibrational "stop signals", often by butting their heads against dancers advertising a different site, inhibiting the rival dance. This cross-inhibition prevents deadlock and premature lock-in, and mirrors models of decision-making in neural circuits.

The reply says SwarmCompass also aims to avoid early lock-in. The rejoinder (Q. XXIV): the swarm avoids it by conflict among advocates who meet; the instrument avoids it by isolation. Opposite mechanisms, one name.

The tails of a distribution

The extreme regions of a distribution, far from its centre, where events are rare. In anthro-complexity, weak signals — early indications of change — are expected to appear in the tails: the atypical story, the unusual signification.

Thesis 16: recursive learning on harvested narrative erases the tails. The reply: the method makes them visible. The rejoinder (Q. XVI): visible is not protected; and the triad removes the tail of intensity by geometry before any model is trained.

The "theory of the adjacent possible" (TAP) equation describes how the number of possible combinations of existing items grows, producing long periods of slow change followed by explosive, hockey-stick growth. Cortês, Kauffman, Liddle and Smolin (2022) analysed its dynamics and applications.

Conceded in Compass XIII as predicting the timing of novelty's explosion — again form, not content. Kauffman's own point survives: what the new things will be cannot be prestated.

The rejoinder's pre-commitment of the deferred post on power. Each test names a place where capacities meet position and resources in anthro-complexity's own practice, and a thesis that asked about it. Stating them now makes the deferred answer recognisable by others than its author.

If the post meets them, the theses on power will have been answered, whatever the answers are. If it does not, readers will be able to tell. That is the whole point of stating them in advance.

The third position (R30)

Turn over ↻
The third position (R30)

The objection is fair: at scale someone must summarise and decide. The rejoinder's answer is that the third position is not "no maps" but "no map whose maker is exempt from it". Maps can be drawn by those on them, revised by them and held answerable to them — OpenStreetMap is a map of the world drawn by its users.

It costs more, is slower, and hands power away. That is why it is rarely done, and why it belongs at the centre of the postponed post on power.

The three marks of the human

Snowden's three distinguishing capacities of humans in complex systems: we hold multiple identities, we act with intent, and we work with abstractions (language, symbols, models). They are the stated reason for anthro-complexity's distinction from other complexity.

Thesis 12: all three are capacities, and none of them is power. The reply concedes that power differs from agency and defines agency by the three marks. The rejoinder (Q. V) notes that this concedes Thesis 12 and moves the question to where capacities meet position.

Part V of The Compass and the Loom proposed an instrument that keeps what is valuable in SwarmCompass and WRASSE — distributed narrative sensing, attention to what is hard to change, many small acts over one large bet — and removes the observer's privilege, the promise of mapped unknowns and the fantasy of alignment.

The reply finds it looks very like its own method. The rejoinder (Q. XLII; R22) sets out the five threads where it differs, and invites: if the loom is yours, weave it.

The trialectic

Snowden's three-fold account of knowledge, extending Polanyi's tacit/explicit with a third term: entangled knowledge, which exists only in the interaction of people, artefacts and context and disappears when the interaction is broken up. The trialectic is the mediation among the three.

Thesis 18 read it through Peirce's thirdness: the mediation the trialectic celebrates is where the designer of the instrument sits. The rejoinder (Q. XIII) locates the designer between the narrator's signification and the analyst's decision.

Turn over ↻
Thomas Seeley

Cornell biologist whose decades of field experiments, summarised in Honeybee Democracy (2010), showed how a swarm of some ten thousand bees chooses a new home: several hundred scouts inspect sites, advertise them with waggle dances tuned to quality, recruit others, and inhibit rival advertisers; when a quorum of scouts gathers at one site, they trigger the swarm's takeoff.

The brochure used the swarm as an image of "true consensus" that "always" chooses best. Compass II disputed each claim. The rejoinder (Q. XXIV; R16) adds that the swarm's intelligence lies in a mechanism — advocacy and dissent among bees who meet — that an instrument whose nodes never meet cannot keep.

Three faces of an instrument

First face: who decides what is done with the pattern (test 3, the residual). Second face: what the instrument does not ask, and who decided it would not (test 4, the agenda). Third face: how the signifier frame shapes what narrators can notice about their own experience (test 1, the signifier; test 5, obliquity).

An account of power in anthro-complexity that answered only the first face would answer the question least asked by the theses.

Three positions toward a human system
The astrologer, the surveyor, the participant.
Turn over ↻
Three positions toward a human system

Fludd (above, with a vision of the whole); Kepler (outside, with a ruler, corrected by data); Stacey (inside, among others, corrected by their responses). Each has a danger: an untestable picture; losing what cannot be counted; staying local or cliquish.

Anthro-complexity, in the rejoinder's reading, takes its ontology from the first, its practice from the second, and its rhetoric from the third — without yet giving the third a method. Table D in Part II sets the comparison out in full.

Thurstonian IRT
Forced choice that recovers absolute level.
Turn over ↻
Thurstonian IRT

Anna Brown and Alberto Maydeu-Olivares (2011) showed that forced-choice questionnaires can be scored with a Thurstonian item-response model that recovers normative (absolute) trait levels from comparative judgements, avoiding the ipsative problems of classical scoring.

The rejoinder's third obligation (Q. XVII): the choice is not only between independent scales and a simplex. Alternatives exist that keep the protection against yes-to-everything and restore magnitude — including, most simply, an added intensity dial: how much of any of this was there?

Concept
Tools as ritual and defence
Frameworks that soothe the anxiety of not knowing.
Turn over ↻
Tools as ritual and defence

In The Tools and Techniques of Leadership and Management (2012), Stacey argued that management tools cannot deliver the control they promise, because human futures are not predictable; they can support competent performance but not expertise, which goes beyond rules. Chris Mowles developed the idea that tools and frameworks often work as rituals and social defences — ways of managing the anxiety of uncertainty by offering the appearance of a view from above.

Applied to diagrams like Stacey's matrix or Cynefin, the question becomes: what do they do in the room, for whom, and what do they protect people from feeling?

Tu quoque

An argument that rejects a criticism on the ground that the critic is guilty of the same thing. It does not show the criticism false; it shows, at most, that the critic is inconsistent.

The rejoinder (Q. XL) grants that the reply's irony is a tu quoque and nonetheless accepts it as R21 — because the reflexive answer to "your story about the harvest is also a harvest" is not to deny it but to say yes, and to let the theses apply to oneself.

A SenseMaker practice in which, instead of setting numerical targets, an organisation identifies a direction of travel in its narrative landscape — more stories of one kind, fewer of another — and acts to shift it. Voloshinov: the sign as arena

Valentin Voloshinov (Marxism and the Philosophy of Language, 1929; English 1973), associated with Bakhtin's circle, argued that the sign is "an arena of the class struggle": different social groups use the same signs with different accents, and the dominant group strives to make the sign uniaccentual, eternal and above conflict.

Applied to the reply's analogy (Q. XIII): even language, the frame no speaker chose, is a site of contest. A signifier set fixed by its designers and closed to its speakers' re-accenting is a sign made uniaccentual by construction.

Weak measurement

Aharonov, Albert and Vaidman (1988) introduced measurements in which the coupling between device and system is so weak that each measurement barely disturbs the system, at the cost of large uncertainty in each reading; averaging many weak measurements yields information without collapsing the state.

"Measure weakly" in Compass XIV meant: touch lightly and seldom. The reply's "oblique" capture "built into existing operational systems" is indirect but continuous — the opposite of weak (Q. XXXIII). The physics is scaffolding; the distinction stands without it.

Concept
Wisdom of crowds
Independent estimates aggregate well; influenced ones herd.
Turn over ↻
Wisdom of crowds

James Surowiecki (The Wisdom of Crowds, 2004) set out conditions — diversity, independence, decentralisation, aggregation — under which groups estimate better than experts. Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer and Helbing (PNAS, 2011) showed experimentally that even mild social influence reduces the diversity of estimates and undermines the effect.

The rejoinder (Q. XXXV): these are facts about estimation, the domain of statistics and CAS, where independent errors cancel. Building a human-complexity instrument on the independence condition senses humans by first removing the mark that makes them human.

A strategy framework introduced on the Cynefin Company blog in September 2025, crossing natural versus stimulated emergence with fine versus coarse granularity to give four domains (Directed, Opportunist, Hypothesis-based, Distributed), placed on a substrate of technological, cultural, procedural and network elements. The reply says it is still experimental, has not reached market, has no layers, and will acknowledge its sources at publication. The rejoinder accepts the first two as corrections and holds the last two to the record (Q. XXVII, XXXI).

Literally "self-so": spontaneity, naturalness, what is so of itself without external imposition. In the Daodejing the sage's highest achievement is that the people experience their accomplishments as 自然 — their own.
